docs.title: Background model
docs.text:
kore solves for small perturbations of a background. The background has five parts, each chosen by name in the parameter file:

part parameter what it sets structure structure the density \(\rho_0\), \(p_0 = \rho_0 T_0\) and gravity \(g\), functions of \(r\) stratification stratification the entropy gradient \(dS/dr\), with \(S = \delta s/c_p\) (only with thermal = 1) diffusivity diffusivity the radial profiles of the viscosity \(\nu\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa\) rotation diff_rot, diff_rot_type a uniform or a differential rotation \(\Omega(r,\theta)\), and the latitudinal entropy that balances it shape centrifugal, centrifugal_shape a sphere, or a body flattened by its rotation

The equations in which they enter are on the page Anelastic equations. The code is in bin/background.py (the choice, the checks, the stratification and diffusivity types), bin/radial_profiles.py (one class per structure), bin/diff_rot.py (the rotation) and bin/centrifugal.py (the flattening).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
kore is dimensionless (Non-dimensionalization). The unit of length is the radius of the outer wall, \(r = 1\). r_out is that radius in star radii (1 by default), so \(x = r\cdot\)r_out is the radius in star radii, the coordinate of the solar profiles below. The only physical unit kore reads is that of the solar rotation data, in nHz.

bin/units.py turns physical values into the parameters, with the time unit \(1/\Omega\); kore itself never imports it. In a parameter file, after r_out is set:

import units
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
units.set_target(par, omega=-271.2, sigma=-33.2)                 # itau, rtau from ω, σ in nHz

set_physical takes \(\nu\) and \(\kappa\) in cm²/s and uses the solar radius and surface gravity unless radius and gsurf (cgs) are given. For the Sun with r_out = 0.985 in a frame rotating at 456 nHz it gives Beyonce \(= 4.86\times10^4\) and, for \(\nu = 10^{12}\) cm²/s, ViscosD \(= 7.4\times10^{-5}\). In a run directory, python3 bin/units.py prints the eigenvalues as \(\omega\) and \(\sigma\) in nHz, \(\omega = -\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\cdot F/\mathrm{Gaspard}\) and \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\cdot F/\mathrm{Gaspard}\), with \(F\) = diff_rot_frame the frame rate in nHz.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The background of the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun/parameters.py), a full sphere with the observed solar rotation:

par.thermal        = 1
par.r_out          = 0.985                 # outer wall in solar radii
par.structure      = 'model S hydrostatic'
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'            # a radiative interior below a slightly subadiabatic convection zone
par.solar_rz_delta_cz = -4e-7
par.diffusivity    = 'solar_rz'            # ν, κ drop to visc0, therm0 below 0.70 R☉
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04
par.diff_rot       = 1
par.diff_rot_type  = 'tabulated'           # Ω(r, θ) from a table
par.diff_rot_file  = 'bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax  = 4
par.thermal_wind   = 2                     # with its exact thermal wind
par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)

The checked-in bin/parameters.py, a gravito-inertial mode, uses structure = 'Wu 2005' with r_out = 0.99 and stratification = 'top hat', with uniform rotation. Getting started uses an incompressible fluid ('Boussinesq', thermal = 0) with a shellular rotation.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
structure has no default.

structure \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\), \(g\) parameters 'model S hydrostatic' the Sun, for new runs: an even polynomial fit of \(\ln\rho\) of Model S (bin/model_s.at) over the whole Sun, \(g\) from its mass, \(p_0\) from hydrostatic balance structure_deg (30) 'Wu 2005' \(\rho_0 = (1 - x^2)^2\) (Wu 2005, \(\beta = 2\)) with its \(g\) and \(p_0\) r_out < 1, so that \(\rho_0 > 0\) at the wall 'Boussinesq' \(\rho_0 = p_0 = 1\), \(g = r\): the Boussinesq equations – '8-term fit' (legacy) the smooth fit of bin/smoothed_sun.py, up to 48 % off Model S in \(\rho\) near the surface, which moves solar inertial modes by 1.5–8 nHz – 'old model S prototype' (legacy) Chebyshev fits of \(\ln\rho\) and \(\ln p\) of Model S, with the \(g\) of the 8-term fit (not hydrostatic) solar_density_deg, solar_density_window, solar_density_sun_deg
  • Only ratios of \(\rho_0\) and of \(p_0\) enter the equations, so their scale does not matter. \(g\) is 1 at the surface (\(x = 1\)) in the solar structures and in 'Wu 2005'.
  • The three solar structures (the first and the last two rows) also make \(x = r\cdot\)r_out the radius of the solar rotation profiles (diff_rot.solar_x).
  • 'model S hydrostatic' is within 1.0 %, 0.5 % and 0.75 % of Model S in \(\rho\), \(p\) and \(g\) at degree 30, and within 0.14 %, 0.06 % and 0.10 % at degree 50. Use 50 to compare with papers that use Model S itself; degrees of 40 and above need about 16 more lmax for the same \(\ell\)-convergence of the HFR modes.
  • The two legacy structures are kept so that runs made before 'model S hydrostatic' give the same results. For 'old model S prototype', solar_density_window None fits the shell \([\)ricb\(\cdot\)r_out \(- 0.01\), r_out \(+ 0.005]\) when ricb > 0, and is 'sun' when ricb = 0: one even fit over the whole Sun of degree solar_density_sun_deg (60).

docs.title: Stratification
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, stratification sets \(dS/dr\) for \(r \ge 0\), in units of \(1/L\); it has no default then. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) kore uses it as an odd function of \(r\), so it should go to zero smoothly at the centre.

stratification \(dS/dr\) parameters 'top hat' \(\tfrac{A}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_1}{w_1} - \mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_2}{w_2}\right]\) aux1…aux5 = \(x_1\), \(w_1\), \(x_2\), \(w_2\), \(A\) 'odd top hat' the same made odd in \(r\): with \(x_1 = 0\) it rises as \(A\thinspace\mathrm{erf}(r/w_1)\) from the centre aux1…aux5 'solar_rz' the radiative interior of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, below solar_rz_dSdr, solar_rz_steps, solar_rz_core, solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf, solar_rz_os 'linear' \(r\); with 'Boussinesq', \(N^2\) = Beyonce \(r^2\) (Rieutord 2006, Mirouh et al. 2016) – 'inverse square' \(1/r^2\), conduction between the walls needs ricb > 0 'user' stratification_profile, a numpy expression (below) stratification_param (\(p\))
  • 'top hat' in a full sphere needs \(x_1 \gtrsim 6 w_1\), so that \(dS/dr \to 0\) at the centre; otherwise use 'odd top hat'. With ricb > 0 and ThermaD = 0, a \(dS/dr \neq 0\) at the inner wall gives spurious modes trapped there (below).
  • 'odd top hat' with aux1…aux5 = 0, 0.03, 0.68, 0.06, 2.6 fits the \(dS/dr\) of Model S to 10 % rms.

'solar_rz'. With \(x = r\cdot\)r_out in solar radii (their eq. 10, plus the convection zone of Bekki et al. 2024, eq. 2):

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dr} &= \frac{A}{4}\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_1}{d}\right]\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_2}{d}\right]\mathrm{erf}\frac{x}{w_0}\cr &\quad + \delta(x)\thinspace \frac{d\ln p_0}{dr}\thinspace \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_{OS}}{d_{OS}}\right], \end{aligned} \] \[ \delta(x) = \delta_{cz} + (\delta_{sf} - \delta_{cz})\thinspace e^{-((x - 0.985)/0.015)^2}, \]

with \(A\) = solar_rz_dSdr (2.615), \([x_1, x_2, d]\) = solar_rz_steps ([0.61, 0.68, 0.04]), \(w_0\) = solar_rz_core (0.05: makes \(dS/dr\) odd and smooth at \(r = 0\), no effect above \(x \approx 3w_0\)), \([x_{OS}, d_{OS}]\) = solar_rz_os ([0.70, 0.04]) and \(\delta_{cz}\), \(\delta_{sf}\) = solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf (0). \(A\) is their \((\partial s_0/\partial r)_{RZ}\) = 1.32e-2 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ cm⁻¹ times \(L/c_p\), with \(c_p\) = 3.46e8 and r_out = 0.985, so it scales with r_out. \(\delta < 0\) is subadiabatic; kore stops if \(\delta\) is set with another stratification. In the smooth Sun example, \(\delta_{cz} = -4\times10^{-7}\) makes the HFR \(m = 8\) mode 34 nHz more retrograde than \(\delta_{cz} = 0\).

docs.title: Diffusivity
docs.text:
\( u\) = ViscosD \(\hat u(r)\) and \(\kappa\) = ThermaD \(\hat\kappa(r)\); diffusivity sets \(\hat u\) and \(\hat\kappa\).

diffusivity \(\hat u\), \(\hat\kappa\) parameters 'uniform' (default) 1 – 'step' visc0, therm0 below \(r\) = aux3, 1 above, joined by an erf of width aux4 visc0, therm0, aux3, aux4 'solar_rz' visc0, therm0 below \(x_{OS}\), 1 above, as \( frac12[1 + \mathrm{erf}((x - x_{OS})/d_{OS})]\) (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, eqs. 8–9) visc0, therm0, solar_rz_os 'user' diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '...', 'kappa': '...'}, numpy expressions (below) diffusivity_param (\(p\))
  • With 'step' and 'solar_rz', ViscosD and ThermaD are the values above the step (the convection zone of the Sun). Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b use visc0 = 0.01 and therm0 = 0.04.
  • Any type is multiplied by \(( ho_0(x_2)/ ho_0)^p\), \(x_2\) = aux3, with \(p\) = visc_pow for \(\hat u\) and therm_pow for \(\hat\kappa\): 0 (the default) keeps the kinematic diffusivities as set, 1 makes \( ho_0 u\) and \( ho_0\kappa\) follow the profile instead.
  • Forcing 11 (random Reynolds stresses) uses the turbulent part of the viscosity, ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\): the floor \( u_f\) is visc0 with 'step' and 'solar_rz' when visc0 < 1 and 0 otherwise, unless rsf_nu_floor is set.

docs.title: ThermaD = 0
docs.text:
ThermaD = 0 removes the thermal diffusion: the motion is adiabatic, and bci_thermal, bco_thermal are not used (Without thermal diffusion). It works with every structure, stratification and rotation option. What to watch for:

  • Prefer ThermaD = 0 to a very small ThermaD. As ThermaD → 0 the eigenvalues of a resolved diffusive run approach the ThermaD = 0 ones linearly. With the thermal wind and walls that are both stress-free and at fixed entropy (bci_thermal = bco_thermal = 0), a small ThermaD forms a thermal boundary layer of width about \((\mathrm{ThermaD}/\lvert\lambda\rvert)^{1/2}\) at the walls, which below ThermaD ≈ \(10^{-7}\) needs far more radial resolution than the bulk. The ThermaD = 0 run has no such layer, and neither have zero-flux or no-slip walls.
  • Let \(dS/dr\) vanish at the inner wall. In a shell, a \(dS/dr \neq 0\) at the inner wall gives spurious modes trapped there. Their eigenvalues move with N, and spin_doctor flags them (residσ ≈ 1). For an erf top hat, take \(x_1 \ge\) ricb \(+ 3w_1\). If the gradient must reach the wall, raise nev by one or two, because the spurious modes take some of the slots.
  • With a differential rotation, expect a band of eigenvalues near \(\sigma = 0\). Without diffusion, the advection of \(s\) by the rotation has a continuous spectrum, \(\lambda = -i\thinspace m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\), which the discretization shows as many eigenvalues near \(\sigma = 0\) with frequencies in the range of \(m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\). With the thermal wind some of them grow slowly. They peak at \(l \approx\) lmax and change with lmax: discard any mode that fails the ℓ-convergence check of spin_doctor. They disappear with thermal_wind = 0 or with a moderate diffusivity (ThermaD ≈ \(10^{-3}\)). Put the target away from the band, where the solver converges slowly.
  • Check the convergence in N. In a full sphere, eigenfunctions with ThermaD = 0 need more radial resolution than diffusive ones (N = 200 instead of 120 for a smooth solar model). Where \(\rho_0\) nearly vanishes at the outer wall (structure 'Wu 2005' with r_out close to 1), the thermal-wind rows converge slowly in N.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
With diff_rot = 0 (the default) the background rotates uniformly at the rate of the frame. With diff_rot = 1 it rotates at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r)\thinspace P_n(\cos\theta), \quad n = 0, 2, 4, \dots \]

where \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) is the rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves, and \(\Delta\Omega\) the relative departure from it, a sum of Legendre polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) with radial coefficients \(f_n(r)\). Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator. The profiles do not depend on the structure. With thermal = 1, the latitudinal entropy that balances the rotation, the thermal wind, is part of the background too (thermal_wind, below). The terms this adds to the equations are in Anelastic equations.

docs.title: Frame and units
docs.text:
\(\Delta\Omega\) is relative to the frame, and Gaspard converts it to the time unit, so any timescale works. Two things follow:

  • ViscosD, ThermaD and Beyonce must be computed for \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). For 'solar' the frame must rotate at 435 nHz; for 'solar_P4' and 'tabulated' at diff_rot_frame (456 nHz by default). The other types are dimensionless.
  • With thermal_wind = 2 the eigenvalues do not depend on the choice of frame. With thermal_wind = 1 (linear in \(\Delta\Omega\)) they do, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\): by 0.1–0.9 nHz for solar inertial modes.

Eigenvalues are in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), as for uniform rotation.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: parameter default meaning diff_rot 0 1 adds the differential rotation diff_rot_type 'Y20' the profile, see below diff_rot_ampl 1.0 the factor of \(\Delta\Omega\), for every type (table below) diff_rot_param 0.0 the shape parameter: \(\sigma\) of 'shellular', p in 'user' and 'ferraro' expressions diff_rot_term_amp [1.0]*9 \(a_0, a_2, \dots, a_{16}\): factors of the \(P_0, P_2, \dots, P_{16}\) terms of \(\Delta\Omega\), any type, after diff_rot_ampl (missing entries are 1); e.g. [1, 1, 0] drops the \(P_4\) part of 'solar_P4' diff_rot_profiles {} 'user': {n: 'numpy expression'}, the shape \(f_n\) of each even degree (below) diff_rot_frame 456.0 'solar_P4', 'tabulated': \(\Omega_{\rm ref}/2\pi\) in nHz diff_rot_solar [464, -76, -50, 433.5, 0.71, 0.045] 'solar_P4': \(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\) (nHz), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\) diff_rot_file '' 'tabulated': the .npz file, absolute or relative to the run directory diff_rot_nmax 8 'tabulated', 'ferraro': highest degree kept, even (up to 16 with thermal_wind = 2) diff_rot_F 'psi' 'ferraro': \(\Delta\Omega = F(\psi)\), a numpy expression of psi and p diff_rot_rdeg 24 'tabulated': degree of the Chebyshev fit of each \(f_n\) in \(r\) diff_rot_window None 'tabulated': None fits over the shell if ricb > 0 and is 'sun' if ricb = 0; 'sun': one fit over the whole Sun, even in \(r\), the same for any ricb diff_rot_sun_deg 60 'sun': degree of that fit thermal_wind 1 the latitudinal background entropy, see below thermal_wind_radial 1 0 drops \(u_r\thinspace \partial_r S_{tw}\) thermal_wind_amplitude 1.0 factor on \(S_{tw}\) (thermal_wind 1, 2) dSdtheta 0.0 thermal_wind = 3: \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\)

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
\(a\) = diff_rot_ampl, \(p\) = diff_rot_param. For the solar types \(x\) is the fractional solar radius: \(x = r\times\)r_out with a solar structure, \(x = r\) otherwise.

diff_rot_type \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) degrees notes 'rigid' \(a\) \(P_0\) test profile: a uniform offset of the rotation rate, with an exact answer (below); \(a = 0\) gives uniform rotation with the diff-rot machinery on (needed for thermal_wind = 3) 'Y20' \(a\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\) \(P_2\) \(P_2\) unnormalised, despite the name; not regular at \(r = 0\): use ricb > 0 'Y20-wall-bounded' \(a\thinspace (1 - r)(r - r_i)\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\), \(r_i\) = ricb \(P_2\) not smooth at \(r = 0\): use ricb > 0 'shellular' \(a\thinspace (r^\sigma - 1)\), \(\sigma = p\) \(P_0\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 (\(a = 1\)); not smooth at \(r = 0\) unless \(\sigma\) is even and positive 'shellular_boussinesq' \(\tfrac12 N_0^2\thinspace (1 - r^2)\), \(N_0^2 = a\) \(P_0\) Mirouh et al. 2016; use thermal_wind = 0 (their background has no thermal wind), structure 'Boussinesq' and stratification 'linear' 'cylindrical' \(\varepsilon\thinspace r^2\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013; barotropic, \(S_{tw} = 0\) 'conical' \(\varepsilon\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Guenel et al. 2016; not regular at \(r = 0\): use ricb > 0 'solar' \(a\thinspace \times\) helioseismic fit, \(P_0 + P_2\), tanh step at \(x = 0.71\) of width 0.1 \(P_0\), \(P_2\) relative to 435 nHz; 4.5 nHz too fast at the equator and 12 nHz at the pole compared with the observations 'solar_P4' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) the fit below \(P_0\), \(P_2\), \(P_4\) diff_rot_solar, diff_rot_frame; defaults from Mukhopadhyay et al. 2026 'tabulated' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) from diff_rot_file \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) below 'user' \(a\sum_n f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta)\), \(f_n\) from diff_rot_profiles the keys of diff_rot_profiles below 'ferraro' \(a\thinspace F(\psi)\), \(\psi\) the flux function of the poloidal magnetic field \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) magnetic = 1 only: constant along the field lines, so a steady background with the field (Magnetic field)

'rigid'. The eigenvalues are known exactly: with \(\lambda_0\) the diff_rot = 0 eigenvalue,

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i\thinspace m G a , \]

with \(G\) = Gaspard.

'solar_P4'. A rigid radiative zone joined by an erf step at the tachocline \(r_{tc}\) (width \(d_{tc}\)) to a convection zone whose rotation depends on latitude only:

\[ \frac{\Omega}{2\pi} = \Omega_{RZ} + \tfrac12\left[\Omega_{CZ}(\theta) - \Omega_{RZ}\right]\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\thinspace \frac{x - r_{tc}}{d_{tc}}\right], \] \[ \Omega_{CZ} = c_0 + c_2\cos^2\theta + c_4\cos^4\theta , \]

with diff_rot_solar = [\(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\)] (nHz, and fractions of R☉).

'user'. diff_rot_profiles gives the shape of each even degree as a numpy expression (below). For example, the cylindrical rotation as a 'user' profile (it gives the same matrices as 'cylindrical'):

par.diff_rot_type     = 'user'
par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '(2/3)*r**2', 2: '-(2/3)*r**2'}
par.diff_rot_ampl     = -0.25

The degrees must be even. Any degree up to 16 works with thermal_wind = 2 (32 with thermal_wind = 1).

'tabulated'. The file holds ome[θ, r] (nHz), r (R☉) and theta (rad), the layout of data/diff_rot.npz of the Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 data set. tests/diff_rot/ls_to_tabulated.py converts the Larson & Schou 2018 table to it; bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz is the mean of the 83 JSOC HMI 72-day inversions (hmi.V_sht_2drls, NACOEFF 36) from 2010-04-30 to 2026-06-29 in this layout, on the 151 table radii. kore projects \(\Omega\) on \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) at each table radius, fits each \(f_n\) in \(r\) over the table radii within 0.01 of the shell, and prints the fit residuals and the truncation error in nHz (the largest difference between the table and its expansion up to \(P_{n_{\max}}\)); check that line. For the Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 profile the truncation error near the poles at the surface is up to 17 nHz at diff_rot_nmax = 8; 12 is the working choice.

docs.title: Thermal wind
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, thermal_wind chooses the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) and the terms the differential rotation adds to the heat equation. The advection of \(s\) by the rotation is always included.

thermal_wind heat-equation terms \(S_{tw}\) 0 the advection of \(s\) only none (e.g. Mirouh et al. 2016) 1 (default) and the advection of \(S_{tw}\) by the perturbation thermal wind of \(\Omega\) to first order in \(\Delta\Omega\) (\(S_{tw} \propto G^2/\)Beyonce) 2 the same thermal wind of the full \((1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) balance; frame independent 3 the same prescribed: \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), uniform in \(r\) (Bekki et al. 2024)
  • thermal_wind 1 and 2 need Beyonce > 0. With timescale = 'rotation', set_scales() sets Beyonce = 0, so set it after calling set_scales().
  • dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)): dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\), with \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Bekki et al. use \(c_p\) = 4.17e8, Model S has about 3.46e8. Negative values give warm poles. The thermal-wind amplitude does not apply.
  • thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops \(u_r\thinspace \partial_r S_{tw}\), as Bekki et al. 2022 and Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 do. Keeping it is the consistent choice, but it moves the solar columnar and high-frequency retrograde modes by 5–15 nHz.
  • With the thermal wind \(S_{tw}\) is the only latitudinal entropy gradient; in a convection zone with \(dS_0/dr = 0\) it is also the only background entropy gradient, and its effect on the modes is of the same order as the momentum terms.
  • With diff_rot = 1 the default thermal_wind = 1 includes the thermal wind. For the advection of \(s\) by the rotation alone, set thermal_wind = 0.
  • With magnetic = 1, \(S_{tw}\) leaves out the force of the background field: it is the same as in a run without a field (Magnetic field).
  • thermal_wind 3 is uniform in \(r\), so in a full sphere it is not regular at the centre and submatrices.py warns.

docs.title: Resolution and cost
docs.text:
• A differential rotation couples harmonic degrees \(l\) that uniform rotation keeps apart, so the matrices get wider. Let \(n_{\max}\) be the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\). The momentum rows then couple degrees that differ by up to \(n_{\max}\) (\(P \to P\), \(T \to T\)) or \(n_{\max} + 1\) (\(P \leftrightarrow T\)).
  • \(S_{tw}\) has degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 1) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 2), and the heat rows couple degrees that far apart. Matrices are therefore widest with 'tabulated' and a large diff_rot_nmax.
  • With ricb = 0 (a full sphere) each \(f_n\) is evaluated at \(\lvert r\rvert\), and it is smooth at the centre only if it goes as \(r^n\) there (Regularity at the centre). 'Y20' and 'conical' keep their \(P_2\) term at the centre, 'Y20-wall-bounded' and 'shellular' (except even \(\sigma > 0\)) have a kink there, and the fit of a 'tabulated' rotation leaves its \(f_n\) a small value there (about \(10^{-5}\) of the largest for the HMI table); submatrices.py prints a WARNING for each. The 'solar' tachocline step needs N ≈ 400 at ricb = 0.
  • Modes that reach into a radiative interior have short radial wavelengths. In a full sphere with the radiative interior of stratification 'solar_rz', solar inertial modes needed N = 768 to 1024 for the spin_doctor residuals, although their eigenvalues converge at a lower N. Solver has the memory this takes.
  • Check convergence with spin_doctor as for any run; its residuals include the terms of the differential rotation.

docs.title: Centrifugal deformation
docs.text:
A rotating star or planet is flattened at the poles: its surfaces of constant density, pressure and entropy, its level surfaces, are oblate spheroids rather than spheres. centrifugal = 1 gives the background this shape, at first order in the flattening (exactly, for a homogeneous fluid, with 'spheroid'): the walls and the level surfaces become spheroids, and the flow feels them through every term of its equations, the inertia, the Coriolis force, the buoyancy, the viscous force and the diffusion, the walls and a differential rotation, and with a magnetic field the Lorentz force, the induction and the matching at the walls. The equations are on Centrifugal deformation.

How kore does it. kore keeps its spherical grid and its radial profiles, and solves in coordinates that follow the level surfaces. The radius \(r\) labels the level surface that encloses the volume of the sphere of radius \(r\); every background profile is a function of it, and the walls are the level surfaces ricb and 1. A differential rotation is such a profile too: a \(\Delta\Omega\) that depends on \(r\) alone is constant on the level surfaces. In these coordinates each term of the equations gains a part proportional to the flattening, and the buoyancy takes the effective gravity: the gravity less the mean centrifugal acceleration. The new terms couple the degrees as a differential rotation of degree 2 does, so the matrices are as wide as with one (Resolution and cost); with a differential rotation of degree \(n_{\max}\), as wide as with one of degree \(n_{\max} + 2\).

With a magnetic field. The background field follows the level surfaces too: kore's formula for B0 and B0_tor gives the field on the level surfaces, and the deformation carries it into the body, so its field lines are those of the sphere stretched with the level surfaces. It differs from the spherical formula by a fraction of order \(f\): submatrices.py says so. At an insulating wall the field is matched to the potential field outside the deformed wall. The field diffuses in the deformed fluid, and in a conducting inner core, which is deformed with the fluid.

docs.title: Flattening
docs.text:
centrifugal_q or centrifugal_f sets how flat the body is, and centrifugal_shape how the flattening varies inside it.

parameter default meaning centrifugal 0 1 flattens the body centrifugal_shape 'clairaut' how the flattening varies with the radius (below) centrifugal_q 0.0 \(q = \Omega^2R^3/GM\) of the surface: the centrifugal over the gravitational acceleration at its equator. With any shape it also sets the effective gravity of the buoyancy centrifugal_f None the flattening of the outer wall, (equatorial − polar radius)/equatorial radius: the value of 'uniform' and 'spheroid', and for 'clairaut' the scale of its shape in place of centrifugal_q centrifugal_profile '' 'user': the flattening \(f(r)\) as a numpy expression (below) centrifugal_param 0.0 'user': p in centrifugal_profile centrifugal_shape the flattening \(f(r)\) set by 'clairaut' the hydrostatic shape of the structure: Clairaut's equation with its gravity centrifugal_q, or centrifugal_f 'uniform' the same at every radius, as in a homogeneous body centrifugal_f 'user' any profile centrifugal_profile, centrifugal_param 'spheroid' the same at every radius, kept exactly at any flattening centrifugal_f
  • 'clairaut' derives the density from the gravity, so \(g\) must be the gravity of the structure's own mass, as it is in 'model S hydrostatic', 'Wu 2005' and 'Boussinesq'. For 'Boussinesq', a homogeneous body, it gives \(f = 5q/4\) at every radius (the Maclaurin spheroid). The gravity of 'model S hydrostatic' ends at the outer wall, so for it kore applies the surface condition of Clairaut's equation at the wall, neglecting the mass above.
  • submatrices.py prints the flattening at the walls and, for 'clairaut', its ratio \(f/q\) at the surface.
  • 'spheroid' is the body of 'uniform' without the first-order approximation: the walls and the level surfaces are exact spheroids, for strong flattenings, or with \(f < 0\) elongated bodies. It suits a homogeneous fluid in a fast-rotating body or in a rigid container, such as a planet with a rigid mantle. It needs 'Boussinesq' with uniform diffusivities and centrifugal_q = 0, and kore stops with a differential rotation; the buoyancy is that of a homogeneous body in hydrostatic equilibrium. With a field, the potential field beyond an insulating wall is the exact one of the spheroid. Its viscous terms and its magnetic diffusion couple degrees four apart (The exact spheroid).

Typical values:

body centrifugal_q flattening of the surface Earth 3.5e-3 3.4e-3; the core-mantle boundary 2.5e-3 Jupiter 0.089 0.065 Saturn 0.155 0.098 Sun 2e-5 8e-6

A Jupiter-like body, with the flattening of its structure:

par.structure         = 'Wu 2005'
par.r_out             = 0.99
par.centrifugal       = 1
par.centrifugal_shape = 'clairaut'
par.centrifugal_q     = 0.089

The level surfaces of the Earth's core are set by the whole planet, so give the flattening of the core-mantle boundary instead (and, with thermal = 1, centrifugal_q = 1.7e-3, its value at that boundary, for the effective gravity):

par.structure         = 'Boussinesq'
par.centrifugal       = 1
par.centrifugal_shape = 'uniform'
par.centrifugal_f     = 2.5e-3

docs.title: What it covers
docs.text:
The deformation is complete at first order in \(f\): the inertia, the Coriolis force and the buoyancy, the viscous force with no-slip or stress-free walls, the thermal diffusion with fixed-entropy or fixed-flux walls, a differential rotation, and with a field the Lorentz force, the induction and the magnetic diffusion, insulating walls and a conducting inner core, with any background field, poloidal or toroidal, in shells and in full spheres. 'spheroid' keeps the inertia, the Coriolis force, the buoyancy, the viscous force, the thermal diffusion and, with a field, the Lorentz force, the induction and the magnetic diffusion, with all their walls and a conducting inner core, exactly.

  • submatrices.py warns about a flattening above 0.1, where the first order loses accuracy (not with 'spheroid'), and with thermal_wind 1 or 2: the thermal-wind entropy keeps the balance of the sphere, so that balance misses its terms of order \(f\thinspace\Delta\Omega\).
  • A viscous full sphere with \(m \neq 0\) needs rpower_v = 4: the deformation gives its toroidal rows a term that is a polynomial in \(r\) only once multiplied by \(r^4\). kore stops and says so.
  • kore stops with a forcing, with walls of zero radial stress (bco or bci = 2) in a viscous run, and with a conducting inner core whose permeability differs from the fluid's (mu_i2o must be 1).

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• The eigenvectors are normalised to the kinetic energy of the deformed body (plus its magnetic energy with a field), and the budgets of spin_doctor (residσ, residω, resid𝑠, resid𝐛) include the terms of the deformation. The full energy budget resid𝐄 closes only at second order in \(f\), so it is of order \(f^2\) rather than round-off; with 'spheroid' it closes to round-off too. The enstrophy and viscous residuals (residens, residD) are not computed.
  • The field files hold the flow and the field in the coordinates of the level surfaces. tools/plot_field.py draws the flow, the field and the entropy where they are in the body.
  • magnetic.dat gains a column with the part of the magnetic energy that the deformation adds (Output files).
  • params.dat records the deformation in its columns 108–112 (Output files).

docs.title: 'user' profiles
docs.text:
stratification_profile, the two diffusivity_profiles, the diff_rot_profiles and centrifugal_profile are numpy expressions of r (the kore radius), x (\(r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure, \(r\) otherwise) and p (stratification_param, diffusivity_param, diff_rot_param or centrifugal_param), with sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, log10, sqrt, abs, sign, pi, where, minimum, maximum, erf, erfc. For example:

par.stratification = 'user'
par.stratification_profile = '2.5*exp(-((r - 0.75)/0.06)**2)'      # dS/dr in 1/L for r >= 0
par.diffusivity = 'user'
par.diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '0.01 + 0.99*0.5*(1 + tanh((x - 0.70)/0.015))', 'kappa': '1'}

kore evaluates them at \(\lvert r\rvert\), so in a full sphere \(dS/dr\) is odd and \(\hat\nu\), \(\hat\kappa\), the \(f_n\) and the flattening are even whatever the expression. They are smooth at the centre only if the expression is: an odd power of \(r\) in an even profile, or an even one in \(dS/dr\), makes a kink, and \(dS/dr\) must vanish there as \(r\), \(f_n\) as \(r^n\). submatrices.py warns about both (Regularity at the centre). The expressions must not contain #: spin_doctor writes them at the end of each params.dat row, after a #.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: Before anything is built, kore stops on a background that cannot work: an unknown type, a parameter name of an older version of kore (the message gives the replacement), 'Wu 2005' without \(0 <\) r_out \(< 1\), 'inverse square' with ricb = 0, \(\delta\) without 'solar_rz', a centrifugal deformation with what it does not cover (above) or without its flattening, or a 'user' expression that does not evaluate. submatrices.py also warns about any name in the parameter file that kore does not define, so a misspelt name is not ignored without notice, and in a full sphere about each profile that is not smooth at the centre (Regularity at the centre). spin_doctor records the background of every solution in params.dat (Output files).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
kore reproduces published eigenvalues of differentially rotating fluids, from an incompressible fluid to the solar convection zone with a radiative interior. This page gives the set-up of each benchmark, the script that runs it, and the result.

benchmark physics result Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 incompressible, shellular and cylindrical rotation reproduced Guenel et al. 2016 incompressible, conical rotation reproduced, including an unstable mode Mirouh et al. 2016 Boussinesq, stably stratified, shellular rotation reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a solar convection zone, observed rotation, thermal wind reproduced, including an unstable mode Bekki et al. 2024 onset of the high-latitude instability reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b solar convection zone with a radiative interior reproduced, except two high-latitude modes

The scripts are in tests/diff_rot/. Each one builds a run directory with a copy of bin/ and its own parameters.py, runs submatrices.py and assemble.py, and solves near the published eigenvalue. Getting started runs one of these benchmarks, fig. 10 of Baruteau & Rieutord, step by step.

Conventions. kore's eigenvalue is \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\) for fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t + im\phi}\) in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (Anelastic equations). The three fluid-dynamics papers work in the inertial frame, with fields \(\propto e^{i\Omega_p t + im\phi}\) (Baruteau & Rieutord, Guenel et al.) or \(e^{(\tau + i\omega)t + im\phi}\) (Mirouh et al.), so their frequency is \(\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda - m\) and their damping rate \(\tau = \mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\), in units of \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The solar papers give frequencies in nHz in the frame rotating at 456 nHz, negative for retrograde modes, and growth rates in nHz.

docs.title: Incompressible and Boussinesq fluids
docs.text:
These three papers use a viscous fluid in a spherical shell with stress-free walls. Their Ekman number is \(E = \nu/(\Omega_{\rm ref}R^2)\), which is ViscosD with timescale = 'rotation'. The common settings are

par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'                 # uniform density
par.bci = par.bco = 0                        # stress-free
par.diff_rot = 1; par.thermal_wind = 0
par.ricb = 0.35                              # their η, unless stated
par.ViscosD = 1e-8                           # their E

tests/diff_rot/lit_bench.py WORKDIR CASE builds and solves one published mode; lit_bench.py WORKDIR list prints the cases (br*, gu*, mi*). The runs take minutes on 8 ranks; the largest needs 26 GB.

docs.title: Baruteau & Rieutord 2013
docs.text:
JFM 719, 47. Shellular rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(r/R)^\sigma\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the surface rate, and cylindrical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon s^2)\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the rate on the axis:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular';   par.diff_rot_param = -0.5   # σ: ΔΩ = r^σ - 1
par.diff_rot_type = 'cylindrical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.4    # ε: ΔΩ = ε r² sin²θ

Result. For the 12 modes compared, the frequencies agree to \(2\times10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\) and the damping rates to 1 %, once kore is resolved (some modes need more resolution than the paper used). Two modes differ in the damping rate: an \(m = 3\) mode in a cluster that does not settle with resolution, and the growing \(m = -6\) mode, whose growth rate is 6 % lower, a shift of 0.4 % in its critical Ekman number. Two modes at \(E \le 5\times10^{-9}\) need about 190 GB and were not computed.

docs.title: Guenel et al. 2016
docs.text:
A&A 589, A22. Conical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon\sin^2\theta)\), in the frame rotating at the pole:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'conical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.25      # ε
par.ricb = 0.71

Result. For the 7 modes compared, the frequencies agree to \(10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (\(5\times10^{-4}\) for one) and six damping or growth rates to 1 %, including the unstable mode with a corotation layer. The seventh, at \(\eta = 0.10\), sits in a cluster and is 6 % off in damping rate.

docs.title: Mirouh et al. 2016
docs.text:
JFM 800, 213. A stably stratified Boussinesq fluid with \(N^2\) uniform, \(g = r\), the temperature fixed at both walls, and the rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \tfrac{N^2}{2}(1 - r^2)\right]\):

par.thermal = 1; par.stratification = 'linear'               # dS/dr = r, so the buoyancy frequency is N² r² with g = r
par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 0
par.Beyonce = 1.5                                            # their N²
par.ThermaD = 1e-7                                           # their E/P
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular_boussinesq'; par.diff_rot_ampl = 1.5   # N² again

thermal_wind = 0 is required: their background is balanced by centrifugal buoyancy, which kore does not carry.

Result. Of the 14 modes, 13 are identified. Their frequencies agree to \(2\times10^{-4}\thinspace\Omega_{\rm ref}\), and the damping or growth rates of 9 to 1 % and of 3 more to 2–4 %. One mode at \(E = 10^{-10}\) needs more resolution than fits in memory. A growing mode in a dense cluster of corotation modes is not identified.

docs.title: The Sun
docs.text: These papers solve the fully compressible equations about Model S; kore is anelastic. The common set-up: the Model S density, \(\nu = \kappa = 10^{12}\) cm² s⁻¹, an adiabatic convection zone, stress-free walls, the frame rotating at 456 nHz and their rotation profile. "With the thermal wind" means thermal_wind = 2 without \(u_r\thinspace\partial_r S_{tw}\) (thermal_wind_radial = 0), as in the papers.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a
docs.text:
A&A, arXiv 2501.16797. The convection zone, 0.71–0.985 R☉, with their tabulated rotation, the file data/diff_rot.npz of their data set (doi:10.17617/3.NP26AI):

import units
par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'old model S prototype'                  # the Model S density
par.r_out = 0.985; par.ricb = 0.71/0.985
par.thermal = 1
par.stratification = 'odd top hat'                       # with aux5 = 0: dS/dr = 0
par.aux1, par.aux2, par.aux3, par.aux4, par.aux5 = 0.0, 0.1, 0.68, 0.06, 0.0
par.bci = par.bco = 0; par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 1
par.diff_rot = 1; par.diff_rot_type = 'tabulated'; par.diff_rot_file = 'diff_rot.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax = 12
par.thermal_wind = 2; par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
par.N = 64; par.lmax = par.m + 63

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py NAME m=… symm=… file=… builds this run for any \(m\) and symmetry, and solve_bekki.py NAME FREQ GROWTH solves it near a frequency and growth rate in nHz. run_bekki.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the five modes below (about a minute each, one core).

Result. For the \(m = 3\) Rossby modes (\(n = 0, 1\)), the \(m = 3\) columnar mode, the \(m = 10\) high-frequency retrograde mode and the unstable \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode, kore agrees with their compressible values to 0.2 nHz in frequency and 0.4 nHz in growth rate. The high-latitude mode is at −95.76 nHz with growth rate +11.30 nHz (theirs: −95.70, +11.69). This needs the thermal wind: without it the frequencies are off by up to 11 nHz and the high-latitude mode is stable.

docs.title: Bekki et al. 2024
docs.text:
The high-latitude mode of the previous set-up becomes baroclinically unstable when the poles are warm enough. With thermal_wind = 3 the latitudinal entropy gradient is prescribed, \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), with dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\) (negative: warm poles):

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py RUN tw=3 ds=-1000 file=diff_rot.npz m=1 symm=-1
tests/diff_rot/solve_bekki.py RUN -93 5

with ds = \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Result. The \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode becomes unstable at \(\lvert\Delta_\theta s\rvert\) = 425 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ with the rotation of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025, and at 546 with the Larson & Schou 2018 table, for \(c_p = 3.46\times10^{8}\). The published value is about 500. The radial shear of the rotation in the lower convection zone sets the onset: a rotation profile uniform in radius needs about four times more.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b
docs.text:
A&A 708, A253. The convection zone extended down to 0.5 R☉ with their stably stratified, rigidly rotating radiative interior:

par.ricb = 0.5/0.985
par.solar_density_window = 'sun'                                # one Model S fit over the whole Sun
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'; par.diffusivity = 'solar_rz'   # their eqs. (8)-(10)
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04                              # ν and κ below 0.70 R☉, relative to the convection zone
par.diff_rot_type = 'solar_P4'                                  # their eqs. (5)-(6)
par.bci_thermal = 1; par.bco_thermal = 0                        # zero entropy flux at the bottom, s = 0 at the top
par.N = 128

the rest as above. tests/diff_rot/mk_rz.py NAME rin=0.5 m=… symm=… builds it for any inner radius rin (in R☉, 0 for the full sphere). tests/diff_rot/solar_checks.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the modes of both Mukhopadhyay papers, with and without the thermal wind (about 40 minutes on one core).

Result. Without the thermal wind, every convection-zone and mixed mode whose counterpart can be identified (8 modes) agrees with theirs to 0.13 nHz, and the two published growth rates to 0.006 nHz. With the thermal wind the convection-zone modes are 2–10 nHz off, so their radiative-interior runs appear to have no latitudinal entropy gradient, unlike those of 2025a. Their two high-latitude convection-zone modes (\(m = 1\) and 2) are not matched: without the thermal wind kore's nearest convection-zone modes are strongly damped, and the paper gives no growth rates to compare.

docs.title: Centrifugal deformation equations
docs.text: This page gives the mathematics behind centrifugal = 1, for readers who want to check the code or extend it: the coordinates that follow the level surfaces, the equations in them and their rows, the magnetic field, the dissipative terms, the differential rotation, the exact spheroid, the flattening of each shape, the effective gravity, the energy budgets, the plots, the accuracy, and the checks. How to set up a run is on Background model. The code is in bin/centrifugal.py, the checks in tests/centrifugal/.

docs.title: Coordinates that follow the level surfaces
docs.text:
kore's flow conserves mass exactly only when the density depends on the radius alone. In a flattened body the density is constant on spheroids, so rather than give every profile a part that depends on latitude, kore maps the body onto a reference space in which the level surfaces are spheres.

A point \( oldsymbol\alpha\) of the reference space, at radius \(r\) and colatitude \( heta\), is at \(\mathbf X = oldsymbol\alpha + oldsymbol\xi\) in the body, with

\[ oldsymbol\xi = \varepsilon(r) hinspace abla\left( frac12 r^2P_2(\cos heta) ight) = \varepsilon(r) hinspace r\left[P_2 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + frac12 rac{dP_2}{d heta} hinspace\hat{ oldsymbol heta} ight], \qquad \varepsilon = - frac23 f , \]

where \(f(r)\) is the flattening of the level surface \(r\), positive for an oblate body. At first order that surface is at the distance \(r(1 + \varepsilon P_2)\) from the centre: its flattening is \(f\) and its volume that of the sphere of radius \(r\). In Cartesian components \( oldsymbol\xi = \varepsilon(r) hinspace(-\alpha_x/2, -\alpha_y/2, \alpha_z)\), an axisymmetric stretch at each radius, so the map is smooth at the centre when \(\varepsilon\) is even and smooth in \(r\); a purely radial \( oldsymbol\xi\) would not be. Every background profile is a function of \(r\), and the walls are the level surfaces \(r\) = ricb and \(r = 1\).

With the deformation gradient \(\mathsf F = \partial\mathbf X/\partial oldsymbol\alpha = \mathsf I + abla oldsymbol\xi\) and \(J = \det\mathsf F\), kore's poloidal and toroidal scalars describe the flow carried back to the reference space,

\[ \mathbf w = J hinspace\mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf u . \]

This transform keeps what kore's formulation relies on. Mass: \( abla_\alpha\cdot( ho_0\mathbf w) = J hinspace abla_X\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u)\), so the exact \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf w) = 0\) of kore's scalars is exact mass conservation in the body. Walls: \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n\) is proportional to \(w_r\) on a level surface, and \(\mathbf u = 0\) where \(\mathbf w = 0\), so the impenetrable and no-slip rows are unchanged.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
kore removes the pressure by taking curls of the momentum equation. In the reference space this works when the equation is written with covariant components, \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\) times it: the pressure force stays a gradient, \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T} abla_X\Pi = abla_\alpha\Pi\). So does the buoyancy, which acts along the gradient of the effective potential, constant on the level surfaces. The dimensionless equations of Anelastic equations become

\[ \mathsf M hinspace\partial_t\mathbf w + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace ilde{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w = - abla\Pi + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g_{ m eff} hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + \dots , \qquad \mathsf M = rac{\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathsf F}{J}, \quad ilde{\mathbf z} = \mathsf F^{-1}\hat{\mathbf z}, \] \[ p_0\left(J hinspace\partial_t s + w_r rac{dS}{dr} ight) = \dots , \]

with the dots the viscous force and the thermal diffusion, which take covariant forms too (Dissipative terms). Three terms of the ideal fluid change: the inertia gains the metric \(\mathsf M\), the Coriolis force turns with the map (\(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathsf F\mathbf w)/J = ilde{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w\)), and the rate of change of the entropy gains \(J\). The advection keeps its form, \(\mathbf u\cdot abla_X S = w_r S'/J\), and the buoyancy takes the effective gravity \(g_{ m eff}\) (below).

At first order. With \(\eta = r\varepsilon'\) and \(w_z = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot\mathbf w\),

\[ (\mathsf M - \mathsf I) hinspace\mathbf w = \varepsilon\left(3w_z\hat{\mathbf z} - \mathbf w ight) + \eta\left[ frac32\cos heta\left(w_z\hat{\mathbf r} + w_r\hat{\mathbf z} ight) - w_r\hat{\mathbf r} - P_2 hinspace\mathbf w ight], \] \[ ( ilde{\mathbf z} - \hat{\mathbf z}) imes\mathbf w = -\varepsilon hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w - \eta\left[ frac32\cos^2 heta hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w - frac12\cos heta hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} imes\mathbf w ight], \] \[ J - 1 = \eta hinspace P_2 . \]

A uniform flattening has \(\eta = 0\): the map is then a linear stretch, and \(J = 1\) at this order.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
The new terms have the form of the force of a differential rotation, so kore builds them with the same tools. Each one multiplies the components of \(\mathbf w\) by polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) of degree 2 at most, with the radial factor \(\varepsilon\) or \(\eta\); kore builds their couplings with the recurrence algebra of bin/angular.py and projects them on its rows as it does the force (Spectral form), without the terms that come from the shear of the rotation.

  • Selection rules. A degree \(l\) couples to \(l\) and \(l \pm 2\) of the same kind (poloidal to poloidal, toroidal to toroidal, entropy to entropy), and to \(l \pm 1\) and \(l \pm 3\) of the other kind (poloidal to toroidal).
  • Matrices. \(A\) gains \(2\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace(\tilde{\mathbf z} - \hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf w\) in the momentum rows. \(B\) gains \(-(\mathsf M - \mathsf I)\thinspace\mathbf w\) in the momentum rows and \((J - 1)\thinspace s = \eta P_2\thinspace s\) in the heat rows, with the signs of the inertia and of the entropy. The poloidal–toroidal couplings of the inertia are imaginary, so \(B\) is complex.
  • Radial operators. Their labels are those of the differential rotation with the profile code of \(\varepsilon\) (ce0) or \(\eta\) (ce1) in place of that of \(\Delta\Omega\), and that of \(r\varepsilon'\) (ce1) or \(r\eta'\) (ce2) for the derivative terms (centrifugal.MOMENTUM). The heat rows use the operator of the entropy times ce1. The three codes are Chebyshev fits on kore's grid, even in \(r\).

docs.title: Magnetic field
docs.text:
A field is carried back to the reference space in the same way as the flow, so that kore's poloidal and toroidal scalars of the field keep their meaning and most of its rows keep the form they have in a sphere.

The field as a flux. kore's scalars describe

\[ ilde{\mathbf b} = J hinspace\mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf b, \qquad ilde{\mathbf B}_0 = J hinspace\mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf B_0 . \]

The flux of \(\mathbf b\) through a surface of the body is that of \( ilde{\mathbf b}\) through its image in the reference space, so \( abla\cdot ilde{\mathbf b} = 0\) is exact and the field lines of \( ilde{\mathbf b}\) are those of \(\mathbf b\), moved with the level surfaces. kore's formula for B0 and B0_tor gives \( ilde{\mathbf B}_0\): the background field of the body is \(\mathsf F ilde{\mathbf B}_0/J\), the field of the sphere stretched with the level surfaces.

Equations. The Lorentz force is written with covariant components, as the rest of the momentum equation, and the induction equation for the flux:

\[ \mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf F_L = rac{\mathrm{Hendrik}}{ ho_0 J}\left[ abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b}) imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 + abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf B}_0) imes ilde{\mathbf b} ight], \qquad \partial_t ilde{\mathbf b} = abla imes\left( rac{\mathbf w imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0}{J} - \mathrm{MagnetD} hinspace\mathsf M hinspace abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b}) ight) . \]

Two identities of the map give them. The current of the body, carried back as a flux, is \( abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b})\); and the cross product of two fields carried back as fluxes, \(\mathbf a = \mathsf F ilde{\mathbf a}/J\) and \(\mathbf c = \mathsf F ilde{\mathbf c}/J\), has the covariant components \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf a imes\mathbf c) = ( ilde{\mathbf a} imes ilde{\mathbf c})/J\). The electric field of the diffusion is MagnetD times the current of the body, whose covariant components are \(\mathsf M hinspace abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b})\) (Dissipative terms).

At first order. With \(\mathsf M - \mathsf I\) and \(J - 1 = \eta P_2\) from above, and the currents \(\mathbf j = abla imes ilde{\mathbf b}\) and \(\mathbf J_0 = abla imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0\) of the sphere, the force and the electric field of the induction gain

\[ \delta\mathbf G = -\eta P_2\left(\mathbf J_0 imes ilde{\mathbf b} + \mathbf j imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 ight) + \left[ abla imes\left((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf B}_0 ight) ight] imes ilde{\mathbf b} + \left[ abla imes\left((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf b} ight) ight] imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 , \qquad \delta\mathbf E = -\eta P_2 hinspace\mathbf w imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 . \]

A uniform flattening has \(\eta = 0\), and only the two currents of the metric remain. A flattening that varies with the radius gives the background field a current even where the spherical formula has none: the axial field, for one, is no longer uniform in the body.

Rows. \(\delta\mathbf G\) enters the momentum rows as the Lorentz force of the sphere does (times Hendrik), and \( abla imes\delta\mathbf E\) the rows of \(f\) and \(g\) as the induction does; both are built with the recurrence algebra of bin/mag_algebra.py. A background of degrees up to \(n\) couples a degree \(l\) to \(l \pm (n + 3)\) at most, two more than in the sphere. The radial factors are products of the profile codes of the deformation and of the background: a label carries the amplitude E (\(\varepsilon\)), N (\(\eta\)), C (\(r\eta'\)) or Q (\(r(r\eta')'\)), then p or t and the degree of the poloidal or toroidal profile (centrifugal.product_code).

Insulating walls. Outside an insulating wall the field is a potential field \( abla\phi\) of the body, and the wall is a level surface, so the matching happens on the spheroid. In the reference space, at the wall \(r = R\), the flux through the wall and the tangential field are continuous:

\[ ilde b_r = \left[J hinspace\mathsf F^{-1} abla\phi(\mathbf X) ight]_r, \qquad \left[\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b} ight]_{ m tan} = abla_{ m tan} hinspace\phi(\mathbf X( oldsymbol\alpha)) . \]

At first order, with \(m_s\) and \(m_t\) the spheroidal and toroidal parts of \((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf b}\) at the wall, \(\delta s = ( oldsymbol\xi\cdot abla\phi)/R\) and \(\delta q = -[ abla imes( oldsymbol\xi imes abla\phi)]_r\) (each of degree \(l\)), eliminating the potential gives the rows

\[ (l+1)F + RF' + R(m_s - \delta s) - rac{R hinspace\delta q}{l+1} = 0, \qquad G + m_t = 0 \qquad ext{(outer wall)}, \] \[ lF - RF' - R(m_s - \delta s) - rac{R hinspace\delta q}{l} = 0, \qquad G + m_t = 0 \qquad ext{(insulating inner core)}, \]

which couple \(F_l\) to \(F_{l\pm2}\), \(G_{l\pm1}\) and \(G_{l\pm3}\), and \(G_l\) to \(G_{l\pm2}\), \(F_{l\pm1}\) and \(F_{l\pm3}\).

Conducting inner core. The inner core is deformed with the fluid, on the same map, and its field is a flux too. With the permeability of the fluid (mu_i2o = 1) the field \( ilde{\mathbf b}\) is continuous at the inner boundary, since \(\mathbf b\) is and the map is smooth across it, so the rows that match the field keep their form. The tangential electric field is continuous too. The flow vanishes at the no-slip boundary, so on each side this field is that of the diffusion, and its row gains the metric part of the diffusion of the fluid and of the core (Dissipative terms).

docs.title: Dissipative terms
docs.text:
The viscous force and the thermal and magnetic diffusion act in the body, so a damped mode feels the deformed walls and the deformed profiles through them. kore carries each back to the reference space as it does the inertia: it keeps its spherical form and gains a part of first order in \(f\).

Viscous force. With \(\mathbf V(\mathbf u) = ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S)\) the force per unit mass (Anelastic equations), its covariant form is, up to a gradient that the curl rows remove,

\[ \mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V\left( rac{\mathsf F\mathbf w}{J} ight) = \mathbf V(\mathbf w) - oldsymbol\xi imes abla imes\mathbf V(\mathbf w) + \mathbf V\left( abla imes( oldsymbol\xi imes\mathbf w) - oldsymbol\xi hinspace abla\cdot\mathbf w ight) - \xi_r rac{d u}{dr} hinspace abla\cdot\mathsf S(\mathbf w) - abla\left( rac{\xi_r}{ ho_0} rac{d( ho_0 u)}{dr} ight)\cdot\mathsf S(\mathbf w) . \]

The second and third terms carry the force of the sphere along the displacement \( oldsymbol\xi\); the last two come from \( u\) and \( ho_0\), which are constant on the level surfaces rather than on the spheres.

Thermal diffusion. The heat rows are the equation times \(J\), and the diffusion becomes

\[ J hinspace abla_X\cdot\left(\kappa p_0 abla_X s ight) = abla\cdot\left(\kappa p_0 hinspace\mathsf M^{-1} abla s ight), \]

whose first-order part is \(- abla\cdot(\kappa p_0(\mathsf M - \mathsf I) abla s)\).

Magnetic diffusion. The current of the body, carried back as a flux, is \( abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b})\), and the covariant components of the electric field of the diffusion are MagnetD times \(\mathsf M hinspace abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b})\). Its first-order part is MagnetD times \((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) abla imes ilde{\mathbf b} + abla imes((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf b})\). A conducting inner core gains the same terms with its own diffusivity.

Walls. The no-slip, impenetrable and fixed-entropy rows keep their form: \(\mathbf w = 0\), \(w_r = 0\) and \(s = 0\) on a level surface are \(\mathbf u = 0\), \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n = 0\) and \(s = 0\) in the body. The two other walls change:

  • a stress-free wall has no tangential stress on the deformed wall: the tangential part of \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathsf S_X\mathsf F^{-\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf r}\) vanishes, with \(\mathsf S_X\) the rate of strain of the body, \(\mathsf F^{-\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf r}\) the normal to the level surface and \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\) taking the components along its tangents;
  • a fixed-flux wall has no flux through the deformed wall: \(\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathsf M^{-1} abla s = 0\).

Rows. The first-order parts multiply the fields and their derivatives by polynomials in \(\cos heta\) of degree 2 at most, so they couple the degrees as the inertia does: \(l\) to \(l\) and \(l \pm 2\) of the same kind, and to \(l \pm 1\) and \(l \pm 3\) of the other. Their radial factors are products of the amplitudes of the map, of the diffusivity and its derivatives, and of the derivatives of \(\ln ho_0\) (centrifugal.diffusion_build). When \(m eq 0\) the toroidal rows of the viscous force and of the induction reach the third derivative of \(P\) and of \(F\), and kore builds those sections in the basis that has it. In a full sphere these rows have terms in \(P/r\) and \(F/r\), polynomials only once the rows are multiplied by \(r^4\) and \(r^3\): kore does it for the field (in a conducting inner core too), and asks for rpower_v = 4 for the flow.

docs.title: Differential rotation
docs.text:
A differential rotation is a profile like the others: \(\Delta\Omega(r, heta)\) is given in the reference space, so the point of the body at \(\mathbf X(r, heta)\) turns at \(\Delta\Omega(r, heta)\), and a rotation that depends on \(r\) alone is constant on the level surfaces. The flow of the body is \(\mathbf U_0 = \mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf X\). The map commutes with the rotations about the axis, so the flux of this flow is \(J\) times the spherical formula \(\mathbf U_{00} = \mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes oldsymbol\alpha\), and its terms change as follows.

  • Momentum. The force \((\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0\) gains, up to a gradient, with \( oldsymbol\omega_0 = abla imes\mathbf U_{00}\),

$$ \delta\mathbf W = -\mathbf U_{00} imes abla imes\left((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) hinspace\mathbf w ight) + (\varepsilon + \eta P_2) hinspace\mathbf w imes oldsymbol\omega_0 - \eta hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega\left(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w - \cos heta hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} imes\mathbf w ight). $$

  • Heat. The advection of the entropy times \(J\) is \((1 + \eta P_2) hinspace\mathbf U_{00}\cdot abla s\): the heat rows gain \(i m hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\eta P_2 hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace s\).
  • Induction. The electric field of the flow carries back exactly, \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf U_0 imes\mathbf b) = \mathbf U_{00} imes ilde{\mathbf b}\): no new term.

A degree \(n\) of \(\Delta\Omega\) couples \(l\) to \(l \pm (n + 2)\) of the same kind and to \(l \pm (n + 3)\) of the other, two more than in the sphere (centrifugal.rotation_build).

docs.title: The exact spheroid
docs.text:
When every level surface has the same flattening, the body is a stretched sphere, and kore keeps the map exactly, at any flattening: centrifugal_shape = 'spheroid'. It serves a homogeneous fluid in a strongly flattened body or container, such as a fast-rotating planet with a rigid mantle (or, with \(f < 0\), an elongated one), and it can be checked against exact solutions at any \(f\).

The map. The point \( oldsymbol\alpha\) of the reference space is at

\[ \mathbf X = \mathsf F oldsymbol\alpha, \qquad \mathsf F = \mathrm{diag}(a, a, c), \qquad rac{c}{a} = 1 - f, \qquad a^2c = 1, \]

so the level surface \(r\) is the spheroid of equatorial radius \(ar\) and polar radius \(cr\), with the volume of the sphere of radius \(r\). At first order in \(f\) this is the map of 'uniform', \(a = 1 + f/3\) and \(c = 1 - 2f/3\). The metric is constant, \(J = 1\), \(\mathsf M = \mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathsf F = \mathrm{diag}(a^2, a^2, c^2)\) and \( ilde{\mathbf z} = \hat{\mathbf z}/c\), and the Laplacian of the body, written in the reference space, is

\[ D = abla\cdot\left(\mathsf M^{-1} abla ight) = rac{1}{a^2} abla^2 + \left( rac{1}{c^2} - rac{1}{a^2} ight)\partial_z^2 . \]

The terms. Each term that changes gains a part that kore keeps whole. With \(\mathsf Z\mathbf v = \hat{\mathbf z}(\hat{\mathbf z}\cdot\mathbf v)\), \(\partial_z = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot abla\) (on each Cartesian component of a vector) and \(x = \cos heta\), the parts beyond the sphere's are

term its part beyond the sphere's inertia \((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) hinspace\mathbf w = (a^2 - 1) hinspace\mathbf w + (c^2 - a^2) hinspace\mathsf Z\mathbf w\) Coriolis force \(( ilde{\mathbf z} - \hat{\mathbf z}) imes\mathbf w = (1/c - 1) hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w\) viscous force \( u\left[(a^2/c^2 - 1) hinspace\partial_z^2\mathbf w + (c^2 - a^2) hinspace\mathsf Z D\mathbf w ight]\) thermal diffusion \(\kappa p_0\left[(1/a^2 - 1) hinspace abla^2 s + (1/c^2 - 1/a^2) hinspace\partial_z^2 s ight]\) traction on a level surface \((a^2/c^2 - 1) hinspace x hinspace\partial_z\mathbf w + (c^2 - a^2) hinspace\mathsf Z\left[\partial_r\mathbf w/a^2 + (1/c^2 - 1/a^2) hinspace x hinspace\partial_z\mathbf w ight]\) flux through a level surface \((1/a^2 - 1) hinspace\partial_r s + (1/c^2 - 1/a^2) hinspace x hinspace\partial_z s\)

The traction is that of the stress-free wall (Dissipative terms), \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathsf S_X\mathsf F^{-\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf r} = \mathsf M( abla\mathbf w)\mathsf M^{-1}\hat{\mathbf r} + ( abla\mathbf w)^{\mathsf T}\hat{\mathbf r}\), with \(( abla\mathbf w)_{ik} = \partial_k w_i\), less the sphere's. The rest keeps its spherical form: the time derivative of the entropy and its advection (\(J = 1\)), the pressure, and the buoyancy. With the gravity \(g = r\) of 'Boussinesq', the buoyancy of the reference space acts in the body along \(\mathsf F^{-\mathsf T} oldsymbol\alpha = abla_X(r^2/2)\): normal to the level surfaces, as the effective gravity of a homogeneous body in hydrostatic equilibrium (a Maclaurin spheroid), whose effective potential depends on \(r\) alone.

Rows. \(\mathsf Z\) multiplies by polynomials in \(\cos heta\) of degree 2 and \(\partial_z\) raises or lowers the degree by one, so the inertia couples a degree \(l\) to \(l\) and \(l \pm 2\) of the same kind and to \(l \pm 1\) of the other, the viscous force and the stress-free rows reach \(l \pm 4\) and \(l \pm 3\), and the heat rows \(l \pm 2\). The radial operators are kore's own, with no profile (centrifugal.spheroid_build, spheroid_walls), and the blocks reach \(\lvert\Delta l vert\) = 4, one more than at first order.

The field. The field is carried back as a flux, as at first order (Magnetic field). With \(J = 1\) the flow induces the flux \( ilde{\mathbf b} = \mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf b\) as it does in the sphere, while the Lorentz force and the magnetic diffusion keep \(\mathsf M\) whole. With the currents \(\mathbf j = abla imes ilde{\mathbf b}\) and \(\mathbf J_0 = abla imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0\) of the sphere and \(\delta = c^2 - a^2\), so that \(\mathsf M - \mathsf I = (a^2 - 1) hinspace\mathsf I + \delta hinspace\mathsf Z\), their parts beyond the sphere's are

term its part beyond the sphere's Lorentz force, per Hendrik \((a^2 - 1)\left(\mathbf j imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 + \mathbf J_0 imes ilde{\mathbf b} ight) + \delta\left\{[ abla imes(\mathsf Z ilde{\mathbf b})] imes ilde{\mathbf B}_0 + [ abla imes(\mathsf Z ilde{\mathbf B}_0)] imes ilde{\mathbf b} ight\}\) electric field of the diffusion, per MagnetD \((a^4 - 1) hinspace\mathbf j + a^2\delta\left[\mathsf Z\mathbf j + abla imes(\mathsf Z ilde{\mathbf b}) ight] + \delta^2 hinspace\mathsf Z abla imes(\mathsf Z ilde{\mathbf b})\)

The force takes the labels of the sphere's Lorentz force (bin/mag_algebra.py) and couples \(l\) to \(l \pm (n + 3)\) through a background of degree \(n\); the diffusion takes kore's own labels (eta0) and reaches \(l \pm 4\) (centrifugal.spheroid_magnetic_build, spheroid_build).

Insulating walls. Outside an insulating wall kore matches the exact potential field of the spheroid. In the spheroidal coordinates confocal with the wall, the wall is a surface \( u = u_0\), and on it the angle of these coordinates is the reference colatitude. A potential of degree \(l\) on the wall therefore meets the degree \(l\) of the field alone, and the matching keeps one row per degree, as in the sphere. The flux through the wall and the tangential field are those of the potential \(\Phi_l\) on it,

\[ ilde b_{r,l} = rac{\lambda_l}{R} hinspace\Phi_l, \qquad \left[\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b} ight]_{{ m tan}, hinspace l} = abla_{ m tan}\Phi_l, \qquad \lambda_l = rac{a^2}{k} hinspace rac{d\ln R_l}{d u}( u_0), \qquad k = \sqrt{\lvert a^2 - c^2 vert}, \qquad u_0 = rac{c}{k} , \]

with \(kR\) the focal distance of the wall \(r = R\) and \(R_l\) the radial function of the potential: \(Q_l^m(i u)\) outside an oblate wall, \(Q_l^m( u)\) outside a prolate one, and \(P_l^m\) of the same argument inside an insulating inner core (the level surfaces are similar, so \( u_0\) is the same). In the sphere \(\lambda_l\) is \(-(l + 1)\) outside and \(l\) inside. Eliminating \(\Phi_l\), with \(m_s\) and \(m_t\) the spheroidal and toroidal parts of \((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf b}\) at the wall, gives the rows

\[ l(l + 1) hinspace F = \lambda_l\left(F + RF' + Rm_s ight), \qquad G + m_t = 0 , \]

which kore divides by \(l + 1\) outside and by \(l\) inside, as the rows of the sphere. They couple \(F_l\) to \(F_{l\pm2}\) and \(G_{l\pm1}\), and \(G_l\) to \(F_{l\pm1}\). kore computes the logarithmic derivatives by recurrence, forward for \(P_l^m\) and backward for \(Q_l^m\) (centrifugal.spheroid_lambda, spheroid_field_walls).

Conducting inner core. With mu_i2o = 1 the field is continuous at the inner boundary, as at first order, and the row of the tangential electric field gains the part of the diffusion above on each side, with the conductivity of each (centrifugal.spheroid_icb).

Scope. The fluid is homogeneous (structure = 'Boussinesq', diffusivity = 'uniform'), with centrifugal_q = 0 (the effective gravity is already kore's \(g\)), and any \(f < 1\); with a field, any background, insulating walls and an inner core that is insulating or conducting with mu_i2o = 1. kore stops with a differential rotation. The budgets of spin_doctor and the plots use the exact metric and map, and every budget closes to round-off (Energy budgets).

docs.title: The flattening
docs.text:
The flattening of each level surface follows from hydrostatic balance in the rotating body. 'clairaut' solves for it, 'uniform' and 'user' take it as given.

'clairaut'. Clairaut's equation, in Radau's form for \(\eta_R = d\ln f/d\ln x\), with \(x\) the radius in units of the radius of the body:

\[ x\frac{d\eta_R}{dx} = 6 - 6\thinspace\frac{\rho}{\bar\rho}\thinspace(\eta_R + 1) - \eta_R^2 + \eta_R, \qquad \eta_R(0) = 0, \]

with \(\bar\rho\) the mean density inside \(x\). kore takes the density ratio from the gravity alone, by Poisson's equation,

\[ \frac{\rho}{\bar\rho} = \frac{x g' + 2g}{3g}, \]

so the structure's \(g\) must be its self-gravity. kore integrates from the centre and fixes the scale of \(f\) by the surface condition \(x f' + 2f = \tfrac52 q\), that is

\[ f(x_t) = \frac{5\thinspace q_t}{2\left(\eta_R(x_t) + 2\right)}, \qquad q_t = q\thinspace x_t^3 , \]

at the top \(x_t\) of the structure: the surface \(x = 1\), or the outer wall for 'model S hydrostatic', whose gravity ends there (the mass above it neglected). With centrifugal_f set, the scale instead makes \(f\) = centrifugal_f at the outer wall. A homogeneous body has \(\eta_R = 0\) and \(f = 5q/4\), the Maclaurin spheroid at first order; a polytrope of index 1 has \(f/q = 15/(2\pi^2)\) at the surface. Since \(\eta = \varepsilon\thinspace\eta_R\), the codes ce1 and ce2 follow from \(\eta_R\) without differentiating:

\[ r\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\thinspace\eta_R, \qquad r\left(r\varepsilon'\right)' = \varepsilon\left[6 - 6\thinspace\frac{\rho}{\bar\rho}\thinspace(\eta_R + 1) + \eta_R\right]. \]

'uniform' and 'user'. 'uniform' has \(f\) = centrifugal_f and \(\eta = 0\). 'user' evaluates centrifugal_profile at \(\lvert r\rvert\) and takes \(r\varepsilon'\) and \(r(r\varepsilon')'\) from the derivatives of the Chebyshev fit of \(\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Effective gravity
docs.text:
The buoyancy acts along the gradient of the effective potential, the gravitational plus the centrifugal one, which is constant on each level surface. At first order its parts in \(P_2\) cancel there, and what remains is

\[ \Phi_{\rm eff} = \Phi_0(r) - \tfrac13\Omega^2r^2, \qquad g_{\rm eff} = \frac{d\Phi_{\rm eff}}{dr} = g - \tfrac23\Omega^2 r . \]

In kore's units the second term is \(-\tfrac23\thinspace q_t\thinspace g(x_t)\thinspace x/x_t\) (centrifugal.g_monopole), which radial_profiles.graviX adds to \(g\) when centrifugal_q > 0, with any shape.

docs.title: Energy budgets
docs.text:
The energies of the deformed body are integrals over the body. Written in the reference space they gain the metric, so spin_doctor adds the metric parts to its budgets, computed from the fields on its own grid (utils4pp.centrifugal_terms), independently of the matrices. In the conventions of Energy balance:

\[ K = \int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf w^*\cdot\mathsf M hinspace\mathbf w hinspace dV, \qquad T = \int p_0 hinspace J hinspace\lvert s vert^2 hinspace dV , \]

and the power of the Coriolis force is \(2\int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf w^*\cdot[2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace ilde{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w] hinspace dV\), imaginary: it still does no work. solve.py normalises the eigenvectors to this \(K\). spin_doctor adds the metric parts of the viscous power, of the power of a differential rotation and of the entropy diffusion in the same way (utils4pp.centrifugal_dissipation_terms), so the budgets close as well as without the deformation. It computes neither the enstrophy residual nor the viscous one, whose wall terms keep their spherical form (residens and residD are NaN).

With a field. The magnetic energy of the deformed fluid is

\[ frac12\int ilde{\mathbf b}^*\cdot\mathsf M hinspace ilde{\mathbf b} hinspace dV = \mathrm{ME} + \mathrm{MEc}, \]

with MEc the part of the metric (magnetic.dat, column 12), and solve.py normalises to \(K\) plus Hendrik times it. spin_doctor adds the metric parts of the Lorentz work (\(\delta\mathbf G\)) to residσ and residω, and those of the induction work (\(\delta\mathbf E\)) and of the magnetic diffusion to resid𝐛 (utils4pp.centrifugal_magnetic_terms), so these close to round-off. The full budget resid𝐄 also counts the Ohmic loss with the metric current \( abla imes((\mathsf M - \mathsf I) ilde{\mathbf b})\), the energy of the potential field matched on each deformed wall, and the field of a conducting inner core with its metric. It closes at second order in \(f\) only: kore keeps the first order of \(1/J\) and of \(\mathsf M\) in the force, in the induction, in the diffusion and in the matching at the walls, and the energy does not cancel their products. In the exact spheroid, where kore keeps \(\mathsf M\) whole, it closes to round-off: the Ohmic loss there is MagnetD times \(\int abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b})^*\cdot\mathsf M hinspace abla imes(\mathsf M ilde{\mathbf b}) hinspace dV\), and the energy of the potential field beyond each wall is a wall integral with the \(\lambda_l\) of its rows (centrifugal.spheroid_potential).

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
tools/plot_field.py draws the fields where they are in the body (centrifugal.to_physical). The reference point \((r, \theta)\) is at the distance \(\varpi\) from the axis and the height \(z\),

\[ \varpi = r\sin\theta\thinspace(1 - \varepsilon/2), \qquad z = r\cos\theta\thinspace(1 + \varepsilon), \]

and the flow there is \(\mathbf u = \mathsf F\mathbf w/J\), at first order

\[ \mathbf u = \mathbf w + \varepsilon\left(\tfrac32 w_z\hat{\mathbf z} - \tfrac12\mathbf w\right) + \eta\thinspace w_r\left(\tfrac32\cos\theta\thinspace\hat{\mathbf z} - \tfrac12\hat{\mathbf r}\right) - \eta P_2\thinspace\mathbf w , \]

given in the spherical basis of the body point, turned by \(-\tfrac32\varepsilon\sin\theta\cos\theta\) in colatitude from that of \((r, \theta)\). The field \(\mathbf b = \mathsf F\tilde{\mathbf b}/J\) maps in the same way. A scalar, such as \(s\), only moves.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
The map, the transform of the flow and the covariant equations are exact. kore keeps them at first order in \(f\), except for the exact spheroid (The exact spheroid), where the only error is that of the discretization.

  • First order. The error is of order \(f^2\). For the spin-over of a Maclaurin spheroid it is \(f^2/6\) in the frequency (Checks): 0.2 % at Saturn's flattening, where the deformation moves the frequency by 10 %. submatrices.py warns above \(f = 0.1\).
  • Thermal wind. With thermal_wind 1 or 2 the entropy \(S_{tw}\) balances \(\Delta\Omega\) as in the sphere: the terms of order \(f\thinspace\Delta\Omega\) of that balance are missing, while its advection and the other terms of \(\Delta\Omega\) are those of the deformed body. submatrices.py warns.
  • What stops the run. The rows of a wall of zero radial stress (bco or bci = 2) would change on a deformed wall, so kore stops with them in a viscous run. The matching rows of a conducting inner core change too when its permeability differs from the fluid's, so kore stops unless mu_i2o = 1. It also stops with a forcing, and in a viscous full sphere with \(m \neq 0\) unless rpower_v = 4 (Dissipative terms).
  • Shifts measured from a sphere. A body that is not deformed keeps the bases and rows of the sphere (centrifugal.deformed), so that its matrices are those of centrifugal = 0. A deformed body with \(m \neq 0\) writes the rows of the toroidal flow in \(C^{(3)}\) when it is viscous, and those of the toroidal field when the field diffuses (Dissipative terms). A shift taken between a deformed run and one at \(f = 0\) therefore also holds the difference of their errors of discretization, which near the resolution limit can rival the part of the shift that the Ekman layers make: for the nutation of Checks without its field, 1.5e-6 in \(\lambda\) at N 160, 6e-4 of \(f\), as large as that part. Taken between deformed runs, at \(\pm f\), the shift does not carry it: it moves by 1e-6 of \(f\) from N 160 to N 200, 5e-6 with the field.

docs.text:

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The deformation was checked in four ways: its closed forms against a symbolic derivation from the definitions, its couplings, blocks and wall rows against direct quadratures, its eigenvalues against exact results (among them the modes of a spheroid, computed without the map), and the energy budgets. The scripts are in tests/centrifugal/ (README; run_all.sh, about 17 minutes on 16 cores). Results of 2026-11-06:

check script result every closed form above, from the map and \(\mathbf w = J\mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf u\) in Cartesian components (sympy): the level surfaces, the exact identities of the covariant equations, the first-order terms, the plot map, the effective potential derive.py exact the magnetic terms, from \(\mathbf b = \mathsf F\tilde{\mathbf b}/J\) alone (sympy): the covariant Lorentz force and induction, their first-order parts \(\delta\mathbf G\) and \(\delta\mathbf E\), a potential field on the deformed wall; docs.title: Modifying kore
docs.text: After changing kore, two questions matter: do the runs that worked before still give the same results, and is the new part right? kore has a tool for each. Everything below runs from the repository, on one machine; most checks take seconds to minutes.
