docs.text: function returns shapes() {n: f(r)}, the shapes of the degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\) for diff_rot_type, before diff_rot_ampl degrees(), n_max() the even degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\) and the highest one tw_degrees(), tw_nmax() the degrees of \(S_{tw}\): 2 to \(n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 1), \(2n_{\max} + 2\) (2), 2 (3), none (0) codes(n) the profile codes zf, zd, zs, tw, tp + the degree character fX(n, r, Dorder) \(f_n\) (diff_rot_ampl × \(a_n\) × shape) and its derivatives, from the Chebyshev fit (§5.2) raw(n, r) \(f_n\) evaluated directly sigma_coefficients(r) the Legendre coefficients \(\sigma_k(r)\) of \(S_{tw}\) (§5.4) sigmaX(n, r, Dorder) \(\sigma_n\) and its derivatives from its Chebyshev fit profile_functions() {code: f(r, Dorder)} of every diff-rot profile code, for burrito momentum_coefficients(n, m), momentum_coef(...) the coefficients of §3.4, and one of them for a target degree and Δl heat_coefficients(m), heat_coef(...) \(P_n(X)\), \(P_n'(X)\), \(P_n'(X)D\) by diagonal, and one coefficient labels() every radial operator of the terms, with the parity class of its column dl_range(section, component) the Δl of the blocks of a row section and column momentum_block(...), heat_block(...) one block of \(A\) check(), description() stops on settings that cannot work; the 'user' definitions as text for params.dat TYPES the types, in the order of their code in params.dat

docs.title: 5.1 The profiles \(f_n\) of each type
docs.text:
diff_rot.shapes defines the shape of each degree; \(f_n\) = diff_rot_ampl × \(a_n\) × shape, with \(a_n\) = diff_rot_term_amp[n/2] (1 in the table below). With \(a\) = diff_rot_ampl, \(p\) = diff_rot_param, and \(x\) the fractional solar radius (diff_rot.solar_x: \(x = r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure (background.md), \(x = r\) otherwise):

diff_rot_type \(f_0/a\) \(f_2/a\) \(f_n/a\), \(n \ge 4\) 'rigid' 1 'Y20' 1 'Y20-wall-bounded' \((1 - r)(r - r_i)\), \(r_i\) = ricb 'shellular' \(r^p - 1\) 'shellular_boussinesq' \(\tfrac12(1 - r^2)\) 'cylindrical' (\(a\varpi^2\)) \(\tfrac{2}{3}r^2\) \(-\tfrac{2}{3}r^2\) 'conical' (\(a\sin^2\theta\)) \(\tfrac{2}{3}\) \(-\tfrac{2}{3}\) 'solar' \((-7.695/435)\thinspace H(x)\) \((-86.04/435)\thinspace H(x)\) 'solar_P4' \((\Omega_{RZ} + (O_0 - \Omega_{RZ})E)/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1\) \(O_2 E/\Omega_{\rm ref}\) \(O_4 E/\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (\(n = 4\)) 'tabulated' fit fit fit, up to diff_rot_nmax 'user' diff_rot_profiles[0] diff_rot_profiles[2] diff_rot_profiles[n]

Here \(H(x) = \tfrac12\left[1 + \tanh(2(x - 0.71)/0.1)\right]\) (the 'solar' frame is 435 nHz), and for 'solar_P4' \(E(x) = \tfrac12\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}((x - r_{tc})/d_{tc})\right]\) and \(\Omega_{CZ} = c_0 + c_2\cos^2\theta + c_4\cos^4\theta\) projected on Legendre polynomials (\(\cos^2\theta = (1 + 2P_2)/3\), \(\cos^4\theta = 1/5 + 4P_2/7 + 8P_4/35\)): \(O_0 = c_0 + c_2/3 + c_4/5\), \(O_2 = 2c_2/3 + 4c_4/7\), \(O_4 = 8c_4/35\).

'user'. diff_rot_profiles maps each even degree to a string, a numpy expression of r (kore radius), x (fractional solar radius) and p (diff_rot_param), evaluated in a namespace with only sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, log10, sqrt, abs, sign, pi, where, minimum, maximum, erf, erfc (no builtins). For example a cylindrical rotation:

par.diff_rot = 1; par.diff_rot_type = 'user'
par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '(2/3)*r**2', 2: '-(2/3)*r**2'}
par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.25

builds matrices bitwise identical to diff_rot_type = 'cylindrical' with the same amplitude. The degrees must be even integers, and the strings must not contain #: spin_doctor.py ends each params.dat row of a 'user' run with them, after a # (diff_rot.description), so that every row carries its profile and np.loadtxt still reads the numeric columns.

'tabulated' (diff_rot._tabulated_fits). The file holds ome[θ, r] (nHz), r (R☉) and theta (rad). At each table radius, \(\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1\) is interpolated in \(\cos\theta\) by a cubic spline and projected on \(P_n\) with 64 Gauss–Legendre nodes, \(f_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{2}\int(\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)P_n\thinspace dx\). Each \(f_n(r)\) is then fitted by least squares with a Chebyshev series:

  • by default (diff_rot_window = None with ricb > 0), on the table radii within 0.01 of the shell, of degree min(diff_rot_rdeg, half the number of radii);
  • with diff_rot_window = 'sun' (the default at ricb = 0), once over the whole Sun, of degree diff_rot_sun_deg, even in \(r\): the data are mirrored to \(-r\), continued below the first table radius by its value, and the odd coefficients are set to zero.

The fit residuals and, for the shell fit, the truncation error of the expansion up to diff_rot_nmax are printed in nHz.

docs.title: 5.2 Derivatives and the full sphere
docs.text:
The operators need \(f_n\), \(r f_n'\) and \(r^2 f_n''\) on the Chebyshev nodes. diff_rot.fX transforms the shape to \(N\) Chebyshev coefficients on the radial domain (utils.chebco_f, coefficients below \(10^{-14}\) of the largest dropped; cached per degree), evaluates the series or its derivatives (utils.funcheb) and multiplies by diff_rot_ampl and \(a_n\). So \(f'\) and \(f''\) are always consistent with the resolved \(f\), also for tabulated, step-like or 'user' profiles.

With ricb = 0 the radial coordinate is \(r \in [-1, 1]\) and each operator keeps only one parity of Chebyshev polynomials (§6.3). The shapes are therefore evaluated at \(\lvert r\rvert\), which makes \(f_n\) even, \(f_n'\) odd, and \(rf_n'\), \(r^2f_n''\) even. A shape with a kink at \(r = 0\) ('Y20-wall-bounded', 'shellular' unless \(p\) is even and positive, or a 'user' expression such as r) then converges slowly in \(N\); submatrices.py prints a WARNING for the predefined ones.

docs.title: 5.3 Profile codes
docs.text:
Each profile used in an operator has a three-letter code: two letters and the degree character diff_rot.DIGITS[n] (0–9, then a–z for 10–35):

code profile function (diff_rot.profile_functions) zf0, zf2, … \(f_n\) (zonal flow) fX(n, r, Dorder) zd0, zd2, … \(r f_n'\) Chebyshev fit of \(r\thinspace\)fX(n, r, 1) zs0, zs2, … \(r^2 f_n''\) Chebyshev fit of \(r^2\thinspace\)fX(n, r, 2) tw2, tw4, … \(p_0\sigma_n\) Chebyshev fit of \(p_0\thinspace\)sigmaX(n, r, 0) tp2, tp4, … \(p_0\sigma_n'\) (odd in \(r\), in utils.odd_profiles) Chebyshev fit of \(p_0\thinspace\)sigmaX(n, r, 1)

They are not in radial_profiles.proffdir until burrito first meets one and adds diff_rot.profile_functions(). With adiab_tw (ThermaD = 0 with the thermal wind) the tw, tp profiles are \(\sigma_n\), \(\sigma_n'\) without \(p_0\) (diff_rot._ptw), because those heat rows are divided by \(p_0\) (§7.2). A separate tp code is needed: a label such as h1tw21_D0 would mean \(r(p_0\sigma_2)'P\), the derivative of the product, not \(r p_0\sigma_2' P\).

docs.title: 5.4 The thermal-wind coefficients \(\sigma_n\)
docs.text:
diff_rot.sigma_coefficients(r) solves (2.9) in Legendre space at all the radii at once, with the \(m = 0\) matrices of angular.py (the Schmidt harmonics of order 0 are the Legendre polynomials):

  • the Legendre coefficients of \(\Delta\Omega\) and \(\partial_r\Delta\Omega\) are the \(f_n\) and \(f_n'\) (fX); a product of two series is \(\sum_n f_n\thinspace P_n(X)\) applied to the other one, so \(F = 2\Delta\Omega + \Delta\Omega^2\) and \(\partial_r F = 2(1 + \Delta\Omega)\partial_r\Delta\Omega\) (thermal_wind = 2), or \(2\Delta\Omega\), \(2\partial_r\Delta\Omega\) (1);
  • multiplication by \(x\) is \(X\) and \((1 - x^2)\thinspace d/dx\) is \(D\), so the bracket of (2.9) is \(X\thinspace\partial_rF + DF/r\), and \((1 - x^2)\thinspace\partial_x S_{tw} = -\tfrac{r^2G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g}(I - X^2)(X\partial_rF + DF/r)\);
  • that is \(D\sigma\), which is solved for \(\sigma\) (with \(\sigma_0 = 0\), the \(l = 0\) part belonging to \(S_0\)) by forward substitution of \(h_k = (k+2)q_{k+1}\sigma_{k+1} - (k-1)p_{k-1}\sigma_{k-1}\) (_solve_D).

This is exact (no quadrature), for any degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\), and matches the closed forms (2.10) to \(2\times 10^{-16}\) of the natural scale \(r^2G^2\lvert\partial\Delta\Omega\rvert/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\) (§9). The result is multiplied by thermal_wind_amplitude; thermal_wind = 3 gives \(\sigma_2 = -\tfrac23\)dSdtheta. sigmaX differentiates the Chebyshev series of \(\sigma_n(r)\) for \(\sigma_n'\). At ricb = 0, \(\sigma_n\) is even (\(f\) even, \(f'\) and \(g\) odd) and \(\sigma_n'\) odd, hence tp in odd_profiles.

docs.title: 6.1 Label grammar
docs.text:
A label names one radial operator: sX[fu1D1][fu2D2]_DY (utils.decode_label).

  • s: the section, u, v or h.
  • X: lowers the row's power of \(r\): the operator carries \(r^{p - X}\), with \(p\) = rpower_u (5) in u, rpower_v (3) in v, and 2 in h (1 when ThermaD = 0 without adiab_tw). Sections u and v also carry \(\rho_0\) to the power rhopower_u, rhopower_v (1 by default), section h no \(\rho_0\).
  • fu1D1, fu2D2: up to two profiles (§5.3) and their derivative orders. lho1, lho2 are \(h'\) and \(h''\).
  • _DY: the radial derivative order applied to the unknown.

For example, with the defaults, u2zd20lho1_D0 is \(r^3\rho_0\thinspace (r f_2')\thinspace h'\) acting on \(P\), and h1tw20lho1_D0 is \(r\thinspace p_0\sigma_2\thinspace h'\) acting on \(P\). rap.burrito evaluates \(r^{\rm rpower}\rho_0^{\rm rhopower} f_1 f_2\) on the Chebyshev nodes, utils.chebco_f transforms it, and utils.Mlam builds the multiplication matrix in the Gegenbauer basis \(C^{(\lambda)}\) of the section; submatrices.py then multiplies on the right by the derivative matrix and changes the basis: u is \(C^{(4)}\), v \(C^{(2)}\), h \(C^{(2)}\) (\(C^{(0)}\) if ThermaD = 0, \(C^{(1)}\) with adiab_tw). The diff-rot labels need at most \(P''\) in u, \(P'\) in v and \(P'\) in h, so they fit those bases. An operator that several terms share is computed only once.

docs.title: 6.2 The labels
docs.text:
diff_rot.labels() lists every radial operator of the terms, and submatrices.py adds them with the vector parity of their column (vP for \(P\) and \(s\), vT for \(T\)), after diff_rot.check():

  • for each degree \(n\) of \(\Delta\Omega\), the 18 momentum labels of the table of §3.4 (diff_rot.MOMENTUM with the codes of \(n\));
  • with thermal = 1 (_heat_labels): (a) h0pss0zf{n}0_D0 (\(r^2 p_0 f_n\); h0zf{n}0_D0 without pss if ThermaD = 0) for each degree of \(\Delta\Omega\); and for each degree \(n\) of \(S_{tw}\): (b) h1tp{n}0_D0 (\(r p_0\sigma_n'\), only if thermal_wind_radial = 1), (c) h2tw{n}0_D0, h1tw{n}0_D1, h1tw{n}0lho1_D0 (\(p_0\sigma_n\) times \(P\), \(rP'\), \(rh'P\)), (c′) h1tw{n}0_D0 (\(r p_0\sigma_n\) acting on \(T\), parity vT).

Like every other operator, each diff-rot matrix has its last chop rows dropped and that many zero rows added at the top, to make room for the boundary-condition rows of its row block, so the boundary conditions are unchanged by the differential rotation.

docs.title: 6.3 Parity in a full sphere
docs.text: At ricb = 0 the vector parity of the unknowns is \(v_P = (-1)^m\)symm for \(P\) and \(s\), and \(v_T = -v_P\) for \(T\). An operator has the parity \((-1)^{\text{rpower} + \text{dorder}_ 1 + \text{dorder}_ 2 + \text{DY} + \text{adj}}\), with adj = 1 for a first profile in utils.odd_profiles. utils.remroco keeps the rows of parity \(v\times\)(operator parity) and the columns of parity \(v\). This is correct only if every profile has the parity assumed: \(f_n\), \(rf_n'\), \(r^2f_n''\), \(\sigma_n\) even, \(\sigma_n'\) odd, \(h^{(k)}\) of parity \((-1)^k\); §5.2 explains how the profiles are made so. If a profile's Chebyshev coefficients of the wrong parity exceed \(10^{-8}\) of the largest, submatrices.py prints a WARNING: that part of the profile is dropped.

docs.title: 7.1 Momentum: diff_rot.momentum_block
docs.text:
operators.differential_rotation(l, section, component, offdiag) calls diff_rot.momentum_block(l, section, component, offdiag, M) with M the operators' namespace, where the matrices of submatrices.npz are loaded under their labels. For the row degree l (= \(l'\)), the section ('u' or 'v'), the column type ('upol' for \(P\), 'utor' for \(T\)) and offdiag = \(l - l'\), it sums over the degrees \(n\) of \(\Delta\Omega\) that couple this Δl (§3.5): \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le\) max_dl(n, …) and the parity of Δl; for each, the coefficient momentum_coef(name, n, l, m, offdiag) times the matrix of each label of momentum_labels(n, …). The result is multiplied by Gaspard and divided by \(L'^3\). Since each stored coefficient carries a factor \(L'\), the block is

\[ \frac{G}{L'^3}\sum(L'\times\text{coefficient})\times(\text{radial operator}) = \mathrm{row}(\mathbf W) \quad\text{of (3.6)} . \]

The \(1/L'^3\) makes these rows consistent with all the other momentum operators (§3.2). It returns [matrix, offd], offd the column block offset (utils.dr_offd, §7.3), or [0, 0] if no degree couples this Δl.

momentum_coefficients(n, m) builds the coefficients once per \((n, m)\), for degrees up to lmax + n + 6 (building beyond lmax keeps the entries near lmax free of truncation errors), and stores them both as sparse matrices and by diagonal (angular.band, \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le n + 3\)), so that momentum_coef is an array lookup. The whole set takes milliseconds at lmax 1025.

docs.title: 7.2 Heat: diff_rot.heat_block
docs.text:
operators.thermal_diffrot calls diff_rot.heat_block(l, component, offdiag, M), which returns the section-h blocks of (3.9) times the row weight. With ThermaD > 0 the rows are \(r^2 p_0\times\)(eq)\(/L'^3\):

term component, \(\Delta l\) expression radial operator (a) 'temp', even, \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le n\) 1j*m*heat_coef('Pn')*M['h0pss0zf{n}0_D0'], times Gaspard \(i m G\thinspace r^2 p_0 f_n\thinspace s\) (b) 'upol', even, \(\le\) tw_nmax Ls*heat_coef('Pn')*M['h1tp{n}0_D0'] \(L_l\thinspace r p_0\sigma_n'\thinspace P\) (c) 'upol', even, \(\le\) tw_nmax heat_coef('dPnD')*(M['h2tw{n}0_D0'] + M['h1tw{n}0_D1'] + M['h1tw{n}0lho1_D0']) \(p_0\sigma_n(P + rP' + rh'P)\) (c′) 'utor', odd, \(<\) tw_nmax -1j*m*heat_coef('dPn')*M['h1tw{n}0_D0'] \(-i m\thinspace r p_0\sigma_n\thinspace T\)

with the sums over the degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\) for (a) and of \(S_{tw}\) for (b), (c), (c′). Ls is \(L_l\) of the source degree (from \(u_r = L_l P/r\)). The angular coefficients come from heat_coefficients(m): \(X\), \(D\) from angular.Algebra up to lmax + max(8, \(n_{hi}\) + 4), and \(P_n(X)\), \(P_n'(X)\), \(P_n'(X)D\) for every even \(n\) up to the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\) and \(S_{tw}\), stored by diagonal. The column offset is the index difference in utils.ell.

Sign. The block is \(-\text{out}/L'^3\). The section-h rows of \(A\) hold the right-hand side of the heat equation (\(B\) = +entropy, thermal_advection = \(-r p_0 S_0' u_r\)), so the left-hand-side terms (2.11) enter \(A\) with a minus sign. In the momentum rows it is the opposite: \(B\) = −inertia, so the left-hand-side term \(\mathbf W\) enters \(A\) with a plus sign, as the Coriolis force does.

Factors of \(G\). (a) carries Gaspard explicitly; (b), (c), (c′) carry \(G^2\) through \(\sigma_n\), except with thermal_wind = 3.

Without thermal diffusion. With ThermaD = 0 the heat rows are divided by \(p_0\), which is about \(10^{-7}\) near the surface of a solar model and spoils the conditioning otherwise.

  • With thermal_wind = 0 the rows are \(r\times\)(eq)\(/p_0\) in \(C^{(0)}\), and (a) is h0zf{n}0_D0 (\(r f_n s\)).
  • With thermal_wind ≥ 1 (adiab_tw), (b) and (c) do not fit there: the weight \(r\) leaves \(P/r\) in (c), and \(C^{(0)}\) cannot hold \(P'\). The rows are then \(r^2\times\)(eq)\(/p_0\) in \(C^{(1)}\) (decode_label, submatrices.py), with the same labels, the tw, tp profiles without \(p_0\) (§5.3), and still no thermal boundary rows.

docs.title: 7.3 Assembly: assemble.py
docs.text:
assemble.py loops over the row degrees of each MPI rank. The unknown vector is [\(P\) blocks][\(T\) blocks][\(s\) blocks], each of N1 Chebyshev coefficients, with nb blocks per type. For row block \(l'\) (row row, diagonal column col0) and each Δl of diff_rot.dl_range(section, component) whose source degree exists, it calls the operator and, unless it returned [0, 0], adds the block at column basecol + col0 + offd*N1:

rows column Δl (dl_range) u \(P\) (basecol = 0) \(-n_{\max}\) … \(n_{\max}\), step 2 u \(T\) (basecol = nb*N1) \(-n_{\max}-1\) … \(n_{\max}+1\), step 2 v \(P\) \(-n_{\max}-1\) … \(n_{\max}+1\), step 2 v \(T\) \(-n_{\max}\) … \(n_{\max}\), step 2 h \(s\) (basecol = 2*nb*N1), term (a) \(-n_{\max}\) … \(n_{\max}\), step 2 h \(P\), terms (b), (c) \(-n_{tw}\) … \(n_{tw}\), step 2 h \(T\), term (c′) \(1-n_{tw}\) … \(n_{tw}-1\), step 2

with \(n_{\max}\) the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\) and \(n_{tw}\) that of \(S_{tw}\). The momentum blocks are added with a plus sign to \(A\), whose momentum rows are Coriolis − viscous − buoyancy + diff rot; the heat blocks carry their sign already (§7.2). \(B\) is unchanged: the differential rotation has no time derivative. Forced runs (\(A - i\omega_f B\)) need no change either. \(A\) and \(B\) are then divided by \(\lVert A\rVert_F\) as usual.

The offset offd counts blocks, not degrees: the poloidal degrees of a symmetry class step by 2, so for a \(P\) (or \(s\)) column offd = \(\Delta l/2\); for a \(T\) column it is the index difference between the toroidal list and the poloidal one, which depends on the symmetry (utils.dr_offd).

docs.title: 8. Diagnostics
docs.text:
spin_doctor.py checks every solution against the energy, frequency and entropy budgets. With differential rotation, the terms couple different degrees, so a per-degree worker cannot evaluate them from its own degree alone. utils4pp.diff_rot_setup, called once per solution by utils4pp.diagnose, therefore:

  1. builds \(\mathbf u\) and \(\partial_r\mathbf u\) on the \((r_k, \cos heta)\) grid from the per-degree components (velocity), with lmax + 10 + max(\(n_{tw}\), \(n_{\max}\)) Gauss–Legendre nodes in \(\cos heta\). The harmonics \(Y_l\), \(\partial_ heta Y_l\) and \(Z_l\) come from angular.ylm_grid: the recurrence of \(X\) started at \(Y_m \propto \sin^m heta\), differentiated in \( heta\) for \(\partial_ heta Y_l\), and started at \(\sin^{m-1} heta\) for \(Y_l/\sin heta\), so that nothing is divided by \(\sin heta\). The recurrence is linear, so it is carried as a mantissa times a power of two per node: for large \(m\) the start \(\sin^{m-1} heta\) would underflow near the poles (from \(m \approx 330\) at \(l\) of a few thousand), and the mantissas are rescaled by \(2^{-600}\) when they grow past \(2^{600}\), which is exact. It is valid at any \(l\) and \(m\) (it matches exact rational values of \(P_l\) to \(\sim 10^{-13}\) up to \(l = 2000\), and keeps the norms to \(\sim 10^{-13}\) at \(m = 1425\), \(l = 3000\)), where scipy.special.sph_harm_y is NaN from \(l = 646\) on; utils.Ylm and utils.Ylm_full use it too;
  2. evaluates \(\Delta\Omega\), \(\partial_r\Delta\Omega\), \(\partial_r^2\Delta\Omega\), \(\partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\) there, as numpy Legendre series of the \(f_n\) (diff_rot.fX);
  3. forms the force \(\mathbf F = -\mathbf W\) of (2.6) and its radial derivative (the force closure), and projects them back on \((q, s, t)\) with (3.4): drforce[l];
  4. with thermal = 1, forms \(p_0[i m G\Delta\Omega s + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw}]\) and projects it on \(Y_l\): drheat[l].

Only the profiles \(f_n\) come from diff_rot.py; the angular part here is independent of its algebra. The \(\sigma_n\) used here are computed by utils4pp.thermal_wind_entropy, which integrates (2.9) in \(x\) with numpy Legendre series at each radius and writes out its \(r\) derivative, not with diff_rot.sigma_coefficients. So the budgets test the assembled operators against a second implementation of the same equations.

The per-degree workers then add:

  • flow_worker: Wdr = \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0\mathbf u^\ast\cdot\mathbf F hinspace dV\), Wdr_im its imaginary part, and Ensdr the enstrophy term \(( abla imes\mathbf u)\cdot( abla imes\mathbf F)\);
  • thermal_worker: Wdr_thm = \(-2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int p_0 s^\ast[i m G\Delta\Omega s + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw}] hinspace dV\).

spin_doctor includes them in the residuals:

\[ egin{aligned} ext{resid}\sigma &: \quad 2\sigma hinspace KE - D_{kin} - W_{thm} - W_{dr} = 0,\cr ext{resid}\omega &: \quad 2\omega hinspace KE + W_{cor,im} - D_{kin,im} - W_{thm,im} - W_{dr,im} = 0,\cr ext{resid}s &: \quad 2\sigma hinspace TE - D_{thm} - W_{adv} - W_{dr,thm} = 0 , \end{aligned} \]

and the enstrophy residual includes Ensdr. By §2.3, only the shear part of \(\mathbf W\) contributes to Wdr; the Doppler and local-Coriolis parts appear in Wdr_im. The diff-rot options are written to params.dat (spin_doctor.param_table: diff_rot_ampl, the \(a_n\), diff_rot_param, and diff_rot_type as its index in diff_rot.TYPES, with a 'user' run's profile definitions at the end of the row after #), and Wdr, Wdr_im, Ensdr, Wdr_thm to flow.dat and thermal.dat.

docs.title: 9. Tests
docs.text:
These scripts test the implementation against itself and against exact results; the comparisons with published calculations are on the page Benchmarks.

  • bin/ru_insane.py, run after submatrices.py (no MPI, seconds; needs N ≥ 96). It packs the diff-rot blocks as assemble.py does and pairs them with random smooth fields, comparing each part against a direct \((r, \cos\theta)\) quadrature of \(\int\rho_0\mathbf x^\ast\cdot\mathbf W(\mathbf y)\thinspace dV\) and of the heat terms. It also checks that term (a) is anti-Hermitian and, for 'rigid', the block identities of §3.6. A 1 % error in one coefficient of one \(\Delta l\) shows up at \(10^{-4}\) to 1. Its grid uses only the profiles of diff_rot.py.
  • tests/diff_rot/angular_check.py (standalone; --quick takes seconds): the harmonics of angular.ylm_grid against exact values, \(X\) and \(D\) and their adjoints, every vector operation of §3.3 against grid projections, and the primitives against the quadrature builder quad_reference.py.
  • tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py [mmax [nmax [lmax]]]: the couplings of diff_rot.py against the closed forms of §3.6, the selection rules of §3.5, and the \(\sigma_n\) against (2.10).
  • tests/diff_rot/regress.sh OLD_KORE: \(A\) and \(B\) against another checkout of kore, on 15 configurations.
  • tests/heat_dr/run_all.sh: the heat-equation terms: the closed forms (2.10) against (2.9), the heat operators against a grid quadrature, the rigid offset (2.12) with the heat equation, budgets built from the matrix rows, and the assembly on 1 to 4 ranks.
  • spin_doctor residuals (§8), for every run: they close to round-off for a resolved mode, and they are the check of resolution in N and lmax.

docs.title: 10. Limitations
docs.text:
• The profiles do not depend on the background model, except that solar_x takes \(x = r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure (background.md).
  • The degree character of the profile codes limits the degrees to 35: \(n_{\max} \le 16\) with thermal_wind = 2 (\(S_{tw}\) up to \(2n_{\max} + 2 = 34\)), \(n_{\max} \le 32\) with thermal_wind = 1; diff_rot.check stops otherwise.
  • 'user' expressions are evaluated with Python's eval in a namespace without builtins: enough to stop accidents, not a sandbox for untrusted input.
  • The inviscid formulation (ViscosD = 0, rows times \(\rho_0^2\)) builds the same labels with different weights, but it has not been validated with differential rotation, and ru_insane.py does not cover it.
  • With thermal_wind = 1 the eigenvalues depend on the choice of frame at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\); thermal_wind = 2 is frame independent.
  • The \(p_b S_0'\) term of the thermal wind is omitted (§1.4); it matters where \(S_0' \neq 0\), e.g. in a radiative interior (stratification 'solar_rz').
  • With ThermaD = 0 and the thermal wind, small-scale growing modes peaking at \(l \approx\) lmax can appear that do not converge in lmax (ThermaD = 0).
  • The matrices widen with the highest degree: the momentum rows couple \(n_{\max} + 1\) degrees on each side, the heat rows \(n_{tw}\) = \(2n_{\max} + 2\) with thermal_wind = 2. 'tabulated' with a large diff_rot_nmax is the most expensive case. Sharp profiles (the 'solar' tachocline at ricb = 0) need large N (about 400).

docs.title: Drag at the outer wall equations
docs.text: This page gives the condition of a drag at a stress-free outer wall (Drag at the outer wall), the drag of the topography, how the condition enters the rows of the wall, and the power and damping rate that spin_doctor reports. They are those of the conductive_IC branch (its topo.py, the drag rows of its assemble.py and utils4pp.cmb_slip_K), written for any density and viscosity profile in bin/topo.py.

docs.title: The condition
docs.text:
The wall pulls on the fluid along it with a stress in proportion to the slip, the flow along the wall relative to the mantle. The tangential viscous stress of the fluid at the outer wall (\(u_r = 0\) there) then meets

\[ ho_0\, u\,\mathrm{ViscosD}\;r\,\partial_r\!\left( rac{\mathbf u_t}{r} ight) = -\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\; ho_w\,\mathsf K\,(\mathbf u_t - \mathbf v_m) \qquad (r = 1), \]

with \(\mathsf K\) the drag coefficient in units of \( ho_w\Omega r_0\) (\( ho_w\) the fluid's density at the wall), \( u\) the viscosity profile of the structure, and \(\mathbf v_m = \omega_M\,\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r\) the velocity of the mantle (rotdyn = 1, 0 otherwise). \(\mathsf K = 0\) is the stress-free wall and \(\mathsf K o\infty\) the no-slip one. \( ho_0 = ho_w\) cancels, and the condition is

\[ r\,\partial_r\!\left( rac{\mathbf u_t}{r} ight) + q\,\mathsf K\,(\mathbf u_t - \mathbf v_m) = 0, \qquad q = rac{\mathrm{Gaspard}}{\mathrm{ViscosD}\, u(1)} . \]

kappa_cmb is \(\mathsf K\) times the unit tensor. For a dimensional drag of stress \(\kappa\,\mathbf u_t\), kappa_cmb \(= \kappa/( ho_w\Omega r_0)\).

docs.title: The drag of the topography
docs.text:
A flow of amplitudes \(U_x\) (zonal) and \(U_y\) (meridional) and frequency \(\omega_0\) along a topography of spectrum \(S(k)\) radiates internal waves of mean power per unit area

\[ P = \frac{\rho\,I_k}{2\lvert\omega_0\rvert}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(U_x^2\cos^2\alpha + U_y^2\sin^2\alpha\right) g\;d\alpha, \qquad g = \sqrt{\max\left[0,\ (\omega_0^2 - N^2)(f^2 - \omega_0^2) + \omega_0^2\,\tilde f^2\sin^2\alpha\right]}, \] \[ f = 2\Omega\cos\theta, \qquad \tilde f = 2\Omega\sin\theta, \qquad I_k = \int_0^\infty S\,k^2\,dk = \frac{h_\text{rms}^2\,k_0\,\Gamma(H - 1/2)}{4\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(H)}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda_0}, \]

with \(\alpha\) the direction of a wave vector of the topography from east, \(\theta\) the colatitude and \(N\) the buoyancy frequency at the wall (Rekier et al. 2025, eqs. B1 and B2). Their eq. (B1) as printed (version 4 of the preprint) lacks a factor \(4\pi^2\), lost between their eqs. (A19) and (10); with it, a sinusoidal ridge gives the classical \(\rho U^2h^2k\sqrt{N^2 - \omega^2}/4\) of Bell (1975), and kore keeps it. The power has no term that mixes the zonal and the meridional flow, so the linear drag of the same mean power is a diagonal tensor on \((u_\theta, u_\phi)\), in units of \(\rho\Omega r_0\):

\[ \mathsf K_{\theta\theta} = \frac{I_k/r_0}{\lvert\omega_0/\Omega\rvert}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\alpha\,\frac{g}{\Omega^2}\,d\alpha, \qquad \mathsf K_{\phi\phi} = \frac{I_k/r_0}{\lvert\omega_0/\Omega\rvert}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\alpha\,\frac{g}{\Omega^2}\,d\alpha . \]

The inputs are topo_hrms \(= h_\text{rms}/r_0\), topo_lambda0 \(= \lambda_0/r_0\) and topo_H \(= H\), with \(N/\Omega\) from the stratification, \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Beyonce}\;g\,dS/dr}/\mathrm{Gaspard}\) at the wall (0 without buoyancy or where it is unstable), or topo_N, and \(\omega_0/\Omega\) = topo_omega, or \(\lvert\)itau\(\rvert\)/Gaspard (eigenvalue problems), or \(\lvert\)forcing_frequency\(\rvert\)/Gaspard (forced runs). The integral over \(\alpha\) is a midpoint rule of 2048 points (topo.kappa). Where \(g\) vanishes for every \(\alpha\) no wave can be radiated and the drag vanishes: near the poles when \(N\) exceeds \(\omega_0\).

docs.title: The rows
docs.text:
At the wall a degree \(l\) of the flow slips along it as

\[ \mathbf u_t = s_l\, abla_1 Y_l + t_l\, abla_1 Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r}, \qquad s_l = P_l' + rac{P_l}{r} + (\ln ho_0)'P_l, \qquad t_l = T_l , \]

with \( abla_1\) the gradient on the unit sphere (Numerical method). The stress-free rows of assemble.bc_u_spherical are \(r^2\) (section u, the second row of the outer wall) and \(r\) (section v, its first row) times the parts of \(r\,\partial_r(\mathbf u_t/r)\) on \( abla_1 Y_l\) and on \( abla_1 Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r}\). The drag adds the same parts of \(q\,\mathsf K\,\mathbf u_t\), which couple the degree \(l\) to \(s\) and \(t\) of every degree \(l'\):

\[ ( ext{row } exttt u)_l + r^2 q\sum_{l'}\left(A_{ss}^{ll'}s_{l'} + A_{st}^{ll'}t_{l'} ight) = 0, \qquad ( ext{row } exttt v)_l + r\,q\sum_{l'}\left(A_{ts}^{ll'}s_{l'} + A_{tt}^{ll'}t_{l'} ight) = 0, \] \[ A_{xy}^{ll'} = rac{\oint x_l^*\cdot\mathsf K\,y_{l'}\,dS}{\oint\lvert x_l vert^2dS}, \qquad x, y \in \{\,s: abla_1 Y,\ \ t: abla_1 Y imes\hat{\mathbf r}\,\} , \]

on the unit sphere (topo.couplings, topo.rows). A constant drag gives $A_{ss} = A_{tt} = $ kappa_cmb and no coupling between degrees. The drag of the topography is even about the equator, so it couples degrees of the same symmetry: \(l\) to \(l\pm2, \dots\) within \(P\) and within \(T\), and for \(m eq 0\) \(P_l\) to \(T_{l\pm1}, \dots\). The integrals are Gauss–Legendre quadratures in \(\cos heta\) with \(\max(4(l_ ext{max} + 2), 2000)\) nodes, many since \(\mathsf K\) has kinks where \(g\) starts to vanish. With the rotating mantle the toroidal flow of degree 1 slips by \(T_1 - r\,\omega_M\), which gives the rows a column of \(\omega_M\) (Rotating solids equations).

docs.title: Power and damping rate
docs.text:
spin_doctor computes the power the drag dissipates from the flow at the wall (topo.dissipation),

\[ D_ ext{topo} = 2\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\; ho_w\oint(\mathbf u_t - \mathbf v_m)^*\cdot\mathsf K\,(\mathbf u_t - \mathbf v_m)\,dS , \]

in the units of its energies (the integral of \( ho_0\lvert\mathbf u vert^2\) of the complex amplitude, whose rate of change is \(2\sigma\) times it), and the damping rate it implies, \(\delta\sigma_ ext{topo} = -D_ ext{topo}/(2E)\), with \(E\) the energy of the mode: the kinetic energy, plus Hendrik times the magnetic energy inside and outside the fluid and that stored in the conducting walls, plus the energy of the rotating solids. With a stress-free wall and no drag, both use \(\mathsf K = 1\): per unit kappa_cmb.

The power through the wall. The viscous stress at the wall works on the fluid at the rate \(W_ u\) (flow.dat column 25), and on the mantle at the rate \(2\,\mathrm{Re}(\omega_M^*\Gamma^ u_M)\) of its viscous torque. The condition above makes their sum minus the drag's dissipation:

\[ D_ ext{topo} = -W_ u - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\left(\omega_M^*\,\Gamma^ u_M ight) . \]

Where the background field also ends in a current sheet at the wall, its push joins the drag in the condition (Magnetic field equations), and \(W_ u\) holds the push's power too, which then adds to the right-hand side. So the budgets need no new term: residσ and resid𝐄 already count the power of the stress at the walls, and the energy budget of the rotating solids the power of their torques. \(\delta\sigma_ ext{topo}\) is the drag's share of the damping rate, one term of that budget.

docs.title: Checks (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
tests/drag/drag_check.py (run_all.sh, about 2 min on 2 ranks):

  • Against conductive_IC (2d84351), eleven runs: a constant drag on the spin-over mode in a shell and in a full sphere; the drag of the topography on the spin-over mode, on an \(m = 2\) mode and in a full sphere; the rotating solids with a stress-free outer wall without a drag, with each drag, with thin conducting layers and a dipole, and with a conducting inner core, a resolved mantle and a field of degree 2; the drag of the topography with a thin layer and a dipole. Eigenvalues to \(6\cdot10^{-14}\), and the rotation of the solids and the torques on the mantle in rotdyn.dat to \(3\cdot10^{-10}\), its precision.
  • Conservation with 'Wu 2005' (r_out 0.9, N 64) and the rotating solids: every mode but \(\lambda = 0\) carries no total angular momentum (\(2\cdot10^{-9}\)) and closes resid𝐋 (\(10^{-9}\)); with kappa_cmb the energy budget of the fluid and the solids closes (\(10^{-10}\)), with the drag of the topography, a dipole, a conducting inner core and a resolved mantle resid𝐄 does (\(10^{-10}\)).
  • Equivalences. A constant tensor given to the drag of the topography (the test hook topo_K) gives the eigenvalues of kappa_cmb (\(2\cdot10^{-14}\)). A rigid differential rotation \(a = 0.3\) with kappa_cmb gives the eigenvalues of a frame turning \(1 + a\) times faster with kappa_cmb\(/(1 + a)\), shifted by \(-i\,m\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\,a\) (\(2\cdot10^{-16}\)): the drag acts on the slip relative to the mantle, in units of the frame's rotation rate.
  • Limits. kappa_cmb = \(10^8\) gives the eigenvalues of a no-slip wall (\(7\cdot10^{-12}\); with the rotating solids \(10^{-10}\), and their rotdyn.dat). A weak drag (kappa_cmb = \(10^{-6}\)) dissipates kappa_cmb times the Dtopo/κ of the stress-free run (\(6\cdot10^{-5}\); with the rotating solids \(2\cdot10^{-5}\)), and with the mantle at rest changes the damping rate of the spin-over mode by kappa_cmb times its δσtopo/κ (\(5\cdot10^{-4}\)). With the rotating solids the change is 0.49 times it for their axial mode: the drag turns the mantle, which changes the other losses at the same order.
  • Frequencies. \(N/\Omega\) and \(\omega_0/\Omega\) in params.dat: topo_N and topo_omega when set, \(\sqrt{10}\) for the stratification 'linear' with Beyonce 10, \(\lvert\)itau\(\rvert\) and the forcing frequency otherwise (\(10^{-9}\)). The same run with a time unit twice as long (Gaspard 2, Beyonce 40, ViscosD, ThermaD and itau doubled) has its eigenvalues doubled (\(10^{-15}\)).
  • The power through the wall closes in every run with a drag but the stiff ones (whose slip is round-off), to \(2\cdot10^{-9}\), and in a forced run (forcing 6) to the printed digits.
  • Stops of background.check_drag.

Also checked once:

  • Calibration. At Ek \(10^{-4}\) (N 64) the Earth's topography (topo_hrms 4.35e-4, topo_lambda0 0.431, topo_H 0.8, \(N = 0\)) adds to the damping of the spin-over mode (\(\omega_0/\Omega\) = 0.995) \(-2.3100\cdot10^{-5}\), and kappa_cmb = 4.5e-6 adds \(-2.3038\cdot10^{-5}\).
  • Weak and strong drag (the spin-over mode, Ek \(10^{-3}\), \(\sqrt{E} = 0.032\)). The change of the damping rate over kappa_cmb times δσtopo/κ is 0.97 at kappa_cmb = \(10^{-3}\), 0.76 at \(10^{-2}\) and 0.47 at \(3\cdot10^{-2}\); the share of the no-slip wall's added damping is 0.72 at \(3\cdot10^{-2}\), 0.94 at 0.1 and 0.998 at 1. With kappa_cmb = \(10^{-4}\) the added damping is \(-5.042\cdot10^{-4}\) at Ek \(10^{-3}\) and \(-5.063\cdot10^{-4}\) at \(10^{-4}\).
  • Quadrature. For the spin-over test (\(\omega_0/\Omega\) = 0.98, \(N/\Omega\) = 0.5) the couplings change by \(6\cdot10^{-7}\) of the largest from 2000 to 16000 nodes, the error of the kinks. The nodes are those of conductive_IC (computed by scipy.special.roots_legendre instead of numpy's leggauss, ten times faster; the couplings agree to \(5\cdot10^{-12}\)).
  • Other forcings. The random Reynolds stress (forcing 11) with kappa_cmb and with the drag of the topography, and the entropy at the inner wall (forcing 13) with kappa_cmb: Dtopo is minus the power of the stress at the wall, to the printed digits.
  • Operators. The drag and the rotating solids change only rows of assemble.py: submatrices.npz is bitwise the same with and without them, so their parameters are not stored in it.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Rekier, J., Triana, S. A., Barik, A., Abdulah, A. & Kang, S. 2025, arXiv:2507.01671 (eqs. 20, 21, B1 and B2).

docs.title: Drag at the outer wall
docs.text:
A stress-free outer wall lets the fluid slip along it freely, and a no-slip wall holds it. A drag lies between the two: the wall pulls back on the slipping fluid in proportion to the slip, and so damps the flow without a viscous layer. kore has two drags, as the conductive_IC branch: a constant drag coefficient, and the drag of the wall's topography, which depends on latitude and on the direction of the flow (Rekier et al. 2025). Either one changes the condition of a stress-free outer wall:

par.bco = 0
par.kappa_cmb = 4.5e-6
setting default meaning kappa_cmb 0.0 the constant drag coefficient, in units of the fluid's density at the wall times the rotation rate times the outer radius; 0: no drag topo_drag None 'rekier': the drag of the topography, instead of kappa_cmb topo_hrms 0.0 the rms height of the topography, over the outer radius topo_lambda0 0.431 the wavelength below which the spectrum of the topography falls off, over the outer radius topo_H 0.8 the Hurst exponent of the topography, which sets how fast its spectrum falls off (above 1/2) topo_N None the buoyancy frequency at the wall, over the rotation rate; None: that of the stratification topo_omega None the frequency of the flow relative to the mantle, over the rotation rate; None: from the run

docs.title: Constant drag: kappa_cmb
docs.text:
kappa_cmb sets a drag that is the same everywhere on the wall and in every direction: the wall pulls on the fluid with a stress of kappa_cmb times the slip, in the units above. The slip is the flow along the wall relative to the mantle, which is at rest, or turns with the rotating solids (Rotating solids).

For the Earth's core-mantle boundary, Rekier et al. (2025) give a drag coefficient of 11.3 kg m⁻² s⁻¹ at the diurnal frequency: kappa_cmb = 4.5e-6, with a density of 9.9e3 kg m⁻³ at the wall, the Earth's rotation rate and a radius of 3480 km.

docs.title: Drag of the topography: topo_drag = 'rekier'
docs.text:
A flow along a wall with topography radiates internal waves into a rotating or stratified fluid, and the waves carry momentum away from the flow. The drag this exerts depends on the latitude, through the Coriolis force, on the direction of the flow, zonal or meridional, on its frequency, and on the buoyancy frequency at the wall. topo_drag = 'rekier' uses the drag that Rekier et al. (2025) derive for a topography with a power-law spectrum, described by its rms height, the wavelength where the spectrum rolls off, and its Hurst exponent. The Earth's core-mantle boundary (an rms height of 1.51 km, a roll-off at 1500 km and a Hurst exponent of 0.8, at a radius of 3480 km):

par.bco = 0
par.topo_drag = 'rekier'
par.topo_hrms = 4.35e-4
par.topo_lambda0 = 0.431
par.topo_H = 0.8

Without buoyancy these values damp the spin-over mode as kappa_cmb = 4.5e-6 does, to 0.3 %.

  • The buoyancy frequency at the wall is that of the stratification (thermal = 1), or 0 without buoyancy or where the stratification is unstable. topo_N sets it instead.
  • The frequency of the flow. The drag depends on the frequency of the flow relative to the mantle, which an eigenvalue problem does not know in advance: kore takes the frequency of the solver's target (itau), or the forcing frequency in a forced run, unless topo_omega sets it. For a mode found away from the target, set itau to its frequency and solve again, until the two agree. The run stops if this frequency is 0.
  • Coupled degrees. The drag varies with latitude, so the wall couples each degree of the flow to the others of the same symmetry, and for m other than 0 the poloidal flow to the toroidal one. Check the convergence in lmax as usual.

The formulas: Drag at the outer wall equations.

docs.title: Weak and strong drag
docs.text: kore applies the drag at a stress-free wall, where the fluid slips. As long as kappa_cmb is small against the square root of the Ekman number (ViscosD/Gaspard), the fluid slips nearly freely, and the drag adds a damping of its own that does not depend on the Ekman number: the regime of a drag on the flow outside the thin viscous layer of a real wall, the one to run in. As kappa_cmb approaches the square root of the Ekman number, the drag holds the fluid at the wall, a viscous layer forms, and the wall acts more and more as a no-slip wall. The Earth's 4.5e-6 is a weak drag down to an Ekman number of about 1e-8. The same holds for each direction of the drag of the topography.

docs.title: With the rotating solids
docs.text: With rotdyn = 1 the outer wall may be stress-free, with or without a drag. The drag then acts on the slip relative to the turning mantle, and pulls the mantle in return: its torque is the viscous torque on the mantle in rotdyn.dat. Without a drag the mantle feels only the magnetic torque and gravity. A fluid slipping along a conducting outer wall (a thin conducting layer or a resolved mantle, Magnetic field) induces its field through the slip relative to the turning mantle too.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
spin_doctor prints two columns for a viscous run with a stress-free outer wall (not with centrifugal = 1):

  • Dtopo, the power the drag dissipates, in the units of the energies;
  • δσtopo, minus Dtopo over twice the energy of the mode (its kinetic energy, its magnetic energy inside and outside the fluid, and the energy of the rotating solids): the drag's share of the damping rate.

Without a drag both are per unit kappa_cmb (the columns Dtopo/κ and δσtopo/κ): the drag a constant kappa_cmb of 1 would exert on the free slip. For a weak drag this estimates the damping it would add, without a run: with the mantle at rest, kappa_cmb times δσtopo/κ is the change of the damping rate of the spin-over mode to 5e-4 of it (Ek 1e-3). A drag also changes the flow, and with it the other losses: with the rotating solids it turns the mantle too, and the damping rate of a mode of the solids changed by about half of the estimate. Run with the drag for its effect.

flow.dat has both (columns 40–41), and params.dat the settings, with the buoyancy frequency and the frequency of the flow that the drag of the topography used (columns 135–141, Output files).

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
Supported: any structure (the density and the viscosity at the wall enter); a full sphere; any m; with or without buoyancy; with or without a field, with any magnetic walls; the rotating solids; a constant drag with a differential rotation; eigenvalue problems, and the forced runs whose outer wall does not move (forcings 6, 11 and 13).

Not supported (the run stops at startup):

  • a drag without the flow (hydro = 0), without viscosity (ViscosD = 0), or at an outer wall that is not stress-free (bco other than 0);
  • Gaspard = 0, centrifugal = 1, or forcings 9 and 10, which move the outer wall;
  • kappa_cmb and topo_drag together;
  • the drag of the topography with a differential rotation, with a frequency of the flow of 0, or in a frequency scan of forcing 11 (rsf_frequencies) without topo_omega, since it is built for one frequency;
  • kappa_cmb negative or not finite, topo_drag other than None and 'rekier', topo_hrms or topo_lambda0 not positive, topo_H not above 1/2, topo_N or topo_omega negative.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Rekier, J., Triana, S. A., Barik, A., Abdulah, A. & Kang, S. 2025, arXiv:2507.01671 (the drag of the topography, their eqs. 20, 21, B1 and B2).

docs.title: Convective forcing
docs.text: The inertial modes of the Sun are observed with finite amplitudes because the convection keeps exciting them while it also damps them. Forcing 11 adds this excitation to kore's linear equations as a random body force: the fluctuating part of the Reynolds stress of the convective eddies. Its strength is tied to kore's viscosity, which in a convection zone stands for the same eddies, so that a mode receives from the eddies the energy that their viscosity takes away. kore returns the power spectrum of the kinetic energy of the forced flow at the frequencies you choose, and from it the energy that each mode reaches. Where the force comes from and why its strength follows from the viscosity is explained on Reynolds-stress forcing. This page shows how to run it and how to read the result.

docs.title: What a run computes
docs.text:
The force is random, so a single solution means nothing: only its statistics do. For each forcing frequency \(w\), kore solves

\[ (A - i\thinspace w\thinspace B)\thinspace\mathbf x_j = \mathbf b_j, \qquad j = 1, \dots, K, \]

where \(A\) and \(B\) are the matrices of the eigenproblem (Numerical method) and the \(K\) = rsf_nsamp right-hand sides \(\mathbf b_j\) are independent realisations of the random force. The mean of the kinetic energies of the \(K\) solutions is the power spectral density of the kinetic energy at \(w\). It is an estimate, whose standard error goes as \(1/\sqrt K\). The matrix is factored once per frequency, and each realisation then costs only a back-substitution, so the cost of a run is set by the number of frequencies.

The flow goes as \(e^{iwt}\), so that \(w\) is the frequency \(-\omega\) of the Anelastic equations in kore's units: negative \(w\) is prograde, as for forcing_frequency. A mode of eigenvalue \(\lambda\) resonates at \(w = \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\). Near a damped mode that is well separated from the others, the spectrum is a Lorentzian centred there, with a half-width at half maximum of \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\), and the area under it is the kinetic energy of the mode.

docs.title: Example: a Rossby mode
docs.text: This example forces the sectoral Rossby mode \(l = m = 2\) of an incompressible fluid in a uniformly rotating spherical shell, and recovers its resonance. It takes less than a minute on four cores.

docs.title: 1. Write the parameter file
docs.text:
Make a run directory as in Getting started, and write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-5
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek

# Incompressible fluid in a uniformly rotating shell, stress-free walls
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.thermal = 0
par.ricb = 0.35
par.bci = 0
par.bco = 0

# m = 2; the sectoral Rossby mode is equatorially antisymmetric
par.m = 2
par.symm = -1

par.N = 96
par.lmax = 49
par.ncpus = 4

# Random Reynolds-stress forcing, 16 realisations
par.forcing = 11
par.forcing_frequency = 0.0
par.rsf_nsamp = 16
par.rsf_taper = 0.2               # the default, 0.04, needs N of about 256 here
par.petsc_opts['mat_mumps_icntl_14'] = 100

# Target of the eigenvalue solve of step 3
par.rtau = 0.0
par.itau = 0.667
par.nev = 4

The viscosity is uniform, so all of it counts as turbulent: the turbulent viscosity is \(\nu_t\) = ViscosD = \(10^{-5}\). The strength of the forcing is a turbulent temperature \(\Theta\), the energy of one eddy. With the default law, \(\Theta = 3\rho_0\nu_t^2\ell_c\), and with the default eddy size \(\ell_c = 0.25\) it is \(7.5\times10^{-11}\) here, in kore's units of energy. rsf_taper sets the width over which the force goes to zero at the walls. Keep forcing_frequency = 0: the scan of step 4 sets the frequencies, and \(A\) is then the matrix of the eigenproblem, which step 3 uses.

docs.title: 2. Build the matrices
docs.text:
./bin/submatrices.py 4
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/assemble.py > log_asm

assemble.py writes A.npz and B.npz, and the \(K\) right-hand sides as the columns of B_forced.npz. log_asm describes the forcing:

 Random Reynolds-stress forcing (forcing = 11): 16 realisation(s), seed 0
 20 noise centres on r = -0.1803 .. 1.4990, l_c = 0.25 .. 0.25, nu_t floor 0 ViscosD
 max Theta nu_t = 7.500e-16 at r = 1.000 (theta = nu, scale 1)
 Chebyshev tail of the rows (max over the last 10% / max): 3.5e-07

The last line checks that N resolves the force. Above \(10^{-6}\) it ends with "WARNING: under-resolved, raise N or l_c": then raise N, or widen the sharpest edge of the force (rsf_taper, or rsf_rcut_width below). With the default rsf_taper this line reads 0.13 at N = 96.

docs.title: 3. Find the mode
docs.text:
The eigenvalue problem can reuse the same matrices. In a subdirectory:

mkdir eig
cp -r bin eig/
ln -s $PWD/A.npz $PWD/B.npz eig/
echo "par.forcing = 0" >> eig/bin/parameters.py
cd eig
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve.py
./bin/spin_doctor.py 4
cd ..

The first eigenvalue is the Rossby mode, \(\lambda = -6.934\times10^{-5} + 0.66666674\thinspace i\), with residσ about \(10^{-12}\). Its frequency is close to the inviscid value \(\omega = -2/(m+1)\), retrograde.

docs.title: 4. Scan the frequencies
docs.text:
Add the frequencies to bin/parameters.py, 21 points over five half-widths on each side of the resonance:

import numpy as np
w0, s = 0.66666674, 6.93e-5       # Im λ and |Re λ| of the mode
par.rsf_frequencies = w0 + s*np.linspace(-5, 5, 21)

and solve:

mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve.py

solve.py prints one line per frequency as it goes, for example

w = 6.666667400e-01   mean KE 4.442305e-07 +- 1.1e-07   (0.7 s)

and appends the same numbers to rsf_spectrum.dat, and the kinetic energy of each realisation to rsf_ke.dat. A scan writes no fields.

docs.title: 5. Read the spectrum
docs.text:
rsf_spectrum.dat has one row per frequency: \(w\), the mean kinetic energy and its standard error.

# w  mean_KE  stderr   (forcing = 11, nsamp 16, seed 0, rsf_split None)
6.663202400000e-01 1.711741196503e-08 4.052316136428e-09
...
6.665974400000e-01 2.222626974507e-07 5.266390856613e-08
6.666320900000e-01 3.554873668819e-07 8.423321121690e-08
6.666667400000e-01 4.442304926635e-07 1.052621556910e-07
6.667013900000e-01 3.554458399913e-07 8.422364035422e-08
6.667360400000e-01 2.222297651836e-07 5.265642773220e-08
...

The peak is at \(w = \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\), and the spectrum falls to half the peak at \(w = \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda \pm \lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\): the Lorentzian of the mode. The energy of the mode is the height of the Lorentzian times \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert/2\), here \(4.44\times10^{-7}\times6.93\times10^{-5}/2 = 1.5\times10^{-11}\). In the limit of eddies much smaller than the mode and of a force that reaches the walls, the mode would reach \(\Theta\), since all of its damping is turbulent (Reynolds-stress forcing). The finite eddy size and the wide taper lower it here to a fifth of \(\Theta\).

The standard error is a quarter of the mean, as expected for 16 realisations. The spectrum is nevertheless smooth, because every frequency uses the same realisations: the shape of a spectrum is much better determined than its level.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• ViscosD > 0: the force is the partner of the viscous force.
  • In a full sphere (ricb = 0), N must be even, and rpower_u ≥ 5, rpower_v ≥ 3 (the defaults).
  • forcing_amplitude_cmb is not used: the power scales with rsf_scale instead.
  • The heat equation is not forced: the right-hand side is zero in its rows, also with thermal = 1.
  • With magnetic = 1 the perturbation of the field is solved with the flow, and a scan needs the inner core 'conducting, Chebys' rather than 'conducting, Bessel' (Magnetic field).

assemble.py stops with a message if one of the first two is not met.

docs.title: Where the force acts
docs.text:
The force follows the turbulent part of the viscosity, \( u_t\) = ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\), clipped at 0, with \(\hat u\) the viscosity profile of Background model and \( u_f\) the part that is not turbulent. By default \( u_f\) is visc0 for the diffusivities 'step' and 'solar_rz' when visc0 < 1, the viscosity of the radiative zone, and 0 otherwise. Where \( u_t = 0\) there is no force at all.

  • With a 'user' viscosity profile, set rsf_nu_floor to its radiative-zone value, or the radiative zone is forced too.
  • To keep the force out of the tail of a viscosity step, cut it below a radius with rsf_rcut. The force is zero below rsf_rcut and full above rsf_rcut + rsf_rcut_width, joined smoothly. Do not raise rsf_nu_floor for this: the clipped \( u_t\) then has a corner that the Chebyshev expansion cannot resolve.
  • The edges need radial resolution. In a full sphere, an edge near \(r = 0.7\) of width 0.04 needs N of about 1280, and one of width 0.08 about 900. The tail line of log_asm tells you when an edge is under-resolved.
  • The force goes to zero over rsf_taper below the outer wall and above an inner core, and over rsf_taper_in above \(r = 0\) in a full sphere, so that it needs no traction at the walls.
  • rsf_split = a radius adds the kinetic energy below that radius to the output, for example the energy in a radiative zone.

docs.title: Strength of the force
docs.text:
The variance of the force is proportional to \(\Theta u_t\). rsf_theta sets the law for \(\Theta\):

rsf_theta \(\Theta\) depends on \( u\) 'nu' (default) \(3 ho_0 u_t^2\ell_c\): eddies of size \(\ell_c\) whose mixing-length viscosity \(u_c\ell_c/3\) is \( u_t\) as \( u_t^2\) 'mlt' \( frac13 ho_0u_c^2\ell_c^3\), with the mixing-length velocity \(u_c = (\alpha F_c/10 ho_0)^{1/3}\) of the convective flux \(F_c\), \(\alpha\) = rsf_alpha no a number that constant no
  • rsf_scale multiplies \(\Theta\), and with it the whole spectrum.
  • 'mlt' needs rsf_lum, the luminosity \(L_\star\) in kore's units, \( ho_u L^5/ au^3\), with \( ho_u\) the unit of density of the structure (the central density for the Model S structures) and \(L\), \( au\) the units of length and time: \(7.0 imes10^{-7}\) for the Sun with a Model S structure, r_out = 0.985 and \( au = 1/\Omega\), \(\Omega/2\pi\) = 456 nHz. It takes the convective flux as \(L_\star/(4\pi r^2)\) times \( u_t/\max u_t\), and needs visc_pow = 0.
  • The eddy size \(\ell_c\) is a smooth minimum of rsf_alpha \(H_p\) (\(H_p\) the pressure scale height) and rsf_lc_max, or the constant rsf_lc. With rsf_angular = 1 (the default) the eddies also have a finite horizontal size, which weakens the force at degrees \(l \gtrsim r/\ell_c\).
  • The Sun. The observed amplitudes of the solar Rossby modes (Löptien et al. 2018) correspond to \(\Theta_{ m eff} \approx (0.6 ext{–}3) imes10^{34}\) erg, \((0.3 ext{–}1.6) imes10^{-11}\) in kore's units with the solar values above. That is about \(10 hinspace(10^{12} hinspace\mathrm{cm^2 hinspace s^{-1}}/ u_t)^2\) times the 'nu' law, or \(1/20\) of the 'mlt' law, for eddies much smaller than the modes. With the default eddy size and angular factor the same modes are forced a few times less, so rsf_scale must be larger by as much. Treat these as starting values for rsf_scale.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
• Around a mode: about 20 points over \(\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda \pm 5\thinspace\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\), and one at \(\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\). An eigenvalue solve on the same matrices (step 3) gives the modes.
  • Between modes, a uniform grid. A mode whose half-width is smaller than the grid step can fall between two points: add a point at each resonance you care about.
  • rsf_frequencies takes any list or array, for example np.loadtxt('freqs.txt') for a file with one frequency per line.
  • For \(m = 0\) the spectrum is even in \(w\): scan \(w > 0\) only.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: parameter default meaning rsf_nsamp 1 number of realisations; 16 to 30 is usual rsf_seed 0 realisation \(j\) uses numpy.random.default_rng([rsf_seed, j]) rsf_theta 'nu' the law of \(\Theta\) (above) rsf_scale 1.0 multiplies \(\Theta\) rsf_lum None luminosity in kore's units, for 'mlt' rsf_alpha, rsf_lc_max 2.0, 0.25 the eddy size, a smooth minimum of rsf_alpha \(H_p\) and rsf_lc_max rsf_lc None a constant eddy size instead rsf_angular 1 1: eddies of finite horizontal size; 0: white in angle rsf_nu_floor None the part \(\nu_f\) of \(\hat\nu\) that is not turbulent; None: visc0 for 'step' and 'solar_rz' with visc0 < 1, else 0 rsf_taper 0.04 width over which the force goes to zero at the walls rsf_taper_in 0.2 the same above \(r = 0\) in a full sphere rsf_rcut, rsf_rcut_width None, 0.04 no force below rsf_rcut, full force above rsf_rcut + rsf_rcut_width rsf_frequencies None the frequencies of the scan, in kore's units (negative prograde) rsf_split None a radius: also report the kinetic energy below it

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
file columns rsf_spectrum.dat \(w\), the mean kinetic energy and its standard error; with rsf_split, then the mean kinetic energy below rsf_split and its standard error rsf_ke.dat \(w\), the kinetic energy of each realisation; with rsf_split, then the kinetic energy below rsf_split of each realisation

Each scan first writes a line starting with #, which np.loadtxt skips.

  • Power spectral density. The mean kinetic energy at \(w\) is a two-sided power spectral density, in kore's units: for \(m \neq 0\), \(\int(\text{mean KE})\thinspace dw/2\pi\) is the mean kinetic energy of the forced flow. For \(m = 0\) the flow is real, the spectrum is even in \(w\), and that integral over all \(w\) is twice the energy: integrate over \(w > 0\) only.
  • One symmetry class. The force drives the two equatorial symmetries independently, and a run solves one of them (symm). The energy at one \(m\) is the sum of a symm = 1 and a symm = -1 run.
  • Noise. The standard error goes as \(1/\sqrt K\), \(K\) = rsf_nsamp: about a quarter of the mean with 16 realisations near a mode, 18 % with 30. Realisation \(j\) is the same at every frequency, in every scan and for any rsf_nsamp, so the shape of a spectrum is less noisy than its level, and scans of the same configuration can be joined.
  • Energy of a mode. Fit a Lorentzian plus a smooth background to the peak: the energy of the mode is the height of the Lorentzian times \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert/2\). Its half-width should be \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\). Other modes add a background to the raw peak.
  • Non-normal operators. With a differential rotation the modes are not orthogonal, and the forced response can differ from the sum of the modes' Lorentzians, or exceed the energy that the fluctuation–dissipation relation gives a single mode. The forced solve includes this.
  • Unstable modes have no stationary response: the spectrum near a growing mode means nothing. Check the eigenvalues near the frequencies you scan.

Without rsf_frequencies, solve.py solves at forcing_frequency only and writes the fields of the forced flow, one column per realisation, as for the eigenvectors of an eigenvalue run (Output files).

docs.title: Large runs
docs.text:
• Several scans in parallel. Each scan needs only bin/ and the matrices. Copy bin/ into a new directory, link A.npz, B.npz and B_forced.npz into it, append par.rsf_frequencies = ... to its parameter file, and run solve.py there. Split the list of frequencies between such directories and run them at the same time.
  • Restarts. A row is appended as soon as its frequency is solved, so a scan can be read while it runs, and a stopped scan only needs the remaining frequencies. Rerun in the same directory only with the same B_forced.npz: with another number of realisations the rows differ in length and np.loadtxt cannot read the file.
  • Failed frequencies. A frequency whose realisations are all NaN or Inf prints "Solver crashed at w = …, got nan's!", and the scan goes on with the next one. The cause is a MUMPS factorisation that ran out of workspace: set par.petsc_opts['mat_mumps_icntl_14'] = 100 from the start, as in the example, and rerun any frequency that still fails with 200 (Solver). A forced run reads the mat_ options, an eigenvalue run the st_ options: use st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 for the eigenvalue solve of step 3.
  • Cost. Each frequency costs one LU factorisation of a matrix of the size of the eigenproblem's, with the same memory, plus one back-substitution per realisation, which is much cheaper than the factorisation.
  • Several forcings at once. \(A\) and \(B\) do not depend on the force, so several configurations of the forcing (other rsf_theta, rsf_rcut, …) can share the factorisations: put their right-hand sides side by side as columns of B_forced.npz. rsf_spectrum.dat then averages over all columns, so read rsf_ke.dat by groups of columns.

The checks of the implementation are in tests/rsf/, with a README.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page goes through one complete run of kore, from the parameter file to a checked eigenvalue. The example is the simplest of the Benchmarks: an inertial mode of an incompressible fluid in a differentially rotating spherical shell, from Baruteau & Rieutord (2013, fig. 10). It takes about a minute on four cores and needs less than 2 GB of memory.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the environment
docs.text:
Install PETSc, SLEPc and their python bindings as described in Installation, then load the environment in the terminal you will use:

source $HOME/kore_env.sh

docs.title: 2. Get the code and make a run directory
docs.text:
git clone -b anelastic_log https://github.com/repepo/kore.git
mkdir br10
cp -r kore/bin br10/
cd br10

kore runs from a directory that holds a copy of bin/, and writes all its files there. Keep the clone itself clean and make one run directory per set of parameters.

docs.title: 3. Write the parameter file
docs.text:
Every script reads its parameters from bin/parameters.py. Replace the content of that file with

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

# Time unit 1/Ω and the Ekman number E = ν/(Ω R²)
par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 8e-7
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek

# Fluid and container: incompressible, a shell with inner radius 0.2, stress-free walls
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'      # ρ0 = 1
par.thermal = 0                   # no heat equation
par.ricb = 0.2
par.bci = 0
par.bco = 0

# Differential rotation Ω = Ω_ref r^σ, with σ = 0.5
par.diff_rot = 1
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular'
par.diff_rot_param = 0.5
par.thermal_wind = 0

# Axisymmetric, equatorially symmetric modes
par.m = 0
par.symm = 1

# Resolution and cores: lmax - m + 1 must be a multiple of 2*ncpus
par.N = 132
par.lmax = 271
par.ncpus = 4

# Look for the 5 eigenvalues nearest the target rtau + i*itau
par.rtau = -0.008
par.itau = 1.23
par.nev = 5

default_params() sets every parameter to its default. bin/params_default.py lists them all, with comments. The parameters used here:

  • timescale and set_scales() choose the unit of time and set the four dimensionless numbers Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD and ThermaD from it (Anelastic equations). The unit of length is the radius of the outer wall.
  • structure, thermal, diff_rot and their options set the background: density, entropy gradient, diffusivities and rotation (Background model).
  • ricb is the inner radius (0 for a full sphere), and bci, bco the conditions at the inner and outer walls (0 stress-free, 1 no-slip).
  • m is the azimuthal wavenumber, and symm the equatorial symmetry of the flow (1 symmetric, −1 antisymmetric).
  • N is the number of Chebyshev polynomials in radius, and lmax the highest spherical-harmonic degree.
  • rtau + i itau is the target: the solver returns the nev eigenvalues nearest to it.

kore's eigenvalue is \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\), for perturbations \(\propto e^{\lambda t + im\phi}\) in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), with \(\sigma\) the growth rate (negative when damped) and \(\omega\) the frequency, here in units of \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The target above is the published mode.

docs.title: 4. Build the matrices
docs.text:
./bin/submatrices.py 4
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/assemble.py

submatrices.py computes one sparse matrix per radial operator of the equations (all in submatrices.npz), using 4 processes. assemble.py combines them over all degrees \(l\) into the matrices \(A\) and \(B\) of the eigenproblem \(A\mathbf x = \lambda B\mathbf x\) (A.npz, B.npz). The number of MPI ranks must equal par.ncpus.

docs.title: 5. Solve
docs.text:
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve.py

solve.py factors \(A - \tau B\) once and finds the eigenvalues nearest the target \(\tau\). It prints them with their residuals:

  -0.007855+1.227914i       5.32254e-12
  -0.019000+1.231247i       3.10986e-11
  -0.019022+1.223615i       5.29565e-11
  -0.019437+1.238668i       3.77176e-11
  -0.019738+1.216233i       1.01615e-10

The first one is the mode of the paper. It writes the eigenvalues to eigenvalues0.dat and the eigenvectors to real_flow.field and imag_flow.field. The residuals printed here only say that the solver converged. They do not say whether the resolution is sufficient.

docs.title: 6. Check the solution
docs.text:
./bin/spin_doctor.py 4

spin_doctor.py rebuilds each solution in physical space and checks the balances it must satisfy. The first columns of its table are

  ★          Re λ              Im λ          𝒯/𝒫       residσ     residω    Peak ℓ   ℓ-Width   ℓ-Convergence
  0      -0.007855111       1.227914453    1.12e+00   1.75e-05   1.01e-08     3         44        4.68e-12
  1      -0.018999641       1.231246928    1.14e+00   3.12e-04   2.23e-06     5         74        2.71e-10

A mode is resolved when its energy residual residσ is below \(10^{-5}\) and its ℓ-convergence below \(10^{-4}\) (with thermal = 1, the entropy residual resid𝑠 must also be below \(10^{-5}\)). The ℓ-convergence is fine, but residσ is \(1.8\times10^{-5}\) for the first mode and \(3\times10^{-4}\) for the others: the radial resolution is not enough. spin_doctor.py also appends one row per mode to params.dat, flow.dat and eigenvalues.dat (Output files).

docs.title: 7. Raise the resolution
docs.text:
Set par.N = 160 in bin/parameters.py and repeat steps 4 to 6. Now

  ★          Re λ              Im λ          𝒯/𝒫       residσ     residω    Peak ℓ   ℓ-Width   ℓ-Convergence
  0      -0.007855595       1.227914636    1.12e+00   7.59e-08   2.45e-10     3         44        4.68e-12

residσ is \(8\times10^{-8}\), and the eigenvalue moved by \(5\times10^{-7}\) from the run at N = 132: the mode is resolved. Its eigenvalue often converges at a lower N than its residual, so judge a run by the residuals. The other four eigenvalues changed completely: at N = 132 they were not solutions of the equations.

docs.title: 8. Compare with the paper
docs.text: Baruteau & Rieutord give \(\lvert\omega\rvert = 1.2279\) and the damping rate \(\tau = -7.86\times10^{-3}\), in units of the surface rotation rate. kore gives \(\lvert\omega\rvert = 1.22791\) and \(\sigma = -7.856\times10^{-3}\). For \(m = 0\) the modes come in pairs \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda^*\), so the sign of the frequency carries no information.

docs.title: Running all steps at once
docs.text:
runKore.sh, at the top of the repository, runs steps 4 to 6 in one go and then moves the results, the matrices and a copy of the parameter files to ../run. Copy it to the run directory and set ncpus in its first lines to par.ncpus:

cp ../kore/runKore.sh .
./runKore.sh

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Change the problem: Background model explains the density, stratification, diffusivity and rotation options, and Benchmarks gives the parameters of the other published cases, including the Sun.
  • Drive the modes with the random stress of convection and compute their spectrum: Convective forcing.
  • A solution that fails the checks, or a run that runs out of memory: Solver.
  • The equations kore solves and how it discretizes them: the pages under Mathematical framework.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To run kore we need the PETSc/SLEPc packages and their python bindings petsc4py/slepc4py. PETSc needs to be compiled with support for complex scalars. MUMPS and SuperLU_dist are external packages that need to be installed together with PETSc.

If you are interested in problems that involve very large matrices, for instance when considering extremely small viscosities, we recommend doing so with a machine with at least 128 GB of memory. The number of processing cores is not critical, eight are fine, 24 are plenty. Small to moderate size matrices can be solved using a laptop, depending on available memory.

docs.title: Installing PETSc/SLEPc on MacOS
docs.text:
It is convenient to have a dedicated python environment to use with kore. It is quite simple to create and activate it:

python3 -m venv kore_env
source kore_env/bin/activate

Then we need to install scipy and cython in that environment: 

pip3 install scipy cython

Now we download the latest PETSc/SLEPc releases using git 

git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/petsc/petsc.git petsc
git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/slepc/slepc slepc

We go now into the newly created petsc folder and configure PETSc: 

cd petsc
./configure --with-petsc4py --download-mpi4py --download-mpich --with-scalar-type=complex --download-mumps --download-parmetis --download-metis --download-scalapack --download-openblas --download-openblas-make-options='USE_THREAD=0 USE_OPENMP=0 USE_LOCKING=1' --with-debugging=0 --download-superlu_dist --download-ptscotch CXXOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' FOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' COPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' --download-bison
We recommend OpenBLAS (--download-openblas) rather than the reference BLAS/LAPACK (--download-fblaslapack). MUMPS spends most of its factorization time in dense BLAS kernels, and with OpenBLAS the LU factorization was 5 to 8 times faster in our tests (Linux, 24-core Threadripper, MUMPS 5.8.2). For example, a torsional-mode run at N = 976 took 4.4 minutes instead of 20. The make options build a single-threaded OpenBLAS, so that it doesn't compete with the MPI processes for cores.

Then we build PETSc: 

make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt all
where you must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path for your case. Before checking that everything works we must tell python where to find petsc4py and mpi4py, which were compiled along in the step above: 
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/petsc/arch-darwin-c-opt/lib
where again we must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path. Now we test the installation: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt check
If no errors appear then you can proceed to install SLEPc. If an error is reported due to python not being able to find PETSc (even though we just updated the PYTHONPATH), but the other MPI tests were successful, then don't worry, it is safe to ignore the error.

We need to setup some environment variables before installing SLEPc: 

export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc

Now go to the slepc folder, configure and build SLEPc: 

cd $SLEPC_DIR
./configure
make
make check
The last step is to install slepc4py, which is distributed along with SLEPc: 
cd $SLEPC_DIR/src/binding/slepc4py
python3 setup.py build
python3 setup.py install
Almost there now. We need to update the PATH environment variable so that we can use the MPI library provided by PETSc instead of the one provided by your system, if any: 
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH

It is a good idea to keep the necessary commands for initialization in a separate file. It should contain the following lines: 

source /path/to/kore_env/bin/activate
export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PYTHONPATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH
We can write that to a file named e.g. kore_env.sh in your home directory, so every time you need to prepare to run kore we do first: 
source $HOME/kore_env.sh

docs.title: Installing PETSc/SLEPc on Linux
docs.text:
The steps are the same as for MacOS, except for the name of the PETSc architecture (arch-linux-c-opt) and the way slepc4py is built. These instructions were tested on Debian 13 with gcc/gfortran 14 and PETSc/SLEPc 3.25.

First we need compilers and a few build tools. On Debian or Ubuntu they can be installed with: 

sudo apt install build-essential gfortran git cmake python3-dev python3-venv

Then we create and activate a dedicated python environment for kore, and install scipy and cython in it: 

python3 -m venv kore_env
source kore_env/bin/activate
pip3 install scipy cython

Now we download the latest PETSc/SLEPc releases using git 

git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/petsc/petsc.git petsc
git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/slepc/slepc slepc

We go now into the newly created petsc folder and configure PETSc, using OpenBLAS as explained in the MacOS section: 

cd petsc
./configure --with-petsc4py --download-mpi4py --download-mpich --with-scalar-type=complex --download-mumps --download-parmetis --download-metis --download-scalapack --download-openblas --download-openblas-make-options='USE_THREAD=0 USE_OPENMP=0 USE_LOCKING=1' --with-debugging=0 --download-superlu_dist --download-ptscotch CXXOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' FOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' COPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' --download-bison
Then we build PETSc: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt all
where you must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path for your case. Before checking that everything works we must tell python where to find petsc4py and mpi4py, which were compiled along in the step above: 
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/petsc/arch-linux-c-opt/lib
Now we test the installation: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt check

We need to setup some environment variables before installing SLEPc: 

export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH

Now go to the slepc folder, configure and build SLEPc. The --with-slepc4py option builds slepc4py along with SLEPc, inside $SLEPC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib: 

cd $SLEPC_DIR
./configure --with-slepc4py
make
make check

As for MacOS, it is a good idea to keep the necessary commands for initialization in a separate file. Note that PYTHONPATH must now include the SLEPc folder too, so that python finds slepc4py: 

source /path/to/kore_env/bin/activate
export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PYTHONPATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib:$SLEPC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH
We can write that to e.g. $HOME/kore_env.sh and do source $HOME/kore_env.sh before running kore.

Several PETSc builds can live side by side in the same petsc and slepc folders, each under its own PETSC_ARCH name (passed as PETSC_ARCH=... to PETSc's ./configure). Switching between them only requires changing PETSC_ARCH.

docs.title: Optional: SHTns and pyevtk
docs.text:
Kore itself needs neither. The plotting package koreviz uses SHTns, a fast spherical-harmonic transform library, to evaluate solutions on a grid in physical space, and koreviz.writeVts uses pyevtk to write files for ParaView.

The script tools/install-shtns.sh downloads SHTns 3.5.2, builds it with OpenMP (with MKL if MKLROOT is set, otherwise with FFTW, which must then be installed) and installs it under $HOME/.local, together with its python module. pyevtk can be installed with pip3 install pyevtk in the Kore python environment.

docs.title: Magnetic field equations
docs.text: This page gives the mathematics behind magnetic = 1, for readers who want to check the code or extend it: the equations, the formula of every background field, how the equations become matrix rows, the boundary conditions, what a differential rotation adds, the energy budgets, and the checks. How to set up a run is on Magnetic field; how the rows were derived and fitted is on Derivation tools, part A.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
kore solves for a small perturbation \(\mathbf b\) of the imposed field \(\mathbf B_0\), together with the flow \(\mathbf u\). Two terms couple them: the flow induces \(\mathbf b\) by moving the field lines of \(\mathbf B_0\), and the Lorentz force of the two fields acts on the flow. Both terms are linear in the perturbation, because \(\mathbf B_0\) is fixed.

In units of the time scale \( au\) (timescale), the induction equation and the Lorentz force per unit mass in the momentum equation (Anelastic equations) are

\[ rac{\partial \mathbf b}{\partial t} = abla imes(\mathbf u imes\mathbf B_0) + \mathrm{MagnetD}\, abla^2\mathbf b, \] \[ \mathbf F_L = rac{\mathrm{Hendrik}}{ ho_0}\left[( abla imes\mathbf b) imes\mathbf B_0 + ( abla imes\mathbf B_0) imes\mathbf b ight]. \]

The magnetic diffusivity \(\eta\) is uniform (background.diffusivity(..., 'eta') returns 1). The perturbation field is written with two scalars, as the flow is but without \( ho_0\), since \(\mathbf b\) is solenoidal by itself:

\[ \mathbf b = abla imes abla imes(f\,\mathbf r) + abla imes(g\,\mathbf r). \]

Parameters. The factor Hendrik sets the strength of the Lorentz force and MagnetD that of the magnetic diffusion. set_scales() computes both from the Lehnert number and the magnetic Ekman number:

factor definition set_scales() Hendrik \(( au B_0/r_0)^2/( ho_0\mu_0)\) \((\mathrm{Gaspard}\cdot\mathrm{Le})^2\) MagnetD \(\eta_0 au/r_0^2\) \(\mathrm{Gaspard}\cdot\mathrm{Em}\)

Both numbers are defined with the rotation rate, as Ek is:

\[ \mathrm{Le} = rac{B_0}{\Omega r_0\sqrt{ ho_0\mu_0}}, \qquad \mathrm{Em} = rac{\eta_0}{\Omega r_0^2} = rac{\mathrm{Ek}}{Pm}, \qquad \Lambda = rac{\mathrm{Le}^2}{\mathrm{Em}} \]

(\(\Lambda\) the Elsasser number, \(Pm\) the magnetic Prandtl number). Le and Em must be set before set_scales() is called. Besides 'rotation' and 'viscous', set_scales() knows two magnetic time scales: 'Alfven' (Gaspard \(= 1/\mathrm{Le}\), so Hendrik \(= 1\)) and 'magnetic' (Gaspard \(= 1/\mathrm{Em}\), so MagnetD \(= 1\)).

Equatorial symmetry. The symmetry of \(\mathbf B_0\) about the equator decides which degrees \(\mathbf b\) takes for a given flow. A poloidal field of degree \(n\) has the symmetry \((-1)^n\) and a toroidal one \((-1)^{n+1}\): the dipole is antisymmetric, a toroidal field of degree 1 (\(B_\phi\propto\sin heta\)) is symmetric, one of degree 2 antisymmetric. \(\mathbf b\) has the symmetry of \(\mathbf u\) times that of \(\mathbf B_0\) (ut.bsymm = symm * symmB0): with an antisymmetric \(\mathbf B_0\), \(f\) takes the degrees of the toroidal flow and \(g\) those of the poloidal flow; with a symmetric one, \(f\) takes the degrees of the poloidal flow and \(g\) those of the toroidal flow. A poloidal and a toroidal part can be combined only if they have the same symmetry.

docs.title: Background fields
docs.text: The background field is steady and axisymmetric. It is the sum of a poloidal part (B0) and a toroidal part (B0_tor), each built from radial profiles times Legendre polynomials and scaled by cnorm or cnorm_tor. This section gives the profile of every option (bin/background_field.py) and how the amplitude is fixed.

docs.title: Poloidal fields
docs.text:
Each poloidal option gives a radial profile \(h(r)\) of one degree \(l\) (several degrees for 'general' and 'ferraro'). The field follows from it by two curls,

\[ \mathbf B_0 = c_\mathrm{norm} abla imes abla imes(h(r)\,Y_l^0\,\mathbf r), \]

with \(Y_l^0\) the Schmidt harmonic \(P_l(\cos heta)\). Its radial component and its current are
