docs.title: Magnetic field
docs.text:
With magnetic = 1, kore adds a background magnetic field that you choose, and solves for small perturbations of the flow and of the field together: the field's Lorentz force acts on the flow, and the flow induces a perturbation of the field. The background field is fixed, steady and axisymmetric. It is imposed, not computed: there is no dynamo, and the background flow does not react to it.

kore does not include the field in the thermal-wind balance. The thermal-wind entropy is computed from the imposed rotation alone, as without a field, and the field's force acts only on the perturbations. This is exact for a field that carries no current, such as B0 = 'axial' or 'dipole', and a good approximation when the field's force is weak compared with the Coriolis force of the differential rotation (Validity and caveats).

This page shows how to set up a run and how to choose the background field. The equations, the formula of every field and the checks of the code are on Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Parameters and a first run
docs.text:
Two dimensionless numbers set how strong the field is and how fast it diffuses. Both are measured against the rotation, as the Ekman number Ek is:

parameter meaning Le Lehnert number: the Alfvén speed of the field over the rotation speed of the outer wall Em magnetic Ekman number: the magnetic diffusivity over the rotation rate times the radius squared

Two combinations are common: the magnetic Prandtl number Ek/Em and the Elsasser number Le**2/Em. The exact definitions are on Magnetic field equations.

A first run. A uniform field along the rotation axis, in a shell with insulating walls, with Elsasser and magnetic Prandtl numbers both equal to one. Add these lines at the end of a bin/parameters.py like the checked-in one (which already imports numpy and sets m, symm, N, lmax and the target), so that no later line overrides them:

par.Ek = 1e-3                # Ekman number
par.Em = 1e-3                # magnetic Ekman number: Pm = Ek/Em = 1
par.Le = np.sqrt(1e-3)       # Lehnert number: Elsasser number Le**2/Em = 1
par.set_scales()             # call it again: it sets Hendrik and MagnetD from Le and Em

par.structure = 'Boussinesq' # any structure works (Background model)
par.magnetic = 1
par.thermal = 0              # no entropy equation
par.B0 = 'axial'             # the poloidal background field (tables below)
par.cnorm = 'mag_energy'     # its amplitude: the integral of B0**2 over the fluid is 1
par.B0_tor = None            # no toroidal background field
par.innercore = 'insulator'
par.mantle = 'insulator'
par.ricb = 0.35; par.bci = 1; par.bco = 1   # no-slip walls

set_scales() turns Le and Em into the factors of the equations, Hendrik (Lorentz force) and MagnetD (magnetic diffusion), so call it after setting them. Two values of timescale are magnetic: 'Alfven' (the Alfvén time) and 'magnetic' (the magnetic diffusion time). A run stops if Le or Em is zero.

docs.title: Choosing the background field
docs.text: The background field is one axisymmetric field for the whole domain. It is the sum of two parts: a poloidal part, whose field lines lie in meridional planes like those of a dipole, and a toroidal part, whose field lines are circles around the rotation axis. Choose a shape for each, with B0 and B0_tor, then set their amplitude. B0 defaults to 'axial' and B0_tor to None; for a toroidal field alone, set B0 = None.

docs.title: Equatorial symmetry
docs.text:
The symmetry of the field about the equator decides which parts can be combined, and how the perturbations are paired.

  • A poloidal field of odd degree is dipolar (antisymmetric about the equator), one of even degree quadrupolar (symmetric). For a toroidal field it is the other way round: degree 1 is symmetric, degree 2 antisymmetric.
  • The two parts must have the same symmetry, or the run stops. A dipole therefore combines with a toroidal field of degree 2, not of degree 1.
  • symm still selects the symmetry of the flow. A symmetric background field gives the perturbation field the flow's symmetry; an antisymmetric one gives it the opposite.

docs.title: Poloidal field: B0
docs.text:
Each option is a fixed radial shape (several for 'general'), multiplied by cnorm (Amplitude). The formulas are on Magnetic field equations.

B0 the field extra parameters (default) geometry degree 'axial' (default) uniform, along the rotation axis none shell or full sphere 1 'dipole' the field of a dipole at the centre none shell only 1 'FDM' the slowest free decay mode of the given degree, for insulating walls B0_l (1); beta, the first guess of the root finder shell or full sphere B0_l = 1 or 2 'G21 dipole' a full-sphere dipole (Gerick et al. 2021) B0_ic shell or full sphere 1 'Luo_S1' the shape of 'G21 dipole' (Luo & Jackson 2022), at a larger scale B0_ic shell or full sphere 1 'Luo_S2' a full-sphere quadrupole (Luo & Jackson 2022) B0_ic shell or full sphere 2 'confined' zero outside a spherical layer, going smoothly to zero at its edges B0_l (1), B0_conf_r1 (0.0), B0_conf_r2 (0.6), B0_conf_p (12) the layer must lie in the fluid B0_l = 1 or 2 'general' your own radial profile for each degree B0_profiles = {degree: 'expression of r, p'}, B0_param (p) shell or full sphere any, of one parity 'ferraro' field lines on the surfaces of constant rotation, so that the rotation does not wind it up (below) B0_ferraro_G ('w'), B0_ferraro_nmax (15, odd), B0_param needs diff_rot = 1 odd, up to B0_ferraro_nmax None no poloidal field

Notes:

  • Full-sphere shapes with an inner core. 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1' and 'Luo_S2' are defined for a full sphere. With an inner core, B0_ic = 'potential' (default) continues the field into the core as a potential field; B0_ic = 'frozen currents' keeps the full-sphere formula, whose currents below the inner boundary then stay in the core (fitting only when the core's magnetic decay time is much longer than the periods sought; the name was 'full sphere' before 2026-11-06).
  • 'dipole' is the field of a dipole at the centre, seen from outside its source: it carries no current in the fluid and meets an insulating mantle as it is. Its source is in the inner core, so it needs one, and B0_ic does not apply to it. A conducting inner core that moves with a forced boundary holds it as a regular field instead (A boundary that moves).
  • 'Luo_S1' and 'G21 dipole' give the same run when cnorm is a name ('mag_energy', 'Schmitt2012', 'rms_cmb'). With a numerical cnorm the 'Luo_S1' field is 30 times stronger.
  • 'confined' puts the field in the layer from B0_conf_r1 to B0_conf_r2 and nowhere else. The defaults reach the centre, which suits a full sphere; with an inner core, set B0_conf_r1 at or above ricb. B0_conf_p (at least 3) sets how smoothly the field vanishes at the edges, so that no current sheet forms there.

  • 'general' takes numpy expressions of r and p (sin, cos, exp, sqrt, where, erf, pi, ...). In a full sphere the profile of degree n should go as r**n at the centre. Example:

    par.B0_profiles = {1: 'r/6 - r**3/10', 3: '0.3*r**3*(1 - r**2)'}

  • 'ferraro' takes B0_ferraro_G, a numpy expression of w (the differential rotation) and p: see Four ways to a steady background.

  • At the walls. kore takes 'general' and 'ferraro' as fields of currents in the fluid. Where they do not meet the potential field of those currents beyond an insulating wall, they end there in a sheet of current, which pushes the fluid along the wall (Current sheets at slipping walls). So does a part written into them whose sources lie beyond the wall, such as the uniform field {1: 'r/2'}: use 'axial' for a uniform field and 'dipole' for a dipole at the centre.

docs.title: Toroidal field: B0_tor
docs.text:
The toroidal part is purely azimuthal. A differential rotation does not wind it up, so it suits any rotation. Each option is one radial shape times cnorm_tor; the formulas are on Magnetic field equations.

B0_tor the field extra parameters (default) geometry degree None (default) no toroidal field 'Malkus' grows linearly with the distance to the axis (degree 1), the field of Malkus (1967) B0_tor_l (1) shell or full sphere; degree 2 shell only B0_tor_l = 1 or 2 'wall' zero at both walls B0_tor_l (1) shell or full sphere B0_tor_l = 1 or 2 'user' a radial shape given as an expression of r and p B0_tor_profile, B0_tor_param (p), B0_tor_l (1) shell or full sphere B0_tor_l = 1 or 2 'general' your own radial profile for each degree B0_tor_profiles = {degree: 'expression of r, p'}, B0_tor_param (p) shell or full sphere any, of one parity

A 'user' profile must be smooth, since its second derivative enters the equations. The expressions of 'user', 'general' (poloidal or toroidal) and 'ferraro' are written to params.dat after #, so they must not contain #.

At the walls. A toroidal field that is not zero at a wall ends there in a sheet of current, unless a conductor beyond the wall carries the field on: a conducting inner core, the resolved mantle or a conducting thin layer. The sheet pushes the fluid along the wall (Current sheets at slipping walls). With the rotating solids the field must vanish at both walls, whatever they are (Rotating solids).

docs.title: Amplitude
docs.text:
The shapes above have arbitrary scales, so the size of the field is set separately. The field in the equations is Le times a dimensionless field, whose size is fixed by cnorm (poloidal part) and cnorm_tor (toroidal part). The Lorentz force goes as Le squared.

value meaning for a number (default 1) multiplies the formula of the shape as it is all types 'mag_energy' the integral of the squared field over the fluid is 1 (Luo & Jackson 2022) all types 'Schmitt2012' the integral of the squared field over the fluid is 4 all types 'rms_cmb' the rms radial field over the outer wall is 1 cnorm with 'axial', 'dipole', 'FDM', 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2' only

Use 'mag_energy', as in the example: Le and the Elsasser number then refer to a field of fixed energy, whatever its shape. With a number, the field's size depends on the arbitrary scale of the formula, and Le alone does not say how strong the field is. 'confined', 'general' and 'ferraro' stop with 'rms_cmb'. Formulas: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: With a differential rotation
docs.text:
With diff_rot = 1 the fluid rotates differentially (Background model), and the shear acts on magnetic field lines in two ways:

  • It shears the perturbation field. kore includes this in the linear problem, for any rotation profile.
  • It winds up the background poloidal field: it stretches poloidal field lines around the axis into an azimuthal field, which grows until magnetic diffusion balances the winding. kore holds the background fixed and does not follow this growth. So the background is steady only if nothing is wound up, or if it already holds the azimuthal field at which the winding is balanced; otherwise kore can only assume that something outside the model keeps it steady.

This section says when the background is steady, and gives four set-ups that make it so.

docs.title: The Ferraro condition
docs.text:
A differential rotation winds up a poloidal field line unless the rotation rate is the same all along it. So nothing is wound up when the rotation rate is constant along every poloidal field line: this is Ferraro's law of isorotation. A toroidal field always satisfies it; a poloidal field usually does not.

At the start of a run with a poloidal field and diff_rot = 1, kore prints how far the field and the rotation are from this condition, as a relative number (definition). Above 1e-7 it prints a warning and carries on; to make it stop instead, set ferraro_policy = 'refuse' (default 'warn'). With B0_wound = 1 it prints the residual of the wound field's balance instead.

docs.title: Four ways to a steady background
docs.text:
Three set-ups avoid the winding by making the rotation rate the same along every field line: kore fits the field to the rotation (B0 = 'ferraro') or the rotation to the field (diff_rot_type = 'ferraro'), or you place the field where the rotation is uniform (B0 = 'confined'). The fourth, B0_wound = 1, accepts the winding: it keeps a field that the shear crosses, and adds the azimuthal field that the shear winds up from it.

set-up the winding what kore does other parameters (default) use it when B0 = 'ferraro' avoided uses a poloidal field whose field lines lie on the surfaces of constant rotation, and keeps the rotation B0_ferraro_G ('w'), B0_ferraro_nmax (15, odd) the rotation is given, and any field that it does not wind up will do diff_rot_type = 'ferraro' avoided keeps the field, and replaces the rotation by one that is constant along each field line diff_rot_F ('psi'), diff_rot_param, diff_rot_nmax (8, even) the field is given (e.g. a model of an observed or a dynamo field), and the rotation only has to fit it B0 = 'confined' avoided nothing: the field sits in a layer where the rotation is uniform B0_conf_r1 (0.0), B0_conf_r2 (0.6) the field lives away from the shear (e.g. below the tachocline) B0_wound = 1 balanced by diffusion keeps the field and the rotation, and adds the azimuthal field that the shear winds up from the poloidal field B0_wound_eta (1.0) both are given and do not match (e.g. a tachocline)

B0 = 'ferraro': field lines on the surfaces of constant rotation. This set-up avoids the winding. The rotation winds up any poloidal field line that crosses its surfaces of constant rotation, so kore uses a poloidal field whose field lines lie on these surfaces. Nothing is wound up, no azimuthal field is created, and by itself the field puts no torque on the rotation. The rotation is kept as given. The field lines are set by the rotation, and B0_ferraro_G, a function of the rotation rate w, sets the magnetic flux that passes between the axis and each of these surfaces. Where the rotation is uniform the field vanishes, so this field lives only where the rotation varies. B0_ferraro_G should vanish on the values the rotation takes on the axis and, for a field that stays inside the fluid, at the outer wall; kore prints how well these hold. A toroidal part of even degree can be added. cnorm must be a number, 'mag_energy' or 'Schmitt2012'.

diff_rot_type = 'ferraro': rotation constant along the field lines. This set-up also avoids the winding, the other way round: kore keeps the poloidal field (any B0 type) and replaces the rotation profile by one that is constant along each of its field lines. diff_rot_F gives the rotation rate of each field line (times diff_rot_ampl, as for every profile), as a function of the field's flux function psi, which labels the field lines (and of p = diff_rot_param); the default 'psi' is the simplest. It needs a poloidal field and cannot be combined with B0 = 'ferraro'. kore's rotation is symmetric about the equator, so with a quadrupolar field diff_rot_F must be even (e.g. a function of psi**2); the run stops otherwise.

B0 = 'confined': a field where the rotation is uniform. The poloidal field fills a spherical layer and nothing else. If the rotation is uniform in that layer, as below the solar tachocline, nothing is wound up.

B0_wound = 1: the field wound up by the shear. This set-up accepts the winding. kore keeps the poloidal field (any type) and the rotation as given, although the shear crosses the field lines. It adds to the background the azimuthal field that the shear winds up from the poloidal field, at the strength where magnetic diffusion balances the winding. This wound field is computed at the start of the run and added to any B0_tor. Its strength follows from the physics, not from cnorm, which normalises the poloidal part alone: it grows with the shear, is inversely proportional to the diffusivity, and can exceed the poloidal field many times. B0_wound_eta (positive, default 1) is that diffusivity in units of MagnetD; the perturbation still diffuses with MagnetD. The wound field's torque would brake the shear; kore leaves it out, so this background holds only while something maintains the rotation. It needs a poloidal B0 and diff_rot = 1. Read Validity and caveats before using it.

B0 = 'ferraro' or B0_wound = 1? They describe different states. B0 = 'ferraro', like diff_rot_type = 'ferraro', describes a field and a rotation that have reached isorotation: the rotation rate is the same along every field line, and nothing is wound up. B0_wound = 1 describes a shear that something maintains across the field lines: the shear keeps winding them up, and diffusion keeps the wound field steady.

A conducting inner core must rotate rigidly with the fluid at its surface: the rotation at ricb must not depend on latitude, or the run stops. The method of each set-up is on Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Inner core and walls
docs.text:
The perturbation field is matched at each wall to the field beyond it. The mantle is an electrical insulator, possibly with a conducting layer at its base: a thin one, described by conditions at the wall alone, or one of any thickness whose field kore solves for. Beyond the conducting parts the field is a potential field. The inner core is an insulator (again with or without a thin conducting layer), or a conductor whose field kore then solves for together with the rest.

setting values (default) notes mantle 'insulator' (default), 'TWA' or 'resolved' 'TWA': a thin conducting layer at the base of the mantle; 'resolved': a conducting layer of any thickness (both below) innercore 'insulator' (default), 'conducting, Chebys', 'conducting, Bessel' or 'TWA' need ricb > 0; 'conducting, Bessel' in forced runs only (Forced runs); 'TWA': a thin conducting layer on an insulating inner core N_cic 64 Chebyshev polynomials of the inner-core field with 'conducting, Chebys' (even, at least 4) mu_i2o 1.0 magnetic permeability, inner core over fluid sigma_i2o 1.0 electrical conductivity, inner core over fluid B0_ic 'potential' for 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2' with an inner core (above)

The magnetic diffusivity of the inner core is MagnetD divided by mu_i2o and sigma_i2o. Where the fluid slips along a conducting inner core (a stress-free inner wall, bci = 0), its tangential electric field, that of its flow across the background field included, is continued into the core, as along a thin conducting layer. Matching conditions: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Thin conducting layer
docs.text:
A thin layer that conducts, such as the base of the Earth's mantle, carries currents that couple the field across it. 'TWA' (the thin-wall approximation of Roberts, Glatzmaier & Clune 2010, as in the conductive_IC branch) models such a layer, at the base of an insulating mantle or on an insulating inner core, through the boundary conditions of the field alone: the layer is not resolved and adds no unknowns. It is described by its thickness, conductivity and permeability, through three numbers per wall:

setting default meaning c_cmb, c_icb 1e-5, 0 thickness times permeability of the layer, relative to the radius of the wall and to the fluid's permeability c1_cmb, c1_icb 1e-5, 0 conductance of the layer: thickness times conductivity, relative to the radius and to the fluid's conductivity muw_cmb, muw_icb 1.0 permeability of the layer relative to vacuum; np.inf drops the terms of first order in the thickness mu 1.0 permeability of the fluid relative to vacuum; it enters the thin-wall conditions only B0_cmb 'wall' how the background field meets a thin layer at the outer wall: 'wall' or 'plain' (below)

With c and c1 zero and mu = 1 the layer is an insulator. A layer with the permeability of vacuum (muw 1, the default, as at the Earth's mantle) lets a steady field through unchanged, and its conductance c1 then sets nearly all of its effect. mu other than 1 needs a thin layer or a conducting inner core at every wall of the fluid.

  • Validity. The approximation holds while the layer is thin against its magnetic skin depth at the frequency of the mode. spin_doctor prints the estimated relative error of the layer's effect, εTWA (the larger of the two walls), and writes both to magnetic.dat; keep it small, say below 1%.
  • A fluid slipping along the wall (bco = 0, bci = 0 or ViscosD = 0). The fluid's tangential electric field, including that of the flow across the background field, is continued into the layer in the frame of the solid (condition C.I of Rekier et al. 2023), which turns with the mantle with the rotating solids. The slip stands for a thin viscous layer that is not resolved, which must be thin against the magnetic skin depth: assemble.py prints Pm times the frequency in rotation units (that of the target, or forcing_frequency in a forced run), which should be small. A drag at the outer wall changes nothing here.
  • With a differential rotation the solid turns with the fluid next to it, so the rotation must be uniform in latitude at the wall: the run stops otherwise.
  • B0_cmb. A steady background field drives no current in the layer, but it must meet the layer's condition at the outer wall. 'wall' (default) adds a potential field to the fields of internal currents ('dipole', 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2', 'FDM') so that they do; it changes nothing for muw_cmb 1 and mu 1. 'plain' keeps them as they are. The other fields are used as given.

The conditions and their checks: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Resolved conducting mantle
docs.text:
'TWA' stands for a layer much thinner than the depth to which the field of a mode enters it, its magnetic skin depth. A thicker or better conducting layer, or a slower mode, needs the field inside the layer itself: mantle = 'resolved' puts a conducting layer between the outer wall and r_surface, with an insulator beyond, and solves for its field together with the rest. The layer is solid and at rest (unless a forcing moves the outer boundary: A boundary that moves), and its conductivity may vary with radius.

setting default meaning r_surface 1.83 outer radius of the layer, the outer wall being at 1 (1.83 is the whole mantle of the Earth) N_mantle 64 Chebyshev polynomials of the layer's field (at least 4) sigma_mantle 1.0 conductivity of the layer relative to the fluid's: a number, or a numpy expression of r and p such as '1e-2*exp(-p*(r - 1))' sigma_mantle_param 0.0 the p of that expression
  • Resolution. The run stops if N_mantle polynomials do not resolve the conductivity profile; a step or a kink is never resolved, so smooth it. The field in the layer needs enough of them too, which a second run with a larger N_mantle shows.
  • A fluid slipping along the layer (bco = 0 or ViscosD = 0) gets the same terms as along a thin layer, with the layer's conductivity at the wall.
  • With a differential rotation the mantle turns with the fluid at the outer wall, so the rotation must be uniform in latitude there: the run stops otherwise.
  • A thin layer of thickness h and conductivity σ tends to mantle = 'TWA' with c_cmb = h and c1_cmb = σh as h decreases, also under a forcing that moves the outer boundary, in both pictures of A boundary that moves.
  • The layer and the fluid have the permeability of vacuum (mu = 1).

The equations and their checks: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Current sheets at slipping walls
docs.text:
A background field that does not meet the field beyond an insulating wall ends there in a sheet of current: a toroidal field that is not zero at the wall, or a poloidal one that does not meet the field beyond. 'general' and 'ferraro' need not; where the permeability jumps at the wall (mu other than 1, or a thin layer with c other than 0 and muw other than 1), the other fields of sources inside the wall meet it only at the outer wall, where B0_cmb = 'wall' adjusts them. A conducting inner core, the resolved mantle or a conducting thin layer carries the field on, with no sheet in the fluid. The sheet pushes the fluid along the wall wherever the perturbation's field crosses the wall. A no-slip wall takes that push. Along a stress-free wall (bco or bci 0 or 2) the fluid's viscous stress takes it, and kore includes it in the conditions there (Magnetic field equations).

  • Inviscid fluid. It has no stress to take the push, so a sheet stops an inviscid run. Use a field that meets the wall (B0_tor = 'wall', a poloidal field that matches the potential field or, where the permeability jumps, one that B0_cmb = 'wall' adjusts), a viscous fluid, or a conductor beyond.
  • centrifugal = 1. A sheet at a slipping wall stops the run.
  • Fields that go on through the wall. 'axial', imposed from beyond the outer wall, and at the inner wall 'dipole' and the fields of B0_ic = 'frozen currents', whose sources lie in the core, go on through the wall with no sheet. Where the permeability jumps at a slipping wall they stop: the field beyond then depends on how the jump bends the imposed field or meets the sources, which kore does not model.

docs.title: The field without the flow
docs.text:
Two tools leave the flow out: one checks the walls and the inner core against exact results, the other gives the field that a known flow induces.

Free decay: hydro = 0. Without the momentum equation the field only diffuses, and is carried by the differential rotation with diff_rot = 1. Each mode then decays at a rate that the conductivity, the walls and the inner core alone set, which for a uniform conductivity is known exactly (Checks). The background field does no work, but B0 still sets the equatorial symmetry of the perturbation, as with the flow. With thermal = 1 the same switch gives the free decay of the entropy. Only eigenvalue problems can leave the flow out. solve.py writes no flow files and normalises each eigenvector to a magnetic energy of 1 (plus the entropy's with thermal = 1), without Hendrik; spin_doctor prints resid𝐛 and resid𝐄, for any walls, and none of the flow's columns.

Kinematic induction. bin/just_induction.py and bin/solve_ind.py give the field that a given flow induces in B0, without the force of that field on the flow. Assemble a magnetic eigenvalue problem (submatrices.py, assemble.py), put the flow in real_flow.field and imag_flow.field (written by a run with the same N, lmax, m, symm and ricb, a forced run of the flow alone for instance), then run

./bin/just_induction.py [lambda]
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve_ind.py

The flow varies as \(e^{\lambda t}\): lambda is the optional argument, a complex number such as the eigenvalue of a mode, and its default is \(i\,\)forcing_frequency, the time dependence of the forced runs (a steady flow when it is 0). The field is written as real_magnetic.field, imag_magnetic.field (and the files of a conducting inner core or of a resolved mantle), one column per column of the flow.

docs.title: Forced runs
docs.text:
A forced run gives the response of the flow and the field to a periodic forcing at one frequency, such as a tide or a libration of the walls (forcing other than 0; Tidal forcing, Thermal forcing, Convective forcing). With a field every forcing runs as without one: the field is solved with the flow at the forcing frequency, with any of the walls and inner cores above, and spin_doctor checks the budgets of the solution. The solution is written as solved, with the amplitude that the forcing sets.

  • A conducting inner core at one frequency. At a single frequency the field inside a uniform conducting inner core is a spherical Bessel function of the radius. innercore = 'conducting, Bessel' uses it, so the core adds conditions at the inner wall but no unknowns, and gives the solution of 'conducting, Chebys' without N_cic. Since that field depends on the frequency, it serves the forced runs at forcing_frequency only. With a differential rotation the core turns with the fluid at the inner wall, and the frequency is that in its frame.
  • Budgets. resid𝐄 includes the work of the pressure, with its magnetic part, where the forcing moves a boundary, and the work of a conducting solid that the boundary moves on the field (Energy budgets).
  • Kinematic induction works in the directory of a forced run too: just_induction.py without lambda takes the forced matrix as it is, at forcing_frequency. Another lambda needs B.npz, which forcing 11 alone writes.

The checks: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: A boundary that moves
docs.text:
Forcings 6, 9, 10 and 14, and 7 with m 2, stand for a boundary that moves or is not spherical. The walls stay spheres, and the forcing prescribes the radial flow at the wall instead. A conducting solid behind such a wall moves too, and the currents in it depend on how it moves across B0. forced_walls sets that motion:

forced_walls the solid behind the wall suits 'rigid' is at rest, and only its shape moves past the sphere: the flow passes through the wall a triaxial mantle that librates (7 with m 2), the flattened inner core of forcing 6 'deforming' deforms with the boundary: its surface moves with the fluid across the wall, and its inside moves with it a boundary that moves (9, 10), a tide (14) None (default) 'rigid' for forcings 6 and 7, 'deforming' for 9, 10 and 14

A deforming solid moves in the simplest way that matches the wall:

  • a resolved mantle moves radially only, with a speed that falls as \(1/r^2\) from that of the wall, which keeps the volume of every shell;
  • a conducting inner core ('conducting, Chebys') moves with the simplest flow that is regular at its centre and has no motion along the wall;
  • with 'TWA' the solid moves with the fluid across the wall (and along it where the wall is no-slip), and so does the thin conducting layer at its surface, the only part of it that conducts.

Its motion across the background field, continued into the solid from the wall, induces a field there, which kore solves for with the rest, and spin_doctor adds its work to resid𝐄. In a conducting inner core the background is continued as the simplest field that is regular at the centre, so 'dipole', whose source is at the centre, becomes there a field with currents. With a poloidal field and 'TWA', 'deforming' gives the solutions of the conductive_IC branch. Where a no-slip wall also moves along itself, as in a libration, the solid turns with it in both pictures. With insulating solids forced_walls changes nothing. 'deforming' does not take 'conducting, Bessel' behind a wall that moves, since the core's field is then no longer a Bessel function.

In both pictures a wall that moves, where B0 reaches it, needs the same permeability on both sides: a surface where the permeability jumps would carry magnetized matter through B0 as it moves. So mu must be 1, and mu_i2o 1 with a conducting inner core. A thin layer's muw_cmb or muw_icb must be 1 where the poloidal part of B0 reaches the wall if the layer has a thickness (c not 0) or conducts at rest ('rigid'), and where the toroidal part reaches it if the layer conducts (c1 not 0). Otherwise it takes any value, as in an insulating layer (c and c1 both 0) or a conducting layer without a thickness (c 0) that deforms with the boundary under a poloidal B0. Walls that stay in place take any permeability.

The equations: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
kore checks the combination of options at startup and stops on any it cannot handle.

Supported: a shell or a full sphere (ricb = 0); any structure; eigenvalue problems and forced runs; with or without a differential rotation; ViscosD > 0, or ViscosD = 0 in a full sphere; with or without the flow (hydro = 0, above); insulating walls, a thin conducting layer, a resolved conducting mantle or a conducting inner core; with rotating solids (rotdyn = 1, Rotating solids). The magnetic diffusivity of the fluid is uniform.

Not supported (the run stops at startup):

  • no background field at all (B0 = None and B0_tor = None), or Le or Em zero;
  • ViscosD = 0 with an inner core (ricb > 0);
  • a conducting inner core in a full sphere, with zero radial stress at the inner wall (bci = 2), with an mu_i2o or a sigma_i2o that is not a positive number, with an odd N_cic or one below 4 ('conducting, Chebys'), with a rotation that varies with latitude at its surface, or with centrifugal = 1 and an mu_i2o other than 1 or a fluid slipping along it (bci = 0) across a poloidal field;
  • 'conducting, Bessel' in an eigenvalue problem, in a frequency scan of forcing 11 (rsf_frequencies), or in just_induction.py with a lambda other than \(i\,\)forcing_frequency; just_induction.py with such a lambda in a forced run other than forcing 11;
  • a thin conducting layer on the inner core in a full sphere, with centrifugal = 1, with zero radial stress at the wall (bco = 2 or bci = 2), or with a rotation that varies with latitude at the wall;
  • negative c_cmb, c1_cmb, c_icb or c1_icb, a muw_cmb, muw_icb or mu that is not positive, or mu other than 1 without a thin layer or a conducting inner core at every wall;
  • a resolved mantle with mu other than 1, with centrifugal = 1, with zero radial stress at the outer wall (bco = 2), or with a rotation that varies with latitude at the outer wall; an r_surface that is not above 1, an N_mantle that is not an integer of at least 4, or a sigma_mantle that is not positive everywhere in the layer or that N_mantle polynomials do not resolve;
  • with forced_walls = 'deforming' (the default of forcings 9, 10 and 14), 'conducting, Bessel' behind an inner wall that the forcing moves radially (forcing 6, and 9, 14 and 7 with m 2 where forcing_amplitude_icb is not 0);
  • the libration of the inner core (forcing 7 with m 0 and forcing_amplitude_icb not 0) behind a stress-free inner wall (bci = 0) along a conducting inner core or a conducting thin layer on it, across a poloidal field;
  • a current sheet of the field (a toroidal field that is not zero at the wall, or a poloidal one that does not meet the field beyond) at the wall of an inviscid full sphere, or at a slipping wall with centrifugal = 1, with an insulator or a thin layer that does not conduct (c1_cmb or c1_icb 0) beyond (Current sheets at slipping walls);
  • 'axial' at a slipping wall, or 'dipole' or B0_ic = 'frozen currents' at a slipping inner wall, where the permeability jumps (mu other than 1, or a thin layer whose c_cmb or c_icb is not 0 and whose muw_cmb or muw_icb is not 1), with an insulator or a thin layer that does not conduct beyond;
  • a permeability other than 1 at a wall that the forcing moves radially and that B0 reaches: mu, mu_i2o with a conducting inner core, and a thin layer's muw_cmb or muw_icb where the part of B0 that it acts on reaches the wall (A boundary that moves); the outer wall moves under forcing 10, and under 9, 14 and 7 with m 2 where forcing_amplitude_cmb is not 0, the inner wall under 6, 9, 14 and 7 with m 2 where forcing_amplitude_icb is not 0;
  • a poloidal and a toroidal part of opposite equatorial symmetry;
  • the limits of the options above:
    • 'dipole' in a full sphere;
    • degrees other than 1 or 2 for 'FDM', 'confined' and B0_tor_l, and 'Malkus' of degree 2 in a full sphere;
    • a 'confined' layer that is empty or does not lie in the fluid, or B0_conf_p below 3;
    • B0_tor = 'user' without B0_tor_profile, or 'general' without profiles or with degrees that are not positive integers of one parity; a 'user' or 'general' profile that is not finite at a point where it is interpolated (r = 0 among them in a full sphere, where an expression that is 0/0 needs another form);
    • an expression (B0_tor_profile, B0_profiles, B0_tor_profiles, B0_ferraro_G, diff_rot_F, sigma_mantle) that is empty or contains #;
    • a cnorm other than a number, 'rms_cmb', 'mag_energy' or 'Schmitt2012', or 'rms_cmb' with 'confined', 'general' or 'ferraro'; a cnorm_tor other than a number, 'mag_energy' or 'Schmitt2012'; a field that is zero with 'mag_energy' or 'Schmitt2012';
    • B0 = 'ferraro' without diff_rot = 1, with diff_rot_type = 'ferraro', with a B0_ferraro_G that is not finite on the values the rotation takes, or with B0_ferraro_nmax even or below 1;
    • diff_rot_type = 'ferraro' without a poloidal field, with a diff_rot_F of the wrong equatorial symmetry, or with a negative or odd diff_rot_nmax;
    • B0_wound = 1 without a poloidal field or without diff_rot = 1, with B0_wound_eta not positive, or with a mantle other than 'insulator' or a thin layer on the inner core;
  • with ferraro_policy = 'refuse', a field and a rotation further than 1e-7 from the Ferraro condition;
  • a value of B0, B0_tor, mantle, innercore, mag_couplings, B0_ic, B0_cmb, forced_walls or ferraro_policy other than those listed on this page.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A magnetic run writes the perturbation field next to the flow, and spin_doctor checks each mode with the magnetic energy budgets.

solve.py writes real_magnetic.field and imag_magnetic.field (and real_magnetic_ic.field, imag_magnetic_ic.field for a conducting inner core, real_magnetic_mantle.field, imag_magnetic_mantle.field for a resolved mantle; 'conducting, Bessel' writes no inner-core field). Each eigenvector is normalised so that the kinetic energy plus Hendrik times the magnetic energy is 1 in the fluid (the magnetic energy alone without the flow, hydro = 0); a forced solution is written as solved.

spin_doctor adds the Lorentz work to residσ and residω, and prints two more residuals: resid𝐛, the energy budget of the induction equation in the fluid, and resid𝐄, the full energy budget including the field outside the fluid, in thin layers, in a resolved mantle and in rotating solids (not with thin layers and mu other than 1, with stress-free walls and centrifugal = 1, or with rotating solids unless vtrq and mtrq are 1). Like residσ (Solver), they should be small for a resolved mode; with a thin layer whose c is not zero resid𝐄 closes only to the order of the approximation, about εTWA. It also prints Mag/Kin, the ratio of magnetic to kinetic energy (Hendrik ME/KE, both in the units of the kinetic energy), εTWA with a thin layer, and writes magnetic.dat and the magnetic columns of params.dat (Output files).

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
The field, more than the flow, usually sets the resolution and the memory a run needs.

  • Resolution. Where a poloidal field crosses a no-slip wall, a thin magnetic boundary layer (a Hartmann layer) forms. It, not the bulk flow, usually sets N, and it gets thinner at lower Ekman numbers. A toroidal field alone has no Hartmann layer and converges faster. A full sphere needs about twice the N of a shell. Always compare the residuals at two values of N; examples are in the checks.
  • 'confined' converges more slowly than the other fields, since it is smooth only to a finite order at its edges, and most slowly when its layer reaches the centre of a full sphere.
  • tol_B0 (default 1e-8) is the relative cut of the radial series of the background field. It sets the band width of the magnetic blocks and the fill-in of the LU factors. Lower it for more accurate operators.
  • mag_couplings chooses how the couplings are built. 'closed' (default) uses closed formulas, which exist for fields of degree 1 and 2. 'algebra' builds them for any degree (bin/mag_algebra.py); it is used automatically for 'general' (poloidal or toroidal), 'ferraro' and B0_wound = 1. Both give the same eigenvalues to round-off.
  • Memory. Fields of high degree, and wound fields with a high-degree rotation, couple more degrees and need more LU memory. If MUMPS stops with INFOG(1) = −9, raise st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 in petsc_opts (Solver).

docs.title: Validity and caveats
docs.text:
kore holds the background field and the background flow fixed. This section says what that leaves out and when it matters. Two effects that would change the background are left out:

  • Ohmic decay. A field that carries electric current would decay by diffusion; kore holds it fixed, with or without rotation. Only the wound field is steady by itself, since the winding balances its diffusion.
  • The Lorentz force of the background field on the background flow. The rotation is imposed and is not changed by the field, and the thermal-wind entropy is computed from the rotation alone. With B0_wound = 1 this force is dominated by the wound field, which can be large.

docs.title: When the field leaves the thermal wind unchanged
docs.text:
With thermal_wind 1 or 2, the latitudinal entropy of the background balances the differential rotation alone (Background model). The force of the background field would enter the same balance. The derivations and the estimates are in Magnetic field equations.

Exact: a field without current. A poloidal field that carries no electric current in the fluid, with no toroidal part, exerts no force, so the thermal wind is exact. If the rotation also satisfies the Ferraro condition, the field does not wind up or decay, and the whole background is steady. B0 = 'axial' and 'dipole' are such fields, and so is a 'general' field whose profile of each degree n combines r**n and, in a shell, r**-(n+1).

Approximate: any other field. All other fields carry current: the other poloidal types, any B0_tor, and the wound field. The background is then a good approximation under three conditions.

  1. The meridional force is weak. The field's force in the meridional planes (magnetic pressure, the hoop stress of the azimuthal field, the tension of curved poloidal lines) adds to the thermal-wind balance. It is negligible when

    \[ \frac{\mathrm{Le}^2\,\lvert\mathbf B_0\rvert^2}{\rho_0} \ll 2\,\lvert\Delta\Omega\rvert , \]

    with \(\rho_0\) the background density and \(\mathbf B_0\) the whole dimensionless field, wound part included. A field that varies on a shorter scale than the rotation makes this stricter. Where it fails, the thermal-wind entropy is wrong by about the ratio of the two sides.

  2. The torque is slow. A poloidal field crossed by the shear brakes it (Ferraro's mechanism), at a rate set by the Elsasser number of the poloidal field built on the background diffusivity:

    \[ \Lambda_p = \frac{\mathrm{Le}^2}{\rho_0\,\mathrm{Em}\,\eta_w}, \]

    with \(\eta_w\) = B0_wound_eta. The thermal wind follows the imposed rotation, so the torque does not change it directly, but the rotation must be maintained against it. The torque is negligible when this rate is small compared with the mode frequencies, their damping rates, and the rate of whatever maintains the rotation. If viscous or turbulent stresses hold the rotation, it is tenable only for a Hartmann number of order one or less:

    \[ Ha = \frac{\mathrm{Le}}{\sqrt{\rho_0\,\mathrm{Ek}\,\mathrm{Em}\,\eta_w}} \lesssim 1 . \]

  3. The field is steady. The Ferraro condition holds, or B0_wound = 1 balances the winding. The wound field can be much stronger than the poloidal field that makes it, so it must meet condition 1 too. The Ohmic decay of the field must be slow compared with the modes.

Where the rotation is uniform there is no thermal wind. In a stably stratified region the field's force is then balanced by a small change of the stratification, which kore leaves out. It is negligible when the Alfvén frequency is far below the buoyancy frequency.

What condition 1 means for the modes. The error it leaves in the frequencies is about half the left side of condition 1, in units of the rotation rate, for modes that feel the baroclinicity (more for slower modes). The field's direct effect on a mode, which kore includes in full, is larger by a factor that grows as the square of the number of the mode's wavelengths along the field lines. So a field can change the modes while leaving the thermal wind unchanged.

docs.title: Wound fields and the tachocline
docs.text:
A B0_wound background is a snapshot: it holds only for modes faster than the braking and the decay above. This is the tachocline confinement problem (Gough & McIntyre 1998; MacGregor & Charbonneau 1999). With molecular diffusivities, even a weak poloidal field in the radiative interior has a large Hartmann number, and its torque would impose isorotation along its field lines and spread the shear of the convection zone inward. A wound field that strong would brake the shear that makes it, as self-consistent tachocline models include.

A field below the tachocline is better represented by a 'confined' field whose layer lies there (B0_conf_r2 below the tachocline): the rotation is uniform there, so the Ferraro condition holds. A B0 = 'ferraro' field cannot be put there, since it follows the surfaces of constant rotation and vanishes where the rotation is uniform. A toroidal B0_tor can be added for the tachocline and the convection zone, since a toroidal field is never wound up.

The checks of this code, with a Hartmann number near 30 and a braking time shorter than a rotation period, test the mathematics (closed form, residuals, budgets), not the physical validity of such a background.

docs.title: The Sun, Jupiter and Saturn
docs.text:
Orders of magnitude with published values, where the field and the shear meet. The numbers and references are on Magnetic field equations.

region condition 1: meridional force condition 2: torque the background Sun, convection zone holds: a mean field of a few thousand G in the lower half gives a ratio of 10⁻³ or less, and the mean field is weaker higher up the weak mean poloidal field (about 10 G) brakes the rotation over a century or more; Hartmann number of order one with turbulent values consistent; the rotation does not follow poloidal field lines, so use a toroidal B0_tor, or B0_wound from a weak poloidal field Sun, tachocline holds for 10⁴ G (ratio about 0.005); fails near 10⁵ G (ratio about 0.5) set by the poloidal field and the diffusivity (above) consistent up to about 2×10⁴ G Sun, radiative interior no thermal wind: the rotation is uniform the Ferraro condition holds consistent with a 'confined' field whose layer lies below the tachocline Jupiter, winds (above 0.96 R) holds: ratio about 10⁻⁹ about a century consistent Saturn, winds (above 0.86 R) holds: ratio about 10⁻¹² about 10⁴ years consistent

The Sun is the case for magnetic effects on inertial modes. At the base of its convection zone a 10⁴ G field has a Lehnert number of a few hundredths: enough to matter for modes with several wavelengths along the field, while condition 1 still holds. In Jupiter and Saturn the Lehnert number is 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷. Their fields change neither the thermal wind nor the large-scale inertial modes measurably: kore's background is consistent there, and the field's effect on the modes is negligible.

docs.title: Checklist for solar inertial modes
docs.text:
Solar inertial modes have periods longer than a rotation (Löptien et al. 2018; Gizon et al. 2021). This makes the criteria above stricter: the effect of the field on a mode grows as its frequency falls, and the background must stay steady over the lifetime of the modes.

  • Time scales. The braking rate and the Ohmic decay rate of the poloidal field must be small compared with the damping rate of the modes, not only with their frequency. The wound field needs a diffusion time across its layer to build up (months to years for a thin tachocline with a turbulent diffusivity): on solar-cycle time scales it is a snapshot.
  • Sensitivity. The effect of the field grows roughly as the square of the Alfvén frequency over the mode frequency, so low-frequency modes feel it most. Scan B0_wound_eta and Le rather than trusting one value.
  • Critical layers and continua. Where the mode frequency matches the local advection by the rotation (the critical latitudes) and at Alfvén resonances, the spectrum has continuous parts and the eigenfunctions thin layers. Check convergence in N and lmax, and tell discrete modes from the continuum.
  • Thermal wind. Keep the thermal-wind entropy on (thermal_wind 1 or 2) and check condition 1 above: the background baroclinicity does not include the forces of the field.
  • Consistent diffusivities. The observed line widths constrain the turbulent viscosity (Ek). Take a turbulent magnetic Prandtl number near one (Em close to Ek), and build the wound field with the same turbulent diffusivity (B0_wound_eta = 1). A wound field built with a molecular diffusivity under modes damped by turbulence is inconsistent.
  • Radiative interior. With molecular values the Hartmann number there is huge, so a field there must not cross a shear: its torque would remove the shear (Ferraro's mechanism). Keep the field below the tachocline, where the rotation is uniform: use 'confined' with its layer there, not B0_wound.
  • Where the modes live. Most observed modes are concentrated in the convection zone (many near the surface or the equator), so a tachocline field reaches them only through their tails. Test the high-latitude and deep modes first.
  • Measurability. A frequency shift matters only above about 1 nHz, a few thousandths of the rotation rate.
  • Symmetry. A dipolar poloidal field with kore's equatorially symmetric rotation gives a wound field of the same family, so the two mode classes stay separate, as without the field.
  • Practical. The wound field has degrees up to the sum of those of the rotation and of the poloidal field, plus one, so a high-degree 'tabulated' rotation means wide couplings and more memory (see Practical tips). In each run read the printed residual of the induction balance.
  • Field geometry. The field inside the Sun is not known, and each set-up imposes its own geometry. Compute the same modes with more than one (for example a toroidal B0_tor, and B0_wound from a weak poloidal field) at a similar field strength: the spread shows how much the results depend on the field assumed.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Magnetic field equations: the equations, every field profile, the rows, the boundary conditions, the four steady set-ups with a differential rotation, the energy budgets, and the checks against conductive_IC and published results.
  • Derivation tools, part A: how the magnetic rows are derived (tests/magnetic/derive.py), fitted (tools/derive/) and built for any degree (bin/mag_algebra.py).
  • Output files: the columns of magnetic.dat and the magnetic columns of params.dat.

docs.title: Numerical method
docs.text: This page shows how kore turns the anelastic equations into the sparse matrices of an eigenvalue problem: the unknowns, the radial basis, the rows, the boundary conditions and the checks of a solution. The terms of a differential rotation are built in the same way (Differential rotation, §3 to §7).

docs.title: Unknowns
docs.text:
At fixed \(m\) and equatorial symmetry, the velocity is written with a poloidal scalar \(P\) and a toroidal scalar \(T\),

\[ \mathbf u = rac{1}{ ho_0} abla imes abla imes\left( ho_0 P hinspace\mathbf r ight) + abla imes\left(T hinspace\mathbf r ight), \]

so that \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0\) holds exactly and the mass equation is never solved. For one harmonic \(Y = Y_l^m( heta,\phi)\), with \(P = P_l(r) hinspace Y\), \(T = T_l(r) hinspace Y\) and \(\mathcal L = l(l+1)\),

\[ u_r = rac{\mathcal L hinspace P_l}{r} hinspace Y, \qquad \mathbf u_h = \left(P_l' + rac{P_l}{r} + rac{d\ln ho_0}{dr}P_l ight) r abla Y + T_l hinspace abla Y imes\mathbf r , \]

with a prime for \(d/dr\) (utils4pp.cheb2space_pol, cheb2space_tor). With thermal = 1 the third unknown is \(s = s_l(r) hinspace Y\).

docs.title: Radial basis
docs.text: Each radial function \(P_l\), \(T_l\), \(s_l\) is expanded in Chebyshev polynomials: N of them on the shell \([\)ricb\(, 1]\), or, in a full sphere (ricb = 0), the N/2 polynomials on \([-1, 1]\) that have the parity of the field. A radial derivative of order \(k\) maps Chebyshev coefficients to coefficients in the Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) basis \(C^{(k)}\), where it is a sparse matrix, and so is the product with a profile expanded in Chebyshev polynomials. The rows of each section are written in the Gegenbauer basis of its highest derivative: \(C^{(4)}\) for u, \(C^{(2)}\) for v and h (\(C^{(0)}\) for h with ThermaD = 0, \(C^{(1)}\) if a thermal wind is included). This makes \(A\) and \(B\) sparse.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
The pressure is removed by taking the radial components of the curl and of the double curl of the momentum equation; \( abla\Pi\) drops out of both because it is a gradient. Each term becomes a radial operator acting on \(P_l\), \(T_l\) or \(s_l\):

section rows equation used u of \(P_l\) \(r^5 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes( ext{momentum})/\mathcal L^3\) v of \(T_l\) \(r^3 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes( ext{momentum})/\mathcal L^3\) h of \(s_l\) \(r^2 hinspace( ext{heat equation})/\mathcal L^3\)

All rows are projected on \(Y_l^m\) and divided by \(\mathcal L^3\), with \(l\) the degree of the row. The powers of \(r\) are rpower_u (5) and rpower_v (3), the smallest that keep every operator a polynomial in \(r\). The factor \( ho_0\) (rhopower_u = rhopower_v = 1) improves the accuracy of the viscous rows near a surface where \( ho_0\) is small. Without viscosity (ViscosD = 0) the momentum rows are \(r^3 ho_0^2\) and \(r^2 ho_0\) times the equations. With ThermaD = 0 the heat rows are divided by \(p_0\), \(r hinspace(\partial_t s + u_r hinspace dS/dr)/\mathcal L^3\), which is better conditioned where \(p_0\) is small (and \(r^2/p_0\) times the equation with the thermal wind). The Coriolis force couples \(l\) to \(l\pm1\); the other terms keep \(l\).

term function in bin/operators.py profiles \(\partial_t\mathbf u\) inertia \(\ln ho_0\) \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\) coriolis \(\ln ho_0\) \(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u\mathsf S)\) viscous_diffusion \(\ln ho_0\) (up to its 4th derivative), \( u\) (up to its 2nd) \(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) buoyancy \(g\) \(p_0 hinspace\partial_t s\) entropy \(p_0\) \(p_0 hinspace u_r hinspace dS/dr\) thermal_advection \(p_0 hinspace dS/dr\) (\(dS/dr\) if ThermaD = 0) \(\mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s)\) thermal_diffusion \(\kappa p_0\)

submatrices.py writes one sparse matrix per radial operator, for example u1lho2_D0 for \(r^4 ho_0 hinspace(\ln ho_0)''\) times the unknown (the label grammar and the profile codes are in utils.decode_label and radial_profiles.proffdir). For the section h row with ThermaD > 0, for example, the diffusion term is

\[ r^2 abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s) = \left[r^2\kappa p_0 hinspace s_l'' + \left(2r\kappa p_0 + r^2(\kappa p_0)' ight)s_l' - \mathcal L hinspace\kappa p_0 hinspace s_l ight] Y. \]

docs.title: Eigenproblem
docs.text:
assemble.py puts the blocks into \(A\mathbf x = \lambda B\mathbf x\). \(B\) holds \(-\)inertia in the momentum rows and entropy in the heat rows. \(A\) holds coriolis \(-\) viscous_diffusion \(-\) buoyancy in the momentum rows and \(-\)thermal_advection \(+\) thermal_diffusion in the heat rows, so each row reads

\[ \lambda hinspace\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u = \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u\mathsf S) + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}, \] \[ \lambda hinspace p_0 s = -p_0 u_r rac{dS}{dr} + \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s), \]

projected as in the table above. solve.py finds the eigenvalues nearest a target \( au\) by shift-and-invert with SLEPc, factoring \(A - au B\) once with MUMPS (Solver). Forced runs solve \((A - i hinspace\mathrm{wf} hinspace B)\mathbf x = \mathbf b\), with wf the forcing frequency; for the random force of forcing 11, \(\mathbf b\) is derived on Reynolds-stress forcing.

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
The conditions (assemble.bc_u_spherical, bc_theta_spherical) are applied at the outer wall (bco) and at the inner one (bci, when ricb > 0); the full sphere has no condition at the centre:

setting condition rows bco = 0 stress-free \(u_r = 0\), and zero tangential stress \(\partial_r(u_\theta/r) = \partial_r(u_\phi/r) = 0\) \(P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace r^2P_l'' + r^2(\ln\rho_0)'P_l' + \left[r^2(\ln\rho_0)'' + \mathcal L - 2 - r(\ln\rho_0)'\right]P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace rT_l' - T_l = 0\) bco = 0 with a drag (kappa_cmb, topo_drag) \(u_r = 0\), and the tangential stress balances the drag of the wall on the slip the stress-free rows plus the terms of the drag (Drag at the outer wall equations) bco 0 or 2 where the background field ends in a current sheet the tangential stress balances the push of the sheet on the fluid the stress-free rows plus the terms of the push (Magnetic field equations) bco = 1 no-slip \(\mathbf u = 0\) \(P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace P_l' + \left[(\ln\rho_0)' + 1/r\right]P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace T_l = 0\) bco_thermal = 0 fixed entropy \(s_l = 0\) bco_thermal = 1 zero diffusive entropy flux \(s_l' = 0\)

The density enters the stress-free and no-slip rows through \(u_\theta\) and \(u_\phi\). The thermal conditions are used only when ThermaD > 0. Without viscosity only \(P_l = 0\) is imposed. bco = 2 (and bci = 2) replaces \(u_r = 0\) by a zero viscous radial stress, \(\left[r(\ln\rho_0)' - 3\right]P_l + 3rP_l' = 0\), which does not contain the pressure.

docs.title: Regularity at the centre
docs.text:
The centre of a full sphere is not a boundary, but the fields must be smooth there, and kore imposes no condition to make them so. This section says why none is needed, when a solution is still not smooth at the centre, and how to check it.

A field that is smooth at the centre has radial functions that go as \(r^l\) there, for a component of degree \(l\), times a series in \(r^2\). The basis gives \(P_l\), \(T_l\), \(s_l\) (and the \(f_l\), \(g_l\) of a magnetic field) the parity of \(l\), and the equations exclude the lower powers of that parity, as long as the background is smooth at the centre too. Each background profile follows the same rule with its own degree \(n\): the \(f_n\) of a differential rotation, the \(h_n\), \(k_n\) of a magnetic field and the \(\sigma_n\) of a thermal wind go as \(r^n\), \(dS/dr\) and \(g\) as \(r\), and \(\ln\rho_0\), \(p_0\), \(\nu\), \(\kappa\) are series in \(r^2\). kore evaluates every profile at \(\lvert r\rvert\) with the parity of its degree, which gives the parity but neither the power nor the smoothness. A profile can fail in two ways:

  • It lacks the power. The \(P_2\) term of 'Y20' and 'conical', and the entropy of thermal_wind 3, keep their value at the centre. The modes converge in N, but to solutions that are not smooth there either.
  • It has a kink or a jump. Its even or odd continuation to \(r < 0\) is not smooth: 'Y20-wall-bounded', 'shellular' unless \(\sigma\) is even and positive, a 'user' expression in \(\lvert r\rvert\), a \(dS/dr\) that changes abruptly near the centre. The modes then converge slowly in N.

With ricb = 0, submatrices.py checks every profile near the centre and prints a WARNING for each failure (background.centre_check).

Spurious modes. Without viscosity (ViscosD = 0) or with ThermaD = 0, the spectrum of a full sphere also holds modes that do not converge when N or lmax is raised: without viscosity some of them grow, with ThermaD = 0 they crowd near zero frequency. Many of them sit at the centre, where they are not smooth; others sit at the wall. Target the frequency of the mode you want, and keep the modes that stay put in N and lmax.

irreg₀. In a full sphere spin_doctor prints irreg₀ for each solution (column 28 of flow.dat): the largest term \(a_p r^p\) with \(p < l\) of the flow and of the field, at \(r = \pi/\mathrm N\) (about the spacing of the Chebyshev points at the centre), relative to their largest value (utils4pp.centre_irregularity). It is at round-off for a resolved smooth mode and near 1 for a spurious mode at the centre. Values in between come from a background that is not smooth at the centre, or from a mode that is not resolved there. After the table spin_doctor counts the solutions above \(10^{-6}\).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
spin_doctor.py evaluates the budgets of Energy balance for each solution, from the fields and independently of the matrices. The radial integrals use Gauss–Legendre quadrature with \(3N/2\) nodes, the angular ones the orthogonality of the harmonics (\(\int\lvert Y_l vert^2 hinspace d\Omega = 4\pi/(2l+1)\)). The force of a differential rotation and the dissipation \(D_ u\) are computed on an \((r, \cos heta)\) grid, with Gauss–Legendre quadrature in \(\cos heta\), exact for these polynomials. Each residual is relative to the largest of its terms:

residual budget in spin_doctor's names residσ \(2\sigma K - W_ u - W_b - W_\Omega - W_p = 0\) (and the Lorentz work) 2σ KE - Dkin - Wthm - Wdr - Wp residω its imaginary part, with the Coriolis force 2w KE + Wcor_im - Dkin_im - Wthm_im - Wdr_im - Wp_im, \(w = \mathrm{Im} hinspace\lambda\) resid\(s\) \(2\sigma T - W_{ m adv} + D_{ m th} - W_{\Omega, m th} = 0\) 2σ TE - Dthm - Wadv - Wdr_thm (Dthm \(= -D_{ m th}\)) residD \(W_ u - W_ u^{ m wall} + D_ u = 0\) Dkin - (Wv_icb + Wv_cmb) + Dvisc resid𝐋 \(\lambda L\) = the torques on the fluid (Rotating solids equations) lam*angmom - (-vtorq - vtorq_ic - mtorq - mtorq_ic [+ i Gaspard angmom])

residσ and resid\(s\) judge whether a solution is resolved (Solver gives the thresholds), also for forced runs, where \(\sigma = 0\). residD compares two independent computations of the viscous terms: \(W_ u\) from the viscous force of each degree (utils4pp.visforce), and \(D_ u\) from the strain rate on the grid (utils4pp.viscous_dissipation). It is \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-12}\).

The work at the walls (utils4pp.wall_powers). kore does not solve for the pressure. spin_doctor recovers it from the momentum equation: \( abla\Pi = \mathbf F - \lambda\mathbf u\), with \(\mathbf F\) every force but the pressure, and the consoidal component of a gradient is \(\Pi_l/r\), so that for each degree \(l\) of \(P\)

\[ \Pi_l = r\left[\mathbf F - \lambda\mathbf u ight]_{s,l} , \]

the consoidal component of the Coriolis, viscous and differential-rotation forces and of \(\lambda\mathbf u\) (utils4pp.pressure_force). The buoyancy is radial and does not enter. With \(q_l = \mathcal L P_l/r\) the radial velocity, \(s_l\) and \(t_l\) the consoidal and toroidal components of \(\mathbf u\),

\[ W_p = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\sum_l rac{4\pi}{2l+1}\Big[ ho_0 hinspace r^2 hinspace q_l^* hinspace\Pi_l\Big]_{ m inner}^{ m outer}, \]

and the stress on a sphere is

\[ oldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf r} = \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0 u\left[\left(2q_l' + frac23(\ln ho_0)'q_l ight)Y\hat{\mathbf r} + \left(s_l' - rac{s_l}{r} + rac{q_l}{r} ight)r abla Y + \left(t_l' - rac{t_l}{r} ight)r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \]

dotted with \(\mathbf u^*\) and integrated over each wall for \(W_ u^{ m wall}\). flow.dat has these terms for each wall (Output files).

\(\Pi_l\) needs the radial derivatives of \(P_l\) up to the third at the walls. That is where the truncation error of the tau method is largest, and near a surface of low density the \((\ln ho_0)'\) terms of the viscous force amplify it. The wall pressure therefore converges with N more slowly than the volume integrals. For 'Wu 2005' (r_out 0.99) at Ek \(10^{-3}\), residσ of a forced run is \(5 imes10^{-2}\) at N 96 and \(2 imes10^{-10}\) at N 192 in a shell, and 0.36, \(6 imes10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-8}\) at N 192, 288 and 384 in a full sphere, while the kinetic energy and the dissipation have converged at the lowest N. Where \(u_r = 0\) at the walls, \(W_p = 0\) whatever the resolution.

ru_insane.py checks the same pairings on the operators themselves: inertia Hermitian and positive, Coriolis anti-Hermitian, viscous Hermitian and negative, the entropy and diffusion blocks, the buoyancy and the advection against quadratures, and the differential-rotation blocks against an \((r, heta)\) grid. tests/tidal checks the budgets with moving walls, against an exact solution of the forced flow and on runs with a variable density, buoyancy and a differential rotation.
