docs.title: Reynolds-stress forcing
docs.text: This page derives the random force of forcing 11: where it comes from, its statistics, why its strength follows from the viscosity, how kore writes it in its variables, and what the resulting spectrum means. How to run it is on Convective forcing. The notation is that of Anelastic equations, in kore's units.

docs.title: Where the force comes from
docs.text:
In a convection zone the velocity is the sum of a large-scale flow \(\mathbf u\), the modes that kore solves for, and the convective eddies \(\mathbf u'\), which are much smaller and faster. The eddies act on \(\mathbf u\) through the divergence of their flux of momentum, the Reynolds stress: the momentum equation of \(\mathbf u\) contains the force

\[ - rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 hinspace\mathbf u'\mathbf u' ight). \]

This force has two parts.

  1. The response to the large-scale flow. On average the eddies mix momentum down the gradients of \(\mathbf u\), as a viscosity does: the trace-free part of the mean of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) changes by \(- u_t hinspace\mathsf S(\mathbf u)\), with \( u_t\) the turbulent (eddy) viscosity and \(\mathsf S\) the trace-free rate of strain. In a convection zone this is kore's viscous force: kore's viscosity \( u\) is the sum of \( u_t\) and a part \( u_f\) that is not turbulent, such as the viscosity of a radiative zone.
  2. The fluctuation. What is left, \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) minus its mean, does not depend on \(\mathbf u\). It is a random stress, and its divergence is a random force that drives the modes,
\[ \mathbf f = rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 hinspace\mathsf s ight), \]

with \(\mathsf s\) a random symmetric tensor per unit mass. Its sign does not matter, since \(\mathsf s\) and \(-\mathsf s\) have the same statistics.

The two parts come from the same eddies, so they are not independent. The viscous part alone would damp every mode to zero, and the random part alone would let the modes grow without bound. Together they keep each mode at a finite energy, in a statistically steady state. Brownian motion is the same: the friction on a particle and the random kicks it receives come from the same molecules, and their ratio is set by the temperature (Einstein's relation). For a fluid in thermal equilibrium, Landau and Lifshitz add to the viscous stress a random stress whose variance is the temperature times the viscosity, so that the fluctuations of the flow have the energy that equipartition requires. Forcing 11 applies this construction to the eddies: the viscosity is \( u_t\), and the temperature is a turbulent temperature \(\Theta(r)\), about the kinetic energy of one eddy.

docs.title: The random stress
docs.text:
kore takes \(\mathsf s\) trace-free and white, with the covariance

\[ \mathbb E\left[s_{ij}(\mathbf x, t) hinspace s_{kl}^*(\mathbf x', t') ight] = rac{4 hinspace\Theta hinspace u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace\Pi_{ijkl} hinspace\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x') hinspace\delta(t - t'), \] \[ \Pi_{ijkl} = frac12\left(\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} + \delta_{il}\delta_{jk} ight) - frac13\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}, \]

where \(\mathbb E\) is the mean over realisations and \(\Pi\) the projector onto symmetric trace-free tensors. With \(\Theta\) replaced by \(k_B T\) and \( ho_0 u_t\) by the dynamic viscosity, this is the random stress of Landau and Lifshitz (divided by \( ho_0^2\), because \(\mathsf s\) is per unit mass).

  • White. The eddies are much smaller than the modes, and their turnover time is shorter than the periods of the modes, so that on the scales of the modes their stress is uncorrelated in space and time. kore can give the eddies a finite size (below).
  • Trace-free. The trace of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) is the turbulent pressure. Its gradient drops out of the curls that kore takes of the momentum equation, and what is left has no dissipative partner, since kore has no bulk viscosity. Leaving it out keeps the relation of the next section exact.
  • Strength. The factor \(4\Theta u_t/ ho_0\) is what the next section requires. A direct estimate gives the same form. For Gaussian eddies with \(\langle u'_i u'_k angle = frac13 u_c^2\delta_{ik}\), the trace-free part of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) has the covariance \(2(u_c^2/3)^2 hinspace\Pi\). If it is correlated over a volume \(\ell_c^3\) and a time \( au_c = \ell_c/u_c\), it acts on larger scales as a white noise of strength \(2(u_c^2/3)^2 hinspace\ell_c^3 au_c hinspace\Pi\). Equating this with \(4\Theta u_t\Pi/ ho_0\), with the mixing-length viscosity \( u_t = u_c\ell_c/3\), gives \(\Theta = ho_0 u_c^2\ell_c^3/6\); a time correlation \(e^{-\lvert t vert/ au_c}\), whose integral over all lags is \(2 au_c\), gives
\[ \Theta = frac13 hinspace ho_0 hinspace u_c^2 hinspace\ell_c^3 , \]

the value kore uses. \(\Theta\) is thus the kinetic energy of one eddy, up to a factor of order 1, which rsf_scale absorbs.

docs.title: Energy of a mode
docs.text:
With the inner product \(\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf b angle = \int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf a^*\cdot\mathbf b hinspace dV\), kore normalizes its eigenvectors to \(\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf a angle = 1\), a kinetic energy of 1. The random stress vanishes at the walls (below), so for any velocity field \(\mathbf a\) an integration by parts gives

\[ \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle = -\int ho_0 hinspace abla\mathbf a^* : \mathsf s hinspace dV = - frac12\int ho_0 hinspace\mathsf S(\mathbf a)^* : \mathsf s hinspace dV, \]

because only the symmetric trace-free part of \( abla\mathbf a\), which is \( frac12\mathsf S(\mathbf a)\), meets the symmetric trace-free \(\mathsf s\). With the covariance above,

\[ \mathbb E\left[\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle(t) hinspace\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle^*(t') ight] = \int ho_0 hinspace\Theta hinspace u_t hinspace\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\;\delta(t - t'), \]

with \(\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 = \mathsf S^* : \mathsf S\). The viscous force does on the same field the work \(- frac12\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\) (Anelastic equations). The force that a field receives and the energy that it dissipates are the same integral: with a uniform \(\Theta\), the variance of the force is \(2\Theta\) times the dissipation by \( u_t\). This is the fluctuation–dissipation relation.

For a mode \(\mathbf a\) of eigenvalue \(\lambda\), with modes that are orthogonal, the amplitude of the mode obeys \(\dot c = \lambda c + \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle\), with \(-\mathrm{Re} hinspace\lambda = frac12\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\). A white force of strength \(Q\) keeps \(\mathbb E\lvert c vert^2 = Q/(2\lvert\mathrm{Re} hinspace\lambda vert)\), so the kinetic energy of the mode is

\[ \mathbb E\lvert c vert^2 = rac{\int ho_0\Theta u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV} = \Theta_{ m eff} hinspace f_t, \] \[ \Theta_{ m eff} = rac{\int ho_0\Theta u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}, \qquad f_t = rac{\int ho_0 u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}. \]
  • A mode holds the energy of one eddy, \(\Theta_{ m eff}\), averaged with the mode's own dissipation as the weight, times the share \(f_t\) of its damping that the turbulence provides. This is the result of Goldreich & Keeley (1977) for the solar p modes: the energy of a mode is about that of an eddy.
  • For a given \(\Theta\) the energy does not depend on the viscosity: \( u\) sets the width of the resonance, not its area. (With the 'nu' law of rsf_theta, \(\Theta\) itself grows as \( u_t^2\).)
  • A mode that dissipates mostly where the viscosity is not turbulent, in a radiative zone for example, has \(f_t \ll 1\) and receives little energy.
  • The modes are close to orthogonal when they are weakly damped in a uniformly rotating fluid. A differential rotation makes them far from orthogonal: the response to the force then differs from this estimate, and only the forced solve, which kore does, gives it.

docs.title: The force in kore's variables
docs.text:
At degree \(l\), with \(Y = Y_l^m\), \(n_l = \int\lvert Y vert^2 hinspace d\Omega = 4\pi/(2l+1)\), \(\mathcal L = l(l+1)\) and the vector harmonics \(\mathbf B = r abla Y\) and \(\mathbf C = \hat{\mathbf r} imes\mathbf B\), the stress is \(\mathsf s = \sum_k c_k(r) hinspace\mathsf T_k\) with five trace-free tensor harmonics:

\(k\) \(\mathsf T_k\) \(\int\lvert\mathsf T_k vert^2 hinspace d\Omega/n_l\) 1 \(Y hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r} - frac12 Y(\mathsf I - \hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r})\) \(3/2\) 2 \(\hat{\mathbf r}\mathbf B + \mathbf B\hat{\mathbf r}\) \(2\mathcal L\) 3 \(\hat{\mathbf r}\mathbf C + \mathbf C\hat{\mathbf r}\) \(2\mathcal L\) 5 \( abla_1 abla_1 Y + frac12\mathcal L hinspace Y(\mathsf I - \hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r})\), the trace-free Hessian of \(Y\) on the unit sphere \(\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)/2\) 6 the tensor of components \((-b, a, b)\), where \(\mathsf T_5\) has \((a, b, -a)\) \(\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)/2\)

\( abla_1\) is the gradient on the unit sphere, and the components are \(( heta heta, heta\phi, \phi\phi)\). \(\mathsf T_5\) and \(\mathsf T_6\) exist for \(l \geq 2\). The force \(\mathbf f = f^P hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r} + f^B hinspace\mathbf B + f^C hinspace\mathbf C\) then has, with \(h = d\ln ho_0/dr\) and a prime for \(d/dr\),

\[ f^P = c_1' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_1 - rac{\mathcal L hinspace c_2}{r}, \] \[ f^B = - rac{c_1}{2r} + c_2' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_2 - rac{(\mathcal L - 2) hinspace c_5}{2r}, \] \[ f^C = c_3' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_3 - rac{(\mathcal L - 2) hinspace c_6}{2r}. \]

kore's momentum rows are \(r^5 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes(\cdot)/\mathcal L^3\) and \(r^3 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes(\cdot)/\mathcal L^3\) (Numerical method), and the curls of \(\mathbf f\) at degree \(l\) are \((\mathcal L/r^2)[f^P - (rf^B)']\) and \(-(\mathcal L/r)f^C\). The right-hand side in the rows of \(P_l\) and \(T_l\) is therefore

\[ b_u = rac{r^3 ho_0}{\mathcal L^2}\left[f^P - (r f^B)' ight], \qquad b_v = - rac{r^2 ho_0}{\mathcal L^2} hinspace f^C, \]

for the default powers of \(r\) and \( ho_0\) (rpower_u, rhopower_u, rpower_v, rhopower_v in general), and zero in the rows of the heat equation.

  • Only the shear stresses drive the radial vorticity. \(c_3\) is the \(r heta\), \(r\phi\) part of the stress and \(c_6\) its horizontal shear: they force the toroidal rows, and with them the Rossby modes and the other vortical modes. \(c_1\), \(c_2\) and \(c_5\) force the poloidal flow.
  • Statistics. Since \(\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x') = \delta(r - r') hinspace\delta(\Omega - \Omega')/r^2\), the \(c_k\) are independent across \(k\), \(l\), \(m\) and frequency, with
\[ \mathbb E\left[c_k(r) hinspace c_k^*(r') ight] = rac{4\Theta u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace rac{\chi_k}{r^2 n_l} hinspace\delta(r - r'), \] \[ \chi_k = rac{n_l}{\int\lvert\mathsf T_k vert^2 hinspace d\Omega} = frac23,\ rac{1}{2\mathcal L},\ rac{1}{2\mathcal L},\ rac{2}{\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)},\ rac{2}{\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)} . \]

docs.title: Finite eddies and walls
docs.text:
A force that is white in radius cannot be resolved, and real eddies have a finite size. kore therefore smooths the noise over the eddy size \(\ell_c(r)\), and makes it vanish at the walls.

Radial correlation. The white \(\delta(r - r')\) is replaced by a unit-area Gaussian of width \(\ell_c\). kore draws the noise at centres \(r_j\) spaced \(h_j = \sigma_j/2\), with \(\sigma_j = \ell_c(r_j)/\sqrt2\), from below the inner wall (or \(r = 0\)) to above the outer wall, and builds

\[ c_k(r) = au(r) hinspace A_{lk}(r) hinspace S(r)^{-1/2}\sum_j\sqrt{h_j} hinspace\xi_j hinspace g_j(r), \] \[ S(r) = \sum_j h_j hinspace g_j(r), \qquad A_{lk} = \left( rac{4\Theta u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace rac{\chi_k}{r^2 n_l} ight)^{1/2}, \]

with \(g_j\) unit-area Gaussians of width \(\sigma_j\) centred at \(r_j\) and \(\xi_j\) independent complex Gaussian numbers of unit variance. For a uniform \(\ell_c\), \(\mathbb E[c_k(r)c_k^*(r')]\) is \( au(r) au(r')A_{lk}(r)A_{lk}(r')\) times a unit-area Gaussian of width \(\ell_c\) in \(r - r'\). The amplitude \(A_{lk}\) is taken at \(r\), not at the centres, so that the stress vanishes wherever \( u_t\) does: none of it leaks into a radiative zone.

Horizontal size. With rsf_angular = 1 the variance at degree \(l\) is multiplied by \(e^{-\mathcal L\ell_c^2/(2r^2)}\): eddies of size \(\ell_c\) do not force degrees much above \(r/\ell_c\).

Walls. At a stress-free wall the rows carry no surface traction, so the stress must vanish there. The taper \( au\) goes from 1 to 0 over rsf_taper below the outer wall, as \( frac12 hinspace\mathrm{erfc}\) of width rsf_taper/8 centred rsf_taper/2 below it. The same holds above an inner core, over rsf_taper_in above \(r = 0\) in a full sphere, and above rsf_rcut over rsf_rcut_width when a cut is set.

These choices only lower the force: for every field \(\mathbf a\),

\[ \mathbb E\lvert\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle vert^2 \leq \int ho_0 hinspace\Theta u_t hinspace au^2 hinspace e^{-\mathcal L\ell_c^2/(2r^2)} hinspace\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV \]

per unit time, with equality in the white limit. A mode receives less energy than \(\Theta_{ m eff}f_t\) when its radial or horizontal scale approaches \(\ell_c\), and when it dissipates near a wall, inside the taper.

docs.title: Eddy size and turbulent temperature
docs.text:
• Turbulent viscosity. \( u_t\) = ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\), clipped at 0, with \(\hat u\) the viscosity profile and \( u_f\) = rsf_nu_floor (Convective forcing).
  • Eddy size. \(\ell_c = \left(\ell_{\max}^{-4} + (\alpha H_p)^{-4} ight)^{-1/4}\), a smooth minimum of \(\alpha H_p\) and \(\ell_{\max}\), with \(H_p = -p_0/p_0'\) the pressure scale height (infinite at \(r = 0\)), \(\alpha\) = rsf_alpha and \(\ell_{\max}\) = rsf_lc_max; or the constant rsf_lc.
  • Turbulent temperature, rsf_theta, times rsf_scale:
    • 'nu': eddies of size \(\ell_c\) whose mixing-length viscosity is \( u_t\), \(u_c = 3 u_t/\ell_c\), so that \(\Theta = frac13 ho_0u_c^2\ell_c^3 = 3 ho_0 u_t^2\ell_c\);
    • 'mlt': the mixing-length velocity of the convective flux, \(u_c^3 = \alpha F_c/(10 ho_0)\), with \(F_c = L_\star/(4\pi r^2) hinspace u_t/\max u_t\) and the luminosity \(L_\star\) = rsf_lum, and \(\Theta = frac13 ho_0u_c^2\ell_c^3\);
    • a number: a uniform \(\Theta\).

\(\Theta\) is an energy, in units of \( ho_u L^5/ au^2\), with \( ho_u\) the unit of density and \(L\) and \( au\) the units of length and time.

docs.title: The spectrum
docs.text:
Each realisation is the Fourier amplitude of the force at the frequency \(w\), normalized so that, for any quantity \(y\) that depends linearly on the flow, \(\mathbb E\lvert y(w)\rvert^2\) is the two-sided power spectral density of \(y\): \(\int\mathbb E\lvert y(w)\rvert^2\thinspace dw/2\pi\) is the variance of \(y\). The kinetic energy that kore reports for an azimuthal wavenumber \(m\) is that of the real flow \(\mathbf u\thinspace e^{im\phi}\) + c.c., so that for \(m \neq 0\) the integral of the mean kinetic energy over \(dw/2\pi\) is the mean kinetic energy of the forced flow. For \(m = 0\) the flow is real, its spectrum is even in \(w\), and the halves \(w > 0\) and \(w < 0\) are the same motion: the integral over all \(w\) is twice the energy. A white noise is white in every rotating frame, so the frame of the run does not matter.

Near a mode, the forced flow is \(c(w)\thinspace\mathbf a\) with \(c(w) = \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f(w)\rangle/(iw - \lambda)\), and its mean kinetic energy is

\[ \mathbb E\lvert c(w)\rvert^2 = \frac{Q}{(\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda)^2 + (w - \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda)^2}, \]

a Lorentzian centred at \(w = \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\), of half-width \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\) and height \(H = Q/(\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda)^2\). Its area, \(\int\mathbb E\lvert c\rvert^2\thinspace dw/2\pi = Q/(2\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert)\), is the energy of the mode: \(H\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert/2\).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The model is linear: it gives the energy that each mode receives, not the nonlinear saturation or the coupling between modes.
  • An unstable mode has no stationary response.
  • The time correlation of the eddies is neglected. Deep in the solar convection zone the turnover time approaches the periods of the inertial modes. The fluctuation–dissipation relation still holds for a viscosity that depends on frequency: read \(\nu_t\) as the eddy viscosity at the frequency of the modes.
  • Left out: the turbulent pressure (the trace of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\)), the fluctuations of the convective heat flux (the heat equation is not forced) and any anisotropy of the eddies.

Philidet & Gizon (2023) model the same source for the solar Rossby modes on a two-dimensional \(\beta\) plane, with a source taken from the observed surface turbulence and a damping set separately. Here the source and the damping are tied by the fluctuation–dissipation relation, and the source has a depth profile.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Goldreich, P. & Keeley, D. A. 1977, ApJ 212, 243.
  • Landau, L. D. & Lifshitz, E. M. 1987, Fluid Mechanics, 2nd ed., Pergamon, chapter XVII (Fluctuations in fluid dynamics).
  • Löptien, B., Gizon, L., Birch, A. C. et al. 2018, Nature Astronomy 2, 568.
  • Philidet, J. & Gizon, L. 2023, A&A 673, A124.

docs.title: Rotating solids equations
docs.text: This page gives the equations of the rotating solids (rotdyn = 1, Rotating solids), the torques that couple them to the fluid, and the angular momentum balance that spin_doctor checks (resid𝐋). They are those of the conductive_IC branch (its rows in assemble.py, utils.gamma_visc, gamma_magnetic, utils4pp.angrymom and torque_walls), written for any density profile and any poloidal background field in bin/rotdyn.py.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
The mantle and the inner core turn about the rotation axis at the rates \(\omega_M\) and \(\omega_{IC}\) relative to the frame, and \(\varphi\) is the angle of the inner core relative to the mantle. Each solid's angular momentum changes by the torques on it. For a mode \(e^{\lambda t}\)

\[ \lambda I_M\,\omega_M = \Gamma_M + K\varphi, \qquad \lambda I_{IC}\,\omega_{IC} = \Gamma_{IC} - K\varphi, \qquad \lambda\varphi = \omega_{IC} - \omega_M - c\,\varphi , \]

with \(I_M\), \(I_{IC}\) = MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC, \(K\) = gTorque Gaspard² and \(c\) = Gaspard/OmgtauIC in the units of the run. \(\Gamma_M\) and \(\Gamma_{IC}\) are the torques of the fluid on the mantle and on the inner core (below): the viscous ones times vtrq, the magnetic ones times mtrq. These are the last three rows of \(A\) and \(B\), after all the fields (utils.offset['rot']).

The walls. The fluid follows the solids through the no-slip walls. A rigid rotation \(\omega\) about the axis is the toroidal flow of degree 1 with \(T = \omega r\) (\(u_\phi = T\sin\theta\), kore's \(Y_1^0\) being \(\cos\theta\)), so the no-slip rows of that degree become

\[ T(1) = \omega_M, \qquad T(r_i) = r_i\,\omega_{IC} , \]

and every other wall condition is unchanged. At a stress-free outer wall (bco = 0) the row of \(T_1\) stays the stress-free one, and a drag acts there on the slip relative to the mantle, \(T_1(1) - \omega_M\) (Drag at the outer wall equations); without a drag only the field couples the fluid to the mantle. A rigid rotation carries an axisymmetric field without changing it, so the rotating solids leave the conditions on the field, and the field of a conducting inner core or mantle, as they are for solids at rest, but for a fluid slipping along a conducting outer wall, whose electric field enters the wall through the slip relative to the mantle (assemble.bc_b_slip).

docs.title: Torques
docs.text:
The torques are the moments of the stresses on each wall. With \(T\) the toroidal flow of degree 1, the axial angular momentum of the fluid is

\[ L = \int ho_0\,s\,u_\phi\,dV = rac{8\pi}{3}\int_{r_i}^{1} ho_0\,r^3\,T\,dr . \]

Viscous. The shear stress on a sphere is \(\sigma_{r\phi} = c_ u\,(T' - T/r)\sin heta\) with \(c_ u = ho_0\, u\,\)ViscosD, so that

\[ \Gamma^ u_M = - rac{8\pi}{3}\,c_ u\,r^2\left(rT' - T ight)\Big|_{r=1}, \qquad \Gamma^ u_{IC} = rac{8\pi}{3}\,c_ u\,r^2\left(rT' - T ight)\Big|_{r=r_i} . \]

Magnetic. The magnetic stress on the fluid's side of each wall, with \(B_{0\phi} = 0\) there:

\[ \Gamma^B_M = -\mathrm{Hendrik}\oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS\,\Big|_{r=1}, \qquad \Gamma^B_{IC} = \mathrm{Hendrik}\oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS\,\Big|_{r=r_i} . \]

It acts on everything beyond the wall: a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core (at an insulating wall \(b_\phi = 0\)). With \(b_\phi = -\sum_l g_l\,\partial_ heta Y_l\) and \(B_{0r} = \sum_n n(n+1)\,h_n Y_n/r\) (the degrees \(n\) of the poloidal background, cnorm included),

\[ \oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS = \sum_l C_l\,g_l, \qquad C_l = 2\pi r^2\sum_n n(n+1)\,h_n\, rac{2l(l+1)}{(2l+1)(2n+1)}\left(\delta_{n,l-1} - \delta_{n,l+1} ight), \]

which is \( frac{16\pi}{5}\,r^2 h_1 g_2\) for a dipole (conductive_IC's gamma_magnetic).

Gravitational. \(K\varphi\) on the mantle and \(-K\varphi\) on the inner core, which also relaxes towards alignment at the rate \(c\).

docs.title: The angular momentum balance: resid𝐋
docs.text:
The fluid's angular momentum changes only through the torques on it. spin_doctor computes them from the fields, apart from the matrices, and checks

\[ \lambda L = -\Gamma_M - \Gamma_{IC} , \]

with the viscous torques from \(T\) at the walls and the magnetic ones from the stress \(\mathrm{Hendrik}\,(B_{0r}\,\mathbf b + b_r\,\mathbf B_0)\) on a grid in \(\theta\) at each wall, for any poloidal and toroidal background (rotdyn.viscous_torques, wall_torques), whatever vtrq and mtrq. Both are taken on the fluid's side of the walls: where \(\mathbf B_0\) ends at a wall in a current sheet (Current sheets at slipping walls), the magnetic one holds the torque on the sheet's currents, which the viscous one balances at a slipping wall. The other forces exert no net axial torque: the pressure is normal to the walls, the buoyancy radial, and for \(m = 0\) neither the Coriolis force nor the advection by a differential rotation \(\Delta\Omega\) has one, since \(\int\rho_0\,\mathbf u\cdot\nabla(s^2\Delta\Omega)\,dV = 0\) between impenetrable walls.

Equatorial. For \(m = 1\), symm = -1 the same balance holds for the equatorial angular momentum, with

\[ L = \frac{16\pi}{3}\int_{r_i}^{1}\rho_0\,r^3\,T\,dr = \frac{L_x - iL_y}{N} , \]

\(N = -1/\sqrt2\) the normalisation of kore's \(Y_1^1 = N\sin\theta\,e^{i\phi}\), the torques in the same combination (the viscous ones with \(16\pi/3\) for \(8\pi/3\)), and the Coriolis torque \(-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf L\), which is \(i\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\,L\):

\[ \lambda L = -\Gamma_M - \Gamma_{IC} + i\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\,L . \]

A differential rotation would add a torque here, so this case needs diff_rot = 0.

resid𝐋 is the residual of the balance relative to the largest of \(\lvert\lambda\rvert L_{\rm abs}\), the torques, and Gaspard \(L_{\rm abs}\) for \(m = 1\), with \(L_{\rm abs}\) the same integral of \(\lvert T\rvert\): a mode on which no torque acts (stress-free walls) is then checked to carry no angular momentum.

docs.title: Energy
docs.text:
With a field, resid𝐄 (Magnetic field equations) counts the solids too. In the units of spin_doctor's kinetic energy a rigid rotation \(\omega\) of a body of moment of inertia \(I\) has the energy \(I\lvert\omega\rvert^2\), and the equations above give

\[ 2\sigma\left(I_M\lvert\omega_M\rvert^2 + I_{IC}\lvert\omega_{IC}\rvert^2 + K\lvert\varphi\rvert^2\right) = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\left(\omega_M^*\,\Gamma_M + \omega_{IC}^*\,\Gamma_{IC}\right) - 2Kc\,\lvert\varphi\rvert^2 . \]

The power of the viscous torques is minus the work of the moving walls on the fluid, which the viscous power of the fluid includes; at a stress-free outer wall with a drag the two differ by the power the drag dissipates (Drag at the outer wall equations). The power of the magnetic torques moves energy between the solids and the field: it is minus the flux of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B_0\) through the moving walls (\(\mathbf v\) their velocity), which resid𝐄 leaves out of the induction work with the rest of the flux of \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B_0\) through the walls (utils4pp.INDU_WALLS). So resid𝐄 adds the energy of the solids to the left-hand side, and the power of the viscous torques and the loss \(-2Kc\lvert\varphi\rvert^2\) to the right. It does so when both torques act on the solids (vtrq and mtrq 1).

docs.title: Checks (2026-11-06)
docs.text:
tests/rotdyn/rotdyn_check.py (run_all.sh, about 1 min on 2 ranks):

  • Decoupled solids. With vtrq = 0 and no field the solids feel only each other: two modes are the roots of \(\lambda^2 + c\lambda + K(1/I_M + 1/I_{IC}) = 0\) (\(3\times10^{-15}\)), the others those of fixed walls (\(10^{-14}\)).
  • Heavy solids. Moments of inertia of \(10^{12}\) give the eigenvalues of fixed walls (\(10^{-12}\)).
  • Against conductive_IC (2d84351), five runs: without a field (two sets of solids, one of them Earth-like), thin conducting layers with a dipole, a conducting inner core and a resolved mantle with a field of degree 2, an axial field with an exponential resolved mantle and a thin layer on the inner core. Eigenvalues to \(10^{-14}\), and the rotation of the solids and the torques on the mantle in rotdyn.dat to \(10^{-10}\), its precision.
  • Conservation with 'Wu 2005' (r_out 0.9, N 64): every mode but \(\lambda = 0\) carries no total angular momentum (\(10^{-9}\)) and closes resid𝐋 (\(10^{-9}\)); without a field the energy budget of the fluid and the solids closes (\(10^{-10}\)), with a dipole, a conducting inner core and a resolved mantle resid𝐄 does (\(10^{-10}\)).
  • Equatorial resid𝐋 without the solids: \(10^{-15}\) without a field, \(10^{-14}\) to \(10^{-11}\) with a field (a conducting inner core and a resolved mantle, thin layers, a toroidal field that does not vanish at the walls), and \(10^{-9}\) in a full sphere.
  • Stops of background.check_rotdyn.

Also checked once: the equatorial balance with the opposite sign of the Coriolis torque fails by O(1); the axial resid𝐋 is \(10^{-14}\) with a differential rotation ('conical', 'Wu 2005'); the solids work with buoyancy (thermal = 1, resid𝐋 \(10^{-13}\), total angular momentum \(10^{-10}\)).

docs.title: Rotating solids
docs.text:
An axisymmetric mode of the fluid pulls on the mantle and on the inner core, and their rotation changes in return. rotdyn = 1 lets both solids turn as rigid bodies about the rotation axis, coupled to the fluid by the viscous and magnetic torques at the walls and to each other by gravity, as in the conductive_IC branch.

setting default meaning rotdyn 0 1: the mantle and the inner core turn under the torques MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC 11.16, 9.2e-3 axial moments of inertia of the mantle and of the inner core, in units of the run's density unit times the outer radius of the fluid to the fifth power gTorque 5e-8 gravitational coupling: the torque between the inner core and the mantle per radian of misalignment, divided by that unit and by the rotation rate squared OmgtauIC 2.3e3 the time over which the inner core relaxes viscously back into alignment, times the rotation rate; np.inf for no relaxation vtrq, mtrq 1, 1 0 switches off the viscous or the magnetic torque on the solids; the fluid still follows the walls

The defaults are those of the conductive_IC branch for the Earth (2.3e3 is a relaxation time of one year). A run needs an axisymmetric, equatorially symmetric eigenvalue problem with a no-slip inner wall; the outer wall is no-slip, as here, or stress-free, with or without a drag (Drag at the outer wall):

par.m = 0
par.symm = 1
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1
par.rotdyn = 1

docs.title: How the solids are coupled
docs.text:
Three unknowns join the fields: the rotation rates of the mantle and of the inner core relative to the frame, and the angle of the inner core relative to the mantle.

  • The walls move with the solids. The fluid at each no-slip wall turns with the solid beyond it. At a stress-free outer wall the fluid slips along the mantle; a drag pulls it towards the mantle's rotation.
  • Viscous torque. The stress of the fluid on each wall: at a stress-free outer wall, that of the drag, or none.
  • Magnetic torque. The magnetic stress through each wall, which acts on whatever conducts beyond it: a thin conducting wall, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core. An insulating solid feels none.
  • Gravitational torque. It pulls the inner core and the mantle back into alignment, in proportion to the angle between them, while the inner core relaxes viscously towards alignment over OmgtauIC.

No torque comes from outside, so the fluid and the solids together conserve their angular momentum: every mode with a nonzero eigenvalue carries none in total. The eigenvalue 0 is the rigid rotation of everything, whose residuals mean nothing.

The equations: Rotating solids equations.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• real_rotdyn.field, imag_rotdyn.field: the two rotation rates and the angle, one column per solution, in the normalisation of the eigenvector (the kinetic energy of the fluid, plus Hendrik times its magnetic energy, is 1).
  • rotdyn.dat: one row per solution with the same three, the gravitational torque, and the viscous and magnetic torques on the mantle and on the inner core (Output files).
  • With a field, resid𝐄 also counts the rotational energy of the solids, their gravitational energy and the power of the torques on them (Magnetic field), when both torques act (vtrq and mtrq 1).

docs.title: The angular momentum check: resid𝐋
docs.text: The angular momentum of the fluid changes only through the torques on it, which spin_doctor computes from the fields, apart from the matrices. It prints resid𝐋, the relative residual of that balance, for eigenvalue problems with the flow and either m = 0, symm = 1 (the axial angular momentum) or m = 1, symm = -1 (the equatorial one, which the Coriolis force turns; the spin-over mode is one of these), with or without the rotating solids. It is not computed with centrifugal = 1, nor for m = 1 with a differential rotation. Like residσ, it should be small for a resolved mode. flow.dat has the angular momentum, the torques and resid𝐋 (Output files).

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
Supported: any structure; with or without buoyancy; with or without a field, with any poloidal B0 and a toroidal B0_tor that vanishes at both walls; insulating walls, a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core.

Not supported (the run stops at startup):

  • m other than 0, symm other than 1, a full sphere (ricb = 0), forced runs, or no flow (hydro = 0);
  • ViscosD = 0, an inner wall that is not no-slip (bci other than 1), or an outer wall that is neither no-slip nor stress-free (bco = 2);
  • Gaspard = 0;
  • a differential rotation (diff_rot = 1) or centrifugal = 1;
  • a toroidal B0_tor that does not vanish at a wall;
  • MoIZ_M or MoIZ_IC not positive and finite, gTorque negative or infinite, OmgtauIC not positive, vtrq or mtrq other than 0 or 1, rotdyn other than 0 or 1.

docs.title: Solver: bad solutions and memory
docs.text:
solve.py finds the eigenvalues λ of \(A x = \lambda B x\) nearest a target τ = rtau + i itau (shift-and-invert): each iteration solves a system with \(A - \tau B\), which MUMPS factors once (a sparse LU). That factorization takes almost all the memory and causes most of the numerical trouble. This page lists what to try when a solution looks wrong or a run runs out of memory.

Solver options go in par.petsc_opts in parameters.py, for example

par.petsc_opts['st_mat_mumps_cntl_1'] = 0.1

Eigenvalue runs read the eps_ and st_ keys, forced runs (forcing > 0) the ksp_, pc_ and mat_ keys, so the same MUMPS option is st_mat_mumps_... in one and mat_mumps_... in the other. An option given on the command line (mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve.py -st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 100) wins over parameters.py. The defaults, with notes, are in bin/params_default.py.

docs.title: First, check the solution
docs.text:
Judge each solution with spin_doctor.py, not with the residual that solve.py prints: with the Ruiz prescaling (on by default) that one is for the rescaled problem. Accept a mode when its energy and entropy residuals (residσ, resid𝑠) are below 1e-5 and its ℓ-convergence is below 1e-4. In a full sphere, also check irreg₀: above 1e-6 the mode is not smooth at the centre (Regularity at the centre). The same residuals judge a forced run, where σ = 0. When the walls move radially (forcing 14), residσ also tests the pressure at the walls, which needs more radial resolution than the rest of the budget (Tidal forcing).

A failure is one of two kinds:

  • Resolution. It fails every time, and the eigenvalue moves when N or lmax is raised. Raise N for the residuals and lmax for the ℓ-convergence. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) N counts both parities, so it needs about twice the N of a shell. N must be even.
  • Solver. It comes and goes between identical runs, or between runs with nearly the same parameters. See below.

docs.title: Bad solutions
docs.text:
symptom what to try the mode you want is not among the solutions put the target on it (units.set_target(par, omega=..., sigma=...), in nHz) and raise nev; to look for growing modes, put the target at σ > 0 in a full sphere without viscosity or with ThermaD = 0, modes that move when N or lmax is raised, some of them growing, many with irreg₀ near 1 spurious modes (Regularity at the centre): target the mode you want and keep the modes that stay put in N and lmax the run stops with INFOG(1)=-9 or -20 MUMPS's workspace is too small (with -20, its reception buffer): st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 = 50, then 100–200, or more (extra workspace, in %; the free core nutation of tests/centrifugal/fcn.sh, with a field and a conducting inner core, runs with 1000). On several ranks MUMPS does not repeat a run exactly, so a run near the limit can fail once and pass the next time a forced run returns NaN the same failure, but PETSc does not stop a forced solve: it returns Inf. Set mat_mumps_icntl_14 = 100; mat_mumps_icntl_4 = 1 prints MUMPS's error codes the run stops with INFOG(1)=-13, or is killed out of memory: see below some modes of a cluster of nearly equal ones, such as the r-mode ladders of a radiative interior, fail spin_doctor or move by 0.05–0.5 nHz between identical runs MUMPS on several ranks is not bitwise reproducible, and nearly parallel eigenvectors amplify its round-off. st_mat_mumps_cntl_1 = 0.1 (the pivot threshold, default 0.01) makes such failures about half as frequent, at the same cost. Repeat the run and compare each mode with the repeat or with runs at nearby parameters: spin_doctor misses some of these failures two modes at an avoided crossing split differently from run to run (by up to 0.03 nHz) their eigenvectors are nearly parallel, but the sum of the pair is stable (to 0.002 nHz): quote the sum, or a trend over several runs

A larger maxit, eps_balance twoside or a higher N or lmax do not help with such clusters. Repeated runs on one rank are bitwise identical, so a small case can be debugged on one rank.

Leave MUMPS's own scaling on (st_mat_mumps_icntl_8 = 0 fails), and do not lower the pivot threshold (cntl_1 = 1e-8 cost accuracy in thermal runs). par.prescale = None (the default) turns the Ruiz prescaling on, except in thermal runs with ThermaD = 0, where it hurts; 0 or 1 force it.

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
As a reference, the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun: m 8, N 640, lmax 79, rotation to degree 4 with thermal_wind 2, drop_tol 1e-14) peaks at 21 GB on 4 ranks.

For the smooth Sun the memory grows roughly as \(N^2 (l_{\max} - m + 1)^{1.35}\) (within about 15 %, more above N ≈ 1800). Wider angular couplings add to it: rotation to degree 12 needed 2.2 times the memory of degree 4 at the same N, and thermal_wind 2 about 1.7 times thermal_wind 1 (below, how this grows with the degree).

What to try, cheapest first:

  1. Resolution. Use the smallest N and lmax that pass the checks above. The eigenvalue usually converges at a lower N than the residuals need.
  2. drop_tol = 1e-14 removes negligible matrix entries: about 30 % less memory, with the eigenvalues unchanged to about 1e-3 nHz. Part of the drop is done after the Ruiz prescaling, and only when that is on.
  3. Block low-rank factors (BLR): st_mat_mumps_icntl_35 = 2, with the tolerance st_mat_mumps_cntl_7 = 1e-14 (set by default): about 13 % less memory and up to twice as fast. Check the residuals: a tolerance of 1e-12 broke the eigenvectors at N ≥ 640, and with ThermaD = 0 BLR and Ruiz together degraded them.
  4. Out of core: st_mat_mumps_icntl_22 = 1 writes the factors to disk, for about half the memory and a slower run. Put them on a real disk with st_mat_mumps_ooc_tmpdir, not on a /tmp held in memory. A full-sphere run at N 1024 needed about 90 GB on 8 ranks this way.
  5. More ranks spread the factors: less memory per rank, a little more in total. lmax − m + 1 must be a multiple of 2 ncpus.

icntl_14 adds workspace, so set it only as high as INFOG(1)=-9 requires.

docs.title: The cost of a differential rotation
docs.text:
A rotation profile with Legendre terms up to degree n couples each degree l of the solution to the degrees l − n to l + n (to l ± (n + 1) between its poloidal and toroidal parts). With the heat equation the thermal wind reaches further: to l ± (n + 2) with thermal_wind 1, and to l ± (2n + 2) with thermal_wind 2. The matrices get wider, and the factorization in solve.py needs more memory and time. tests/diff_rot/dr_cost.py measures this on one problem: N 96, lmax 97, m 2, structure 'Wu 2005' with stratification 'top hat', ricb 0.35, and a 'user' rotation of degree n, on 4 ranks of a laptop (Apple M4 Pro). The peak memory and the time of solve.py:

degree n momentum only with the heat equation, thermal_wind 1 thermal_wind 2 no rotation 0.9 GB, 1 s 1.0 GB, 2 s 1.0 GB, 2 s 0 0.9 GB, 1 s 1.4 GB, 2 s 1.4 GB, 2 s 2 1.3 GB, 2 s 2.3 GB, 4 s 2.8 GB, 6 s 4 1.8 GB, 3 s 3.1 GB, 7 s 4.3 GB, 12 s 8 2.5 GB, 5 s 5.0 GB, 17 s 6.9 GB, 29 s 12 3.5 GB, 9 s 7.1 GB, 31 s 8.5 GB, 35 s 16 4.6 GB, 13 s 8.4 GB, 49 s 11.9 GB, 67 s 24 6.1 GB, 43 s 10.4 GB, 63 s 32 8.1 GB, 29 s 15.3 GB, 95 s

How to read it:

  • The memory grows about linearly with n, here by 0.2 GB per degree with the momentum equation alone and 0.4 GB per degree with the heat equation. At n 32 the solve needs 9 times the memory of the run without rotation, and 15 times with the heat equation.
  • thermal_wind 2 costs a little less than thermal_wind 1 at twice the degree: its heat rows reach about twice as far.
  • submatrices.py (2 s) and assemble.py (7 s at most) stay small: the factorization is what grows.
  • The time is noisier than the memory, since it also depends on how many iterations the eigensolver needs: in the momentum case n 24 took longer than n 32.

The memory also grows with N and lmax (above). To plan a large run, run the script at its resolution:

python3 tests/diff_rot/dr_cost.py WORKDIR N LMAX NCPUS [LIMIT_GB]

It kills any step that goes above LIMIT_GB (default 30) and then skips the larger degrees of that case.

docs.title: Thermal forcing
docs.text: Forcing 13 heats the inner wall unevenly in latitude, as the Sun heats the ground of a planet more at the equator than at the poles. kore returns the flow that this heating drives: an overturning circulation in the meridional plane, like the Hadley cells of the Earth's atmosphere, and the zonal winds that the Coriolis force makes of it.

docs.title: What it imposes
docs.text:
The entropy at the inner wall \(r = r_i\) is

\[ s(r_i, \theta) = A\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta), \qquad P_2(\cos\theta) = \tfrac12 (3\cos^2\theta - 1), \]

with \(A\) = forcing_amplitude_icb. With bci_thermal = 1 the condition is on the gradient instead, \(\partial_r s(r_i, \theta) = A\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\), a prescribed heat flux. \(P_2\) is \(-\tfrac12\) at the equator and \(1\) at the poles, so a negative \(A\) makes the equator warmer. The pattern is axisymmetric and equatorially symmetric, so the run needs m = 0 and symm = 1, and also ricb > 0, thermal = 1 and ThermaD > 0. The problem is linear: the flow is proportional to \(A\). With magnetic = 1 the perturbation of the field is solved with the flow (Magnetic field).

With forcing_frequency = 0 the solution is the steady flow. At least one wall must then be no-slip (bci = 1 or bco = 1): with two stress-free walls a rigid rotation of the fluid also solves the equations, and the solution is not unique. A non-zero forcing_frequency \(w\) gives the response to a heating that oscillates as \(e^{iwt}\).

docs.title: Example: a Hadley cell
docs.text:
Write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-3
par.Etherm = 1e-3
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek, ThermaD = Etherm

# Boussinesq fluid in a thin rotating shell, conductive and stably stratified: N² = Beyonce/r
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.stratification = 'inverse square'
par.thermal = 1
par.Beyonce = 10.0
par.ricb = 0.9
par.bci = 1                       # no-slip ground
par.bco = 0                       # stress-free top
par.bci_thermal = 0               # the entropy of the ground is imposed
par.bco_thermal = 0

# axisymmetric and equatorially symmetric
par.m = 0
par.symm = 1

par.N = 48
par.lmax = 47
par.ncpus = 2

# steady heating of the ground, the equator warmer than the poles
par.forcing = 13
par.forcing_frequency = 0.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = -1.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py

It takes a few seconds. The solution is in real_flow.field, imag_flow.field, real_thermal.field and imag_thermal.field (Output files).

The figure shows the northern hemisphere. The fluid rises over the warm equator, moves poleward aloft, sinks at high latitudes and returns to the equator along the ground: one cell per hemisphere. The Coriolis force turns the poleward flow aloft into a prograde (westerly) jet, and the return flow near the ground into retrograde (easterly) winds at low latitudes. Poleward of about 25° the winds near the ground are prograde, because a steady flow exerts no net torque on the ground.

A linear, axisymmetric flow has no eddies. As a result, the cell reaches from the equator to the pole, and there are no Ferrel cells. At lower Ekman numbers the circulation retreats into the Ekman layer at the ground and towards the equator. A stress-free top wall then also has a weak reversed cell above it.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
For m = 0 each field is its coefficient times \(P_l(\cos\theta)\), plus the complex conjugate. With the poloidal and toroidal scalars \(P_l(r)\), \(T_l(r)\) and the entropy \(s_l(r)\) (Chebyshev series in \(r\) over \([r_i, 1]\), one block of N coefficients per \(l\); \(l\) even for \(P\) and \(s\), odd for \(T\)), and with \(\rho_0 = 1\) as in the example,

\[ \psi = -2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l r\thinspace P_l(r) \sin\theta\thinspace \partial_\theta P_l(\cos\theta), \qquad u_\phi = -2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l T_l(r)\thinspace \partial_\theta P_l(\cos\theta), \qquad s = 2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l s_l(r)\thinspace P_l(\cos\theta), \]

where the meridional streamfunction \(\psi\) gives \(u_r = \partial_\theta\psi/(r^2\sin\theta)\) and \(u_\theta = -\partial_r\psi/(r\sin\theta)\). In the northern hemisphere \(\psi < 0\) is a cell that rises at the equator.

docs.title: Tidal forcing
docs.text: Forcing 14 moves the walls radially in the pattern of a degree-2 tide, as the tidal bulge raised by a companion moves the surface of a star or a planet. kore returns the flow this drives in the fluid: the tidally forced inertial and gravito-inertial waves, with their dissipation and the power that the tide puts in. A scan of forcing_frequency gives the frequency spectrum of the response.

docs.title: What it imposes
docs.text:
At each wall \(r_w\) the radial velocity is

\[ u_r(r_w, \theta, \phi, t) = A_w\thinspace Y_2^m(\theta)\thinspace e^{i(m\phi + wt)} + \text{c.c.}, \]

with \(A_w\) = forcing_amplitude_cmb at the outer wall and forcing_amplitude_icb at the inner wall, \(w\) = forcing_frequency, and \(Y_2^m\) kore's Schmidt harmonics. The physical radial velocity at the wall is therefore

tide m, symm \(u_r\) at the wall eccentricity, \((l, m) = (2, 0)\) 0, 1 \(2A\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\cos wt\), with \(P_2(\cos\theta) = \tfrac12(3\cos^2\theta - 1)\) obliquity, \((2, 1)\) 1, −1 \(-2\sqrt3\thinspace A\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos(\phi + wt)\) eccentricity and asynchronism, \((2, 2)\) 2, 1 \(\sqrt3\thinspace A\sin^2\theta\cos(2\phi + wt)\)

The tangential velocity at the walls is zero: forcing 14 keeps the no-slip conditions and replaces only \(u_r = 0\) by the imposed value. The pattern turns at the angular velocity \(-w/m\) in the frame, so a negative \(w\) is prograde, as everywhere in kore. For a body spinning at the frame rate \(\Omega\) and a companion on a circular orbit of angular velocity \(n\), the \((2, 2)\) tide has \(w = 2(\Omega - n)\tau\) in kore's units (Anelastic equations). If the wall follows a tidal displacement \(\xi\thinspace Y_2^m e^{i(m\phi + wt)}\) + c.c., its velocity is \(iw\xi\): set the amplitude to \(w\xi\) (the factor \(i\) shifts the phase and changes no power). The problem is linear: the flow is proportional to the amplitudes, and every power to their square.

Requirements: bco = 1 and bci = 1 (also in a full sphere, where bci is otherwise ignored), and one of the three pairs (m, symm) above. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) only the outer wall moves. assemble.py stops with a message when a requirement is not met. The forcing works with any structure, with thermal = 1, with a differential rotation and with a field (Magnetic field).

docs.title: Example: the (2, 2) tide in a rotating shell
docs.text:
Write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-3
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek

# incompressible fluid in a rotating shell, no-slip walls
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.thermal = 0
par.ricb = 0.35
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1

# the (2, 2) tide: m = 2, equatorially symmetric
par.m = 2
par.symm = 1

par.N = 96
par.lmax = 49
par.ncpus = 2

# radial velocity Y_2^2 at the outer wall, at the frequency w = 1 (retrograde in the frame)
par.forcing = 14
par.forcing_frequency = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_cmb = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = 0.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py
./bin/spin_doctor.py 2

It takes a few seconds. spin_doctor prints residσ \(1\times10^{-14}\), the power the walls put in (P_in) and the viscous dissipation (Dν), and its flow.dat holds the whole energy budget (Output files):

import numpy as np
f = np.loadtxt('flow.dat', ndmin=2)[-1]
P_in  = f[20] + f[21] + f[23] + f[24]   # work of the pressure and of the viscous stress at both walls
D_nu  = f[25]                           # viscous dissipation
print(P_in, D_nu)                       # 0.1416912 0.1416912

The outer wall puts in \(W_p = 0.1618\) through the pressure and \(W_\nu^{\rm wall} = -0.0201\) through the viscous stress, and the viscosity dissipates the sum, \(D_\nu = 0.1417\): with a uniform rotation and no buoyancy nothing else can take it. The viscous wall work does not depend on the flow inside. On a no-slip wall the tangential velocity is zero, so \(\nabla\cdot(\rho_0\mathbf u) = 0\) fixes \(\partial_r u_r\) there, and \(W_\nu^{\rm wall} = -\tfrac{32\pi}{5}\thinspace\mathrm{ViscosD}\thinspace\lvert A\rvert^2\) at the outer wall of an incompressible fluid. All the dynamics of the response is in \(W_p\).

A spectrum is a loop over forcing_frequency: submatrices.py does not depend on it, but assemble.py and solve.py must be run again for each frequency.

docs.title: The energy of the response
docs.text:
spin_doctor evaluates the kinetic energy budget of Energy balance. For a forced, periodic response (\(\sigma = 0\)) it reads

\[ P_{ m in} = W_p + W_ u^{ m wall} = D_ u - W_b - W_\Omega , \]

with, in flow.dat and thermal.dat:

quantity columns meaning \(P_{ m in}\) flow.dat 21 + 22 + 24 + 25 the power the moving walls put into the fluid: the tidal power \(W_p\) flow.dat 21 (inner wall), 22 (outer wall) its part done by the pressure \(W_ u^{ m wall}\) flow.dat 24, 25 its part done by the viscous stress \(D_ u\) flow.dat 26 the viscous dissipation, the heat released \(-W_b\) thermal.dat 5 (with the opposite sign) the power handed to the entropy perturbation, released by thermal diffusion \(W_\Omega\) flow.dat 18 the power taken from the differential rotation

Which one to report depends on the question:

  • Orbital and spin evolution depend on the energy the tide gives to the fluid, \(P_{ m in}\). With a uniform rotation and no buoyancy it equals \(D_ u\), which is why the viscous dissipation is often called the tidal dissipation. It is not in general.
  • Tidal heating is \(D_ u\), plus the thermal diffusion of the entropy perturbation with thermal = 1.
  • The exchange with the differential rotation, \(W_\Omega\), has either sign. Where the shear feeds the waves (\(W_\Omega > 0\)) the fluid dissipates more than the tide puts in, and \(P_{ m in}\) can even be negative. Where the waves give energy and angular momentum to the mean flow, mostly at critical layers, it dissipates less. kore keeps the background fixed: whatever maintains it (convection, a body force) is assumed to absorb or supply \(W_\Omega\). Report \(W_\Omega\) with the others.

The amplitudes are those of the complex coefficients: every power above is the mean, over a period, of the power of the physical flow.

docs.title: Interpreting the response
docs.text:
• Unstable modes. The forced solve only needs \(A - iwB\) to be invertible, so it gives a response even when the background has growing modes elsewhere. The result is the part of the flow at the forcing frequency, in phase with the tide; in a linear problem the growing modes add to it at their own frequencies. It is meaningful when the instabilities are saturated, for example by the convection that the background represents, and their effect on the tide is in the viscosity. It is not meaningful near a growing mode: check with an eigenvalue solve (forcing = 0, itau = forcing_frequency) that no eigenvalue with \(\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda \geq 0\) is close to \(i w\). A spectrum computed this way is not causal: do not transform it back into a response in time.
  • Critical layers. With a differential rotation, where \(w + m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) vanishes the waves meet a critical layer, which only the viscosity resolves. Check that the response converges with N and lmax there.
  • No-slip walls. Forcing 14 imposes zero tangential velocity on the moving walls. Each wall then has an Ekman layer, whose dissipation scales as \(\mathrm{Ek}^{1/2}\), more than a smooth flow inside (\(\propto\mathrm{Ek}\)). On the solid surface of a core this is physical. At the free surface of a star or a giant planet, or at the boundary of a convective envelope over a radiative zone, it is not: there the tangential flow of the tide does not vanish. Compare runs at several Ekman numbers to tell the wall layers from the waves inside.
  • Resolution of the wall pressure. \(W_p\) needs the pressure at the walls, which converges with N more slowly than the volume terms when the density varies (Numerical method). For 'Wu 2005' (r_out 0.99) at Ek \(10^{-3}\), N 96 gives a 5 % error on \(W_p\) in a shell, and N 192 in a full sphere a 40 % error, while the kinetic energy has converged. residσ shows it: accept a response when it is below \(10^{-5}\).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameter meaning forcing 14 forcing_frequency \(w\), in units of \(1/\tau\) in the rotating frame; negative is prograde forcing_amplitude_cmb \(A\) at the outer wall: the amplitude of the radial velocity forcing_amplitude_icb \(A\) at the inner wall (not used in a full sphere) m, symm (0, 1), (1, −1) or (2, 1) bci, bco 1

The fields are written as for any forced run (Output files), and tests/tidal checks the forcing against an exact solution of the forced flow.
